  **No novel algorithm in any cell.** Every correct program outside the catalogue from every arm of this experiment went through an audit: 38 correct programs (23 from the long-form cells, 10 from the walk, 5 from the lists) plus 15 seeded failing ones. Two blind judges (gemini-2.5-flash-lite and gpt-4.1-mini; each passed a 6-program control gate at 5 of 6 after a prompt fix) compared each program with its three nearest known solutions from the declared dataset's 472 human and textbook programs and its three nearest catalogue references, and the executor read each one and ran it on three extra random inputs. The 38 correct programs were 30 labeller misses (mostly counting sort on kth smallest written with a dictionary or Counter), 7 catalogue variants (counting plus binary search on cumulative counts; a last-in-first-out label correcting search on the shortest path task) and 1 degenerate quadratic brute force. Judge A called 10 programs novel and judge B none (kappa 0.27); the manual pass found 5 of those 10 degenerate (XOR or sum tricks, broken loops), 3 labeller misses and 2 catalogue variants. The exact one-sided 95% upper bound on the novel rate is 0.058 per cell of 50, 0.113 per cell of 25 and 0.26 per thinking-on cell of 10. Together with the record audit (0 of 78), the run's direct answer to the novelty question is that no instruction or knob produced a correct algorithm outside the catalogue and its known variants.

  **Deviations and checks.** Distinctive n-grams had to be lexical (a veto of an indentation-tailed n-gram was bypassed by re-indenting in 20 of 20 unit tests), and shams could not be constructed for kth smallest and find duplicate. The analysis code was edited after its hash was committed (corrected compositions, a post hoc sensitivity, a claim mechanism check); an unchanged rederivation script reproduced every preregistered number from raw rows with no mismatch. Dropped: placement of the walk landings on the manifold, the thinking-on temperature sweep, and extending the path task thinking cells to N = 25. Judge spend was USD 0.49.

  ## 3.9 Comparisons across this iteration's experiments

  **The same modal bench ban, drawn three times in Qwen3-8B and once in Llama.** Three Qwen3-8B artifacts sampled the modal bench bans with the five frozen templates and 20 samples each, on different engines: vLLM in bf16 (bench forecast experiment), HF in bf16 with common random numbers (bench route experiment, full ban arm) and HF with 8-bit linears (locus experiment, four bench tasks). Table 119 sets them side by side with Llama. With the wording fixed, avoidance replicates within a few points and the landing replicates in kind. The same five tasks pass the gate in both artifacts that ran all twelve. Every Qwen3-8B draw sends kth smallest to quickselect and size-k heap, two sum to brute force, find duplicate to index marking, connected components to BFS, and merge intervals to a failing merge without sorting. Llama lands elsewhere on two of the shared tasks (two sum to sort and two pointers, connected components to DFS), on both of which Llama's own association answer matches its landing.

  **One wording, everywhere.** The fourth template of Table 40, which states only that X is not allowed here, is the weakest wording in every artifact that measured it. In the bench forecast experiment it accounted for 197 of 240 banned programs, against 85 to 135 for the other templates. In the bench route experiment its pooled avoidance was 0.19, against 0.42 to 0.62, and it produced 29% of all ban failures. In the exposure template arm its mean avoidance was 0.81, against 0.93 to 0.96. In the locus experiment it kept the default in 20 of 20 bench samples and carried all 61 grid BFS programs under the ban, which is why every within-ban decoder there reduced to a template decoder. In Llama, dropping the fourth template alone flips the frozen branch from no family advancing to substitution. Wording is the largest measured source of variance in compliance, and any analysis that pools templates without modelling them pools different experiments.

  **Signature vetoes, five times.** Every artifact that vetoed a default's distinctive n-gram found the default carried by more than its surface tokens. The default survived every round on 9 of 12 bench tasks in the bench forecast experiment, and Y re-emerged after three rounds for 25 of 33 shown algorithms in the exposure experiment. Only one Llama default (the heap of top-k frequent) was removed, the one-shot veto's avoidance was at most 0.41 in the bench route experiment, and the token walk stalled on all six tasks of the reach experiment although the veto was exact. On both path tasks no veto variant moved the default at all, in Qwen3-8B or in Llama, while a single prompt ban moves them by about 85 points. The subtraction forecast was therefore undefined on most events, and the test of whether a ban-free veto reproduces a ban's landing was undetermined everywhere it was planned.

  **Three forecast contests.** Table 120 summarises the contests that decide the title claim, each under the same frozen rule. On the Qwen3-8B modal bans no family's forecast beats uniform by a decisive margin, and in neither model does a family advance once undefined forecasts are not counted as wins. On the exposure bans, where the default is still available, the ladder (that is, the default) wins: snap-back. Association is never better than the ban-free families in Qwen3-8B, and in Llama it ties them.

  ## 3.10 What iteration 3 established, what it ruled out, and what it abandoned

  Everything below is still one model per contest, at most 31 gated events per contest, and labels from labellers that passed their gates; the bench is memorised LeetCode material, and the path tasks are a screen that is never pooled.

  **Established.**

  1. *The likelihood substitution test of iteration 2 cannot decide the title claim.* Its gain and residual argmax hit the realised landing in 0 of 17 Qwen3-8B single bans, against 14 of 17 for the implied mass. No row keeps three estimable survivors, the bootstrap variance of the mean gain is 2.7 times the noise term it subtracted, and a decision on mass would need about 50 programs per algorithm at the lower bound and 129 Qwen3-8B or 43 Llama events. Whether the gains are pure subtraction, whether their specific part is aimed, and whether the generic profiles form a ladder are all undetectable with that instrument.
  2. *Shown a correct program of a non-default algorithm and told not to use it, Qwen3-8B snaps back to its default.* The default's share of attempts rises from 0.05 under the copy twin to 0.72 under the named ban and 0.82 under the unnamed one. The modal replacement is the default in 24 of 31 gated events, and the ladder forecast wins the frozen contest (7 wins; top-1 0.77). Naming the banned algorithm adds little beyond asking for something else (same modal replacement for 0.88 of Y). *(Correction, iteration 4: the frozen counting rule advances some family in 85% of no-information simulations and in 100% of label-permutation placebo draws (the ladder in 43%), and no paired test survives Holm on the named events, so the 7 wins of the ladder are weak evidence. Wording also changes the landing: under templates one to four the default is modal for 13 of 19 priority algorithms, against 15 of 19 under the fifth, and the replacement flips to the associate for the size-k heap and the Z algorithm. Snap-back rests on one wording. It replicates in the present minor bans of Llama, which return to the default in 0.72 to 0.93 of attempts not banned; Section 4.2.3.)*
  3. *Where the default is not available, the landing is specific to the task and mostly unforeseen.* On the five gated Qwen3-8B modal bench bans, no ban-free or association forecast beats uniform on average, and three of five landings (index marking, BFS, a failing merge without sorting) were named by no family. In Llama the landing is predictable above chance (ladder and association 7 of 13 each), but the families do not separate. *(Correction, iteration 4: the merge intervals landing is residue, failing programs labelled other (29 coverage arrays, 12 unsorted sweeps, 3 others), and that event passes the gate only through them (catalogue-only avoidance 0.14). In Llama, with other excluded, association hits 7 of 13 (p = 0.032) and the ladder 6 of 13 (p = 0.100), so only association is above chance.)*
  4. *A ban's route is task dependent.* On the bench, pooled over five gated tasks, generated tokens reading the ban carry 0.74 of the effect and the prompt states 0.61. The mechanism is redundant on kth smallest and connected components, direct on two sum and find duplicate, and superadditive on merge intervals, and a second draw reproduces every task. The prompt route story of the path tasks does not generalise. *(Correction, iteration 4: the claim that generated tokens carry more of the effect rested on a comparison of point estimates. With their jackknife intervals the fractions are F_direct 0.744 [0.38, 1.11] and F_prompt 0.611 [0.06, 1.17], which overlap, with interaction -0.355. The superadditive class rests on merge intervals, which is gated only through residue; without it F_prompt is 0.648 [-0.08, 1.38] and F_direct 0.865 [0.68, 1.05].)*
  5. *The ban is applied at the opening of the body and not re-read.* Forcing the default's first body token undoes the ban completely on every gated task, while forcing the `def` line undoes none of it. *(Correction, iteration 4: the locus is resolved to a single token only on kth smallest, where one token after the `def` line and its indentation undoes the ban; on the other four gated tasks the shortest forced prefix in the depth sweep that undoes it is 10 to 30 tokens long. Restated: the ban gives way at the opening of the body, to a single token on kth smallest.)*
  6. *Wording dominates compliance.* The fourth template is the weakest in every artifact (template SD about 2.0 logits; likelihood ratio 374), and dropping it flips the Llama branch.
  7. *The default is not carried by any small set of surface tokens.* Exact signature vetoes, one-shot, persistent, iterated or cumulative, almost never remove it; the model renames, respells or breaks the code. A single prompt ban moves the model further than any veto.
  8. *Prompts reach past one rung where the alternatives are interchangeable.* Bans that leave one survivor got BFS 50 of 50 on connected components and quickselect 50 of 50 on kth smallest; on kth smallest quickselect is the answer to every ban list, including lists that ban it and the list that leaves only the default. Elsewhere (Floyd-Warshall, size-k heap, heapify and pop, binary search on values) the model will not write a survivor it can write on request. *(Correction, iteration 4: the kth smallest disconfirmation depends on the rung definition. It uses the fallback rung of the token walk; three bench draws put the landing of the ban on quickselect (59 to 79%), which makes quickselect the behavioural second rung, and under that definition the cell confirms the claim (size-k heap, will 0.00). Connected components disconfirms under either definition.)*
  9. *No instruction or knob produced a correct novel algorithm.* Zero of 78 correct out-of-catalogue programs in the iteration-1 and iteration-2 data and 0 of 38 in iteration 3 are novel; the request's long-form instruction makes 84% of outputs claim novelty, 39% of those contain no code, and 75% of the rest are catalogue algorithms.
  10. *Llama's correct output is as collapsed as Qwen3-8B's on the grid task* (BFS 20 of 20 correct), and more diverse on 9 of 13 bench tasks counted over correct programs.

  **Ruled out, or not supported.**

  - *Substitution by association in Qwen3-8B.* In none of the three contests did association win; it was worse than uniform on all five gated modal bans and lost to the ladder by about 1.3 nats on exposure bans (Holm 0.081 named, 0.0056 unnamed).
  - *A shared prohibition direction as the carrier of the ban.* Adding the leave-one-task-out ban displacement to a neutral prompt passed on 0 of 5 gated tasks against matched random directions, and removing it from a ban never restored the default (pooled -0.026 [-0.07, 0.03]).
  - *A ban-free signature veto as the forecast of the next rung.* It was undefined on 10 of 12 Qwen3-8B modal events and 29 of 33 exposure events, and where defined on the path tasks or the bench it landed elsewhere than the ban.
  - *The prompt route as the general mechanism of a ban.* Disconfirmed on the bench (pooled direct share 0.74, jackknife [0.38, 1.11]).
  - *Prompts move the model exactly one rung.* Disconfirmed on connected components (BFS will 1.00 at can 1.00) and, through the fallback rung, on kth smallest.
  - *The three ban-attending heads as a causal site.* Ablating them moved the grid ban by +0.06 over random heads in the same layers, inside the range of any perturbation of the fragile fourth-template ban.
  - *A locus at generated tokens 1 to 16.* No decoder beat the template-only or written text controls on any testable task; on the shortest path task the choice diverges at a median of about 29 tokens.

  **Dead ends, with the evidence that closed them.**

  - *The forced ratio latent probability as the decision instrument for where a ban sends the mass.* Closed by Table 82 (argmax 0 of 17 against the realised landing) and Table 84 (programs and events needed far beyond the budget).
  - *Signature vetoes and the token walk as a way past the default.* Closed by the bench forecast, exposure, Llama, route and reach experiments: the default survives exact vetoes by renaming and respelling, and the walk stalled at rung 1 or 2 on all six tasks.
  - *The shared prohibition direction.* Closed by Table 110.
  - *Head ablation as a test of the attention heads.* Closed by the random-head control.
  - *Qwen-Scope base SAEs for readouts of the ban.* They now pass a fairer transfer criterion (fraction of cross-entropy recovered 0.989 to 0.994), but their reconstructions keep only a cosine of about 0.3 of the ban displacement, and their latents never beat difference-in-means.
  - *Long-form novelty instructions as a source of novel algorithms.* Closed by Table 118 and the audit (0 novel of 38 correct programs outside the catalogue).

  ## 3.11 What the next iteration takes from this one

  The title claim of the update, that a ban removes the default and the model falls to a next rung that ban-free counterfactuals can read in advance, did not survive in that form. The part that survived is snap-back: with the default available, a ban on a shown algorithm returns the model to its default, which is subtraction in its simplest form. Where the default itself is banned, the counterfactuals meant to expose the next rung either fail to move the model (signature vetoes) or move it somewhere else (random pushes, the shared prohibition direction), and the landing is specific to the task in a way no frozen family foresaw in Qwen3-8B. Substitution by association is not supported in Qwen3-8B and is tied with the ladder in Llama. What decides the replacement under a modal ban remains open, and the run now has two concrete leads for it: the opening of the body, where the prefill sweep localises the ban to the first body token, and the template, which carries more of the variance in compliance than anything else measured. *(Added in iteration 4: a third lead was already in the iteration-3 data, the landing composition per route arm. On connected components either route alone lands mostly on DFS, which is the generic landing of random pushes and the association answer of Qwen3-8B, and BFS is chosen only when both routes act; Section 4.2.2.)*

  Three things follow for the next iteration. First, the contest needs events on which the default is unavailable and the families disagree, in numbers the paired tests can use: the modal bench bans give 5 gated events in Qwen3-8B, so pooling with Llama (11) and adding bench tasks where bans take is the arithmetic, with the template entered as a random effect rather than pooled over. Second, the first body token is now a measured locus in behaviour; a decoder or patch there, in states saved at that position for each task, would ask what is decided when the ban gives way. Third, the generic perturbation rival needs a behavioural test where its runner-up and the associate differ, which the Qwen3-8B bench rarely provides; Llama's present minor events are where the named ban gained the associate about 0.25 of attempts beyond the veto on two of six events, and that is the next place to look.

  Request items still open: a same seed temperature arm with thinking on (dropped again), manifold placement of the walk landings (dropped; the walk stalled), and an SAE readout that keeps the ban displacement. *(Added in iteration 4: the same seed arm with thinking on ran in iteration 4, Section 4.5.)*

  # Iteration 4: plan noise priced against temperature, where the noise must enter, the plan subspace, and a held-out model family

  ## 4.1 Why this iteration ran what it ran

  **The review of the iteration-3 record.** The review was blocking again. It raised six major items, all marked must fix, and three minor ones. The first item went to the answer the record gave to the second question of the request, whether the algorithm a model writes can be influenced. The closing section and Section 3.2.5 said that only the semantic seed and the A* mention buy a second correct algorithm, and that both name or describe it. Table 91 itself held two activation rows that buy one without naming anything, and none of the iteration-3 arms had been entered into the knob table, although random directions written into the task-specification states had reached a Hill-1 near 3 on kth smallest at no pass cost. The second item was an executed result missing from the record: the landing composition of every route arm, which bears directly on what picks the replacement under a ban. The third concerned the Llama contest, which scored its present minor events against a label the record never defined and mislabelled three rows of Table 102; with other excluded, only association hit above chance. The fourth was that the event gate counted failing programs labelled other as avoidance, the defect the record had already corrected for the TOP ban list, and merge intervals passed the gate only through such residue. The fifth was coverage of the request: the activation-space plots with centroids coloured by implemented count existed but had no figure marker, the same seed temperature arm with thinking on had been dropped twice, and the run had located where a ban acts but not where the choice of algorithm itself is represented. The sixth asked for the iteration-3 claims to be set against their nearest published neighbours. The minor items asked for top-1 hit rates under one rule for undefined forecasts, Table 82 per distinct likelihood row, and four sentences of Section 3.10 that said more than their tables. Table 121 maps every item to its answer. The corrections are made in place in Sections 2.3.6 and 3.2 to 3.11, each marked as an iteration-4 correction.

  **The hypothesis update.** The update reframed the run around a result that had sat in the control arms of the iteration-3 locus experiment . Isotropic random directions added to the task-specification states at blocks 12 to 23, at the size of the displacement a ban itself causes, had made Qwen3-8B [5] write two or three different correct algorithms for one prompt at no loss of correctness. On kth smallest, 7 of 15 directions moved at least 20% of programs off the default, and five reached a correct-only Hill-1 of 2 or more. The update read this as evidence that the algorithm is chosen in those states before any code is written. We call that state the *plan* below, with one caveat stated now: the word names a site in the network, and whether a plan representation sits there is what this iteration tested. Temperature never touches the plan, which would explain why it changes wording and not ideas, while a nudge to the plan changes ideas. The question that ran through iterations 1 to 3, substitution against subtraction, becomes a special case: a ban is one large displacement of the plan, plus generated tokens reading the ban. Three claims followed, each with a rule committed before its first decisive sample.

  - *The price claim.* Plan noise moves the algorithm while temperature moves only the wording, and on tasks where the plan is movable it buys correct algorithmic diversity more cheaply than every token-level and prompt-level knob tested. Two sub-claims: the effect is specific to the task-specification states at blocks 12 to 23 (the site claim), and with the token seed held fixed, temperature changes the algorithm in at most 1 of 20 seeds while a change of plan noise draw changes it often (the same seed claim, which is question 1a-c of the request).
  - *The subspace claim.* The choice is represented in a low-dimensional subspace of the task-specification states, spanned by the differences between per-algorithm centroids under forced prompts, and a push changes the algorithm to the extent that it moves the state along that subspace.
  - *The movability claim.* Whether a ban on the default of a task is obeyed is predicted, without any ban sample, by whether random pushes can move that task, and the ban lands where the pushes land unless generated tokens read the ban. The claim was to be confirmed in a model family never run in this study. Two further tests rode along: a norm sweep to the point of breakage with a full audit for novel algorithms, and the top-five prohibition of the request applied as a push at the plan.

  We define the instruments once. A *ban unit* is the norm of the ban minus neutral twin displacement per layer and per task-specification position at blocks 12 to 23, averaged over the five modal ban templates; for a model never banned it is estimated without ban text from the residual norm times the median ratio, in Qwen3-8B, of ban displacement to residual norm at the same relative depth. *Plan noise* at dose alpha is a fresh isotropic random direction per sample, added during prefill at every task-specification position of blocks 12 to 23, with the displacement along it set to alpha ban units at each block, so the edits do not compound. A fixed direction *escapes* when, over its first 10 samples, the share of attempts off the default exceeds that of the twin by at least 0.20 at a pass rate of at least 0.8 times that of the twin; two experiments added a confirmation at N = 30 by an exact binomial test. The *escape fraction* of a task is the share of its fixed directions that escape, and we call a task *movable* when its escape fraction is above zero at some dose of at most 2. The *plan subspace* of a task is the span of the differences between per-algorithm centroids of the task-specification states under 30 forced paraphrases per algorithm, with a name-masked twin built from descriptions. The *push-landing forecast* names the modal catalogue survivor among off-default attempts of escaping directions, and the *opening ladder* ranks survivors by the teacher-forced log probability of their modal forced-program body opening under the neutral twin. We price a knob by its *5-point Hill-1*, the highest correct-only rarefied Hill-1 (depth 25) it reaches at a cost of at most 5 pass points, and by its *price of 1.5* and *price of 2*, the smallest pass cost at which it reaches a Hill-1 of 1.5 and of 2. The plan noise and site experiments compute them on the *randomisation hull* of each knob, the set of mixtures of the reference arm with the settings of the knob, which turns the dial of a knob into a continuous price curve.

  **The strategy.** Seven artifacts ran (Table 122). One evaluation repaired the record from rows on disk and froze the push screen by hash, so that every later analysis cites one screen. Four Qwen3-8B experiments tested the price, site, same seed and subspace claims, and one experiment ran the movability claim in a held-out family. A research artifact positioned the iteration-3 and iteration-4 claims against published work. Two departures from the plan shaped what could be claimed. The held-out family was planned as gemma-2-9b-it, but the only GPU available held 16 GB, so the experiment ran gemma-3-4b-it [76], another family never run in this study. Every Qwen3-8B GPU artifact ran on the same 16 GB card with 8-bit floating point weight and activation linear layers, the engine of the iteration-3 screen; each reproduced the rows of the screen byte for byte, so every plan noise result below is a result for that engine, with no measured gap to bf16. The planned second screen body in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct was first in the drop order and did not run.

  ## 4.2 The record audit: the iteration-3 record repaired from rows on disk

  The record audit  generated no model text. It recomputed every number from the labelled rows of eleven earlier artifacts, citing each source file, and spent USD 0.22 on the blind judges of its audit of other programs. A stdlib-only reimplementation rederived 29 headline checks with no mismatch and reproduced the frozen screen file byte for byte, a second script added 12 checks with no mismatch, and all 7 placebo tests failed as they should.

  ### 4.2.1 One knob table for every iteration-3 arm

  The audit rebuilt the knob table over every iteration-3 arm, 1,120 cells of artifact, task, arm and dial, each priced against its own twin with a Newcombe interval on the pass cost [42], the correct-only rarefied Hill-1 at depth 25 with template and independent-sample 90% intervals, the Good-Turing coverage estimate, catalogue-only avoidance and two flags. A cell *escapes* by the rule of Section 4.1, and we say it *qualifies* when it escapes and reaches a Hill-1 of at least 2 within 20 pass points. Of the 1,120 cells, 752 are knobs, 348 controls, 18 ablations on a ban and 2 ceilings; 945 come from Qwen3-8B and 175 from Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Table 123 gives the verdict per task that the review asked for, read from the table under the class rule of Section 3.2.5. The band patch is listed separately, because it writes the states of the ban itself into the twin and so carries the ban; exposure arms are priced against their own copy twin, in which the shown algorithm is the default.

  The table answers the question of the review in the direction it pointed. On connected components the two routes together choose the substitute, and neither chooses it alone. Each single route removes union find, but the prompt route alone, the direct route alone and the knockout all land mostly on DFS, which is the association answer of Qwen3-8B, the runner-up of the baseline likelihood order and the modal landing of random pushes on the task (DFS 0.83 and BFS 0.17 of the excess-weighted push landing in Section 4.6); BFS becomes the modal landing only when both routes act. On kth smallest the direct route alone almost eliminates the size-k heap (1 against 28 under the full ban), so the size-k heap share travels by the prompt states, and the random pushes of Section 4.6 land on the same two algorithms. On find duplicate the direct route reproduces the index marking of the full ban, and the five programs of the knockout land on Floyd cycle detection 3 times, the association answer. Two sum lands on brute force under every arm, and merge intervals lands mostly on residue. We carry this forward as the route-landing lead: where a single route suffices to remove the default, it lands on the generic neighbour that pushes and the stated alternative of the model agree on, and departures from that neighbour appear when both routes act. *(Correction, iteration 5: this generalises from one task. It is an observation on a single task, connected components, where either route alone lands mostly on DFS, the neighbour that pushes and association agree on, and both routes together choose BFS. Find duplicate is the counterexample in the same table: the direct route alone removes the default and lands on index marking (74 of 78), which is neither the push landing (sort and adjacent check) nor the association answer (Floyd cycle detection). On two sum pushes and association disagree, so there is no agreed neighbour to land on.)*

  ### 4.2.3 The Llama hit rule

  The Llama bench experiment  scored its 12 modal events against the modal landing and its 6 present minor events against the survivor with the largest excess over the renormalised ban-free baseline, a rule written in its scoring code and never stated in the record. Table 129 recomputes the top-1 hits of every family on the 13 gated events under each candidate rule, with Poisson-binomial p values against the per-event chance rates. The ladder nominated other on 3 of the 13 gated events, and on find duplicate both its nomination and the landing were other.

  ### 4.2.4 The audit of other programs, and catalogue-only avoidance

  The audit pooled every program labelled other that iteration 3 produced under a ban: 21 events and 226 unique programs, of which 6 passed the hidden tests (Table 131). Two blind judges from different families classified each as a labeller miss, a variant of a catalogue algorithm, a degenerate or hard-coded program, or a novel algorithm, a third judge broke ties, and the executor read 73 programs by hand: every passing program, every program a judge called novel, all 44 merge intervals programs and a seeded sample of the rest. Judge A (gpt-4.1-mini) fell below the control gate (4 of 6 positive controls in the strict class) and received no weight; judge B (gemini-2.5-flash) passed at 5 of 6 and was weighted; the two agreed at Cohen's kappa [11] 0.77 [0.67, 0.86]. The final classes were 68 catalogue variants, 156 degenerate programs, 2 labeller misses and no novel algorithm. Judges flagged 7 programs as novel and the manual pass confirmed none; the one passing program a judge called novel reran 60 of 60 hidden tests and 3 of 3 stress tests and is a textbook binary search over values after a sort.

  ### 4.2.5 Geometry in activation coordinates

  The request asks for actual geometry plots in activation space, with centroids coloured by implemented count, before and after prohibiting the top five algorithms. The ban list experiment  had drawn them in iteration 2, and the record had only tabulated their counts (Table 85). The figure below plots four of them from the saved centroid coordinates: the Isomap embedding (k = 10) of teacher-forced residual stream states at layer 24, read at the token before the commit token, with each centroid sized by the number of programs implementing it under the condition. The caveat travels with the figure: the token before the commit token is a position whose index depends on the label of the program itself, so part of the separation between centroids can reflect position rather than algorithm. Under the five-name ban, every implemented program sits on a banned centroid (BFS 63, DFS 36, IDDFS 1); under the single BFS ban the mass moves to the DFS centroid, which is far from BFS in this embedding; and on the shortest path task the ban that leaves only Bellman-Ford/SPFA splits between the allowed Bellman-Ford/SPFA centroid (51) and the banned Dijkstra centroid (48). The MDS stress-1 of the centroid geodesic matrix is 0.025 on the grid task and 0.006 on the shortest path task. BFS and bidirectional BFS coincide in this embedding (centroid distance 0.0147 in MDS units).

  ## 4.3 Plan noise priced against every other knob (Qwen3-8B)

  **Why.** The price claim was the primary claim of the iteration and the question of the request in its plainest form: which knob buys correct algorithmic diversity most cheaply. The iteration-3 evidence for random pushes came from fixed directions, three per task on most of the bench, chosen by nobody. This experiment  drew a fresh direction for every sample, which is the form a practitioner would use, and priced it on the six movable tasks of the frozen screen against every token-level and prompt-level knob the run had tried, all under one statistic and one price convention.

  **Design.** Qwen3-8B ran with 8-bit linear layers on the 16 GB card, thinking off, and every arm of a task shared the same uniform stream per template and slot, so arms differ only by the knob. Plan noise ran at alpha 0.5, 1, 2 and 4 (and 8 in the dose sweep). The comparison knobs were temperature 1.3 and 1.6 without truncation, top-k 10, the nonce ban, the novelty instruction, the semantic seed on the path tasks and the iteration-3 signature vetoes (one-shot, persistent and iterated, reused rows); min-p 0.1 at temperature 1.6 and 2.0 and a verbalized sampling prompt [46] were preregistered sensitivities. Every cell had N = 50 (5 templates by 10 slots): 202 cells and 10,100 labelled programs, with no cell dropped. The 5-point Hill-1 and the prices of 1.5 and 2 were computed on the randomisation hull of each knob with 2,000 bootstrap replicates, and the choice of the best setting of a knob was made inside every replicate. The rule, committed by hash before the first sample beyond stage 10, confirmed the price claim if plan noise reached a 5-point Hill-1 of at least 1.5 on at least 3 of the 6 tasks, beat the 5-point Hill-1 of the best non-activation knob on at least 4 of 6, and had a pooled margin with a task-bootstrap 95% interval above 0.

  **The rule returned PARTIAL.** Plan noise is not the uniformly cheapest knob (Table 137). It reaches a 5-point Hill-1 of at least 1.5 on only 2 of 6 tasks, against the 3 required, and beats the best non-activation knob on 4 of 6, but the pooled margin is -0.22 with an interval from -0.89 to 0.30 (one-sided p = 0.76; exact sign test over the six margins p = 0.34). Plan noise wins clearly on kth smallest (2.72 against 1.96 for the novelty instruction, ahead in every bootstrap replicate) and on connected components (2.09 against 1.96 for the iterated veto, ahead in 91%), and on both it reaches Hill-1 of 1.5 and of 2 at no pass cost. It edges two sum and the grid task by margins inside their intervals. It loses decisively on find duplicate, where it does not move the hash set at alpha 2 or less while the reused iterated veto reaches 2.73, and on the shortest path task, where the semantic seed reaches 1.93 against 1.35 for plan noise because pushed Bellman-Ford/SPFA programs cost 14 to 26 pass points.

  **Controls and checks.** The prohibition frame of the neutral twin is inert for the algorithm: a plain prompt with the specification alone and the twin have identical off-default shares on five of the six movable tasks (+0.02 on the shortest path task), although the frame costs 18 pass points on the grid task and adds 22 on cycle detection. *(Added in iteration 5: plan noise was also run on the plain prompt without the prohibition frame of the twin (alpha 1, 350 programs on the same common-random-number slots), and the record did not report it. Its off-default shares were 0.16 on kth smallest (0.28 under the twin frame), 0.24 on connected components (0.12), 0.26 on the shortest path task (0.26), 0.02 on the grid task (0.06) and 0 on two sum, find duplicate and cycle detection. Plan noise does not need the frame on kth smallest, connected components and the shortest path task; under plan noise at alpha 1 the frame costs 10 pass points on the grid task (interval -6 to 28). Table 173 gives the rows.)* A forecast committed before stage 100, which treated fresh noise as an equal mixture of the fixed directions of the screen, predicted the PARTIAL verdict and the alpha-1 composition within the resampling null on 5 of 6 tasks; it over-predicted find duplicate (1.76 forecast against 1.00) and two sum and under-predicted connected components. Two screen rows rerun with the keys of the screen itself agreed slot for slot (label agreement 1.00 on all four cells). The labellers recovered every reference on all 13 bench tasks. The 12 correct programs labelled other were all labeller misses, and no novel algorithm appeared. A judge agreed with the labeller on 1.00 of audited programs everywhere except kth smallest (0.80), and rescoring kth smallest with the labels of the judge left its margin at +0.71 against +0.76. Replacing every plan noise setting by the twin gave margins of 0 or below on all six tasks, and under 100 within-task shuffles of the arm labels the full committed rule never returned CONFIRMED; the count criteria alone fired in 8 of 100 shuffles in the independent rederivation, so the interval criterion is what makes the rule specific. The rederivation matched 12 of 12 checks, and the hash chain shows the commitment preceding the first row beyond stage 10.

  ## 4.4 Where the noise must enter (Qwen3-8B)

  **Why.** If the plan lives in the task-specification states, the same random displacement should change the algorithm there and nowhere else. If any perturbation of matched size does as well, the effect is generic sensitivity, and the word plan names nothing. This experiment  wrote one random displacement per common-random-number slot into six sites at matched per-position dose in ban units and priced each site on the randomisation hull.

  **Design.** The six sites were the task-specification states at blocks 12 to 23 (the plan site of the hypothesis), the read position, the condition sentence, generated tokens 1 to 32 (through teacher-forced shadow rows), the task-specification states at blocks 0 to 11, and the same states at blocks 24 to 35. Each ran at alpha 1, 2 and 4 with N = 30 per cell (twin N = 50) on the six movable tasks, with energy-matched variants of the read position and condition sites and the plan site at alpha 8 for the boundary. One fresh direction and one stream of token uniforms per slot were shared by every arm, so every site contrast is an exact paired flip. In all 4,510 programs ran; 4,460 decisive rows followed the commitment, and none preceded it. The preregistered rule called the site claim confirmed if the plan site had the highest 5-point Hill-1 on at least 4 of 6 tasks.

  **The rule returned PARTIAL, and three sites are inert.** The plan site has the best 5-point Hill-1 on 3 of 6 tasks (kth smallest, the grid task and the shortest path task; p = 0.062 against a binomial with chance 1/6), generated-token noise is best on two sum and find duplicate, and early-block noise on connected components (Table 143). Every per-task margin is a bootstrap close call except the shortest path task, where the plan site is ahead in 97% of replicates. The read position and the condition sentence never changed the algorithm at per-position doses of 1 to 4 ban units (corrected in iteration 5 from the phrase *at any dose*; the energy-matched read position below is weaker but not inert): 0 of 526 and 0 of 527 correct programs off the default at alpha 1 to 4. The late blocks are almost as inert (6 of 521). The outputs at these three sites are often byte-identical to those of the twin, 90% to 100% at alpha 1 on kth smallest, two sum and find duplicate for the read position and the late blocks.

  **The effect is not generic transmission.** Noise at the read position produces as large a displacement at the last block as the plan site does (medians 141, 250 and 474 against 159, 272 and 461 at alpha 1, 2 and 4), yet it flips nothing. A logistic regression of a correct program being off the default on the log of the realised displacement at the read position, with template and task fixed effects, over 2,769 correct programs from the prefill sites, gives the plan site an indicator of +2.15 [1.79, 2.51] beside a displacement slope of +0.88 [0.62, 1.14]. In the matched-dose bins (the upper three quintiles of displacement) the plan site is off the default in 16% to 27% of programs, against 3% to 7% for the other prefill sites. A hand-coded Mantel-Haenszel odds ratio, which pools the odds of an off-default program at the plan site against the other prefill sites across task and displacement quintile strata, gives 5.72 [3.94, 8.30], and its placebo, with plan-site labels shuffled within task, has a median of 0.98. A Bayesian mixed logistic model with random task and template effects puts the site effects relative to the plan site at -3.0 (read position), -2.9 (condition sentence), -3.0 (late blocks), -0.8 (generated tokens) and -1.1 (early blocks), with the slope of the plan site on log2 alpha at +1.11. Concentrating the whole ban energy at the read position (median displacement there 1,002, six times that of the plan site at alpha 1) moved find duplicate by +0.23 and connected components by +0.18 at pass ratios of 0.87 to 0.93; spreading it over the condition span stayed inert. Generated-token noise produces the most phrasing clusters per idea (4.2 and 4.7 at alpha 1 and 2, against 2.8 and 3.4 for the plan site, AST-shingle components at Jaccard 0.8).

  **The boundary.** At alpha 8 the task specification is effectively erased (Table 147): the model echoes the condition sentence, writes placeholder code or asks for clarification, and the pass rate is 0.00 on every task. Correct-only diversity peaks at alpha 2 (kth smallest, grid, shortest path) or alpha 4 (two sum, find duplicate, connected components), and alpha 4 already costs 33% to 97% of the passes. Across every arm 3,555 programs were correct, and exactly one was labelled other: a find duplicate program from generated-token noise at alpha 2 that calls a count of each element over the list. The judges called it degenerate and a labeller miss, and the manual read, beside its three nearest known solutions, called it the textbook quadratic brute force. No novel algorithm appeared (rule-of-three bound 3/3,555 = 0.08% per correct program [67]).

  **The top-five prohibition at the plan.** The request asks what happens when the five most implemented algorithms are prohibited. The prompt version had failed by reimplementation (avoidance 0.00) and the cumulative token veto had stalled. This experiment applied the prohibition as an activation push: the plan states of the grid task were pushed along the per-block direction from the mean of the five banned centroids to the mean of the survivor centroids, estimated from 300 forced prompts in which the centroid of every algorithm was separable from the others (nearest-centroid separability 0.83 to 1.00). The push never moved the model off BFS (Table 148). Correct programs were BFS 30 of 30 at alpha 1 and 19 of 19 at alpha 2, and none passed at alpha 4; fresh random plan noise at the same norm did no better. The test of edge against opposite side could not be computed because no survivor program appeared at any dose, and the plan geometry leaves little to resolve: bidirectional BFS and IDA* sit almost equally far from the banned set (geodesic 0.36 against 0.37; MDS stress-1 0.147; no persistent loop beyond a permutation null).

  ## 4.5 Same seed: temperature against plan noise (Qwen3-8B, question 1a-c of the request)

  **Why.** The request asks three things about temperature: with a tight temperature and top-k 10, does the model produce one idea in many phrasings or many ideas; does loosening it multiply ideas or phrasings; and does the answer hold with the same seed. The run had answered the first two in iteration 1 and the third with thinking off in iteration 2, and had dropped the thinking-on arm twice. This experiment  ran the seed-coupled design on the grid task, the shortest path task and kth smallest, with the thinking-on arm made non-droppable, and added plan noise as the second factor so that the same seed could be varied in temperature or in plan.

  **Design.** Each task had 20 token seeds, one per template and slot, and each seed kept one noise stream across every condition (inverse-CDF sampling with common random numbers). The temperature block ran each seed at 0.3, 0.7, 1.0 and 1.3 (top-p 1) and with top-k 10 at 0.7. The plan noise block ran 6 fixed isotropic directions at alpha 1 and 2 and temperature 0.7 and 1.0. The change count of a task is the number of seeds whose algorithm differs across the conditions of a block; for plan noise it is averaged over the 20 three-direction subsets of the 6 directions. Thinking on ran in vLLM with per-request seeds (an exponential race coupling, confirmed by recomputing the first token in 32 of 32 requests), a 16k cap and the completion rate reported. *(Correction, iteration 5: the top-k 10 answer to the request with thinking off is Table 76 of iteration 2: with seeds coupled, the label changed in 0 of 30 seeds in 10 of 12 cells. The thinking-on arm of this experiment ran without top-k (top-k off, Gumbel-max coupling through per-request seeds, temperatures 0.3, 0.7, 1.0 and 1.3), so the literal cell of the request, thinking on with top-k 10 and the same seed, was not run in iteration 4. It ran in iteration 5, Section 5.7.)*

  **Temperature never changed the algorithm; plan noise changed it in most seeds on the shortest path task.** With thinking off, the algorithm stayed the same across all four temperatures in 20 of 20 seeds on all three tasks, and with thinking on in 20 of 20 seeds on the shortest path task (Table 150); the exact 95% upper bound on the per-seed change rate is 0.168 for each count of 0 in 20. One random plan direction at alpha 1 changed the algorithm in 17.25 of 20 seeds on the shortest path task, 4.55 on kth smallest and 2.5 on the grid task. *(Correction, iteration 5: these are not rates per direction. Each is the mean, over the 20 three-direction subsets of the 6 directions, of the number of seeds whose label differs anywhere among the no-noise arm and the three directions of the subset, a union over three directions. The single-direction counts of changed seeds at alpha 1 and temperature 1.0 are 7, 10, 15, 17, 3 and 8 of 20 on the shortest path task, 2, 0, 0, 7, 2 and 0 on kth smallest, and 0, 0, 1, 1, 3 and 0 on the grid task.)* The paired contrast per seed, plan noise change minus temperature change, pooled over the shortest path task and kth smallest (40 seeds), has a mean of 0.545 [0.41, 0.67] and a one-sided sign-flip p of 1.0e-5. That is the single entry of the experiment in the secondary family of the iteration. A within-seed permutation of conditions puts the observed mean above all 200 placebo means (maximum 0.155; p = 0.005).

  The preregistered verdict is PARTIAL: the temperature, phrasing and coupling predictions hold, and the plan noise prediction (at least 5 of 20 seeds) fails on kth smallest, at 4.55. The plan prescribed the unit of the bench forecast experiment for kth smallest, which is 1/1.30 of the unit the screen used, so alpha 1 here is a weaker push than alpha 1 of the screen; at alpha 2 kth smallest reaches 10.6, and under a Gumbel-max coupling 5.8. Counted over correct programs or with invalid outputs as a label, the temperature count stays 0 on every task; with top-k 10 added as a fifth condition it stays 0; with min-p 0.1 at temperature 2.0 added it becomes 1 on the shortest path task and kth smallest (one Bellman-Ford/SPFA and one quickselect program out of 20) and stays 0 on the grid task.

  **Temperature changes phrasings, not ideas.** Phrasings per idea grow with temperature (Table 151): the pooled slope of log phrasings per idea on temperature is 0.64, 0.70 and 0.81 at Jaccard thresholds 0.7, 0.8 and 0.9, each 95% interval excluding 0. Almost all of the growth is on the grid task (3 to 13 clusters at threshold 0.8). The shortest path task barely moves (1 to 2) and kth smallest does not move (2 at every temperature). At alpha 1 and temperature 0.7, the rarefied Hill-1 of correct ideas is 1.87 on the shortest path task, 1.31 on kth smallest and 1.15 on the grid task, while top-k 10 gives 1.00 on all three. Plan noise lands on Bellman-Ford/SPFA on the shortest path task (52 of 60 off-default programs, 8 other), on quickselect on kth smallest (11 of 11) and on DFS on the grid task (5). It costs correctness on the shortest path task: pass 0.63 at alpha 1 and temperature 1.0 and 0.42 at alpha 2, against 1.00 without it. Once a seed has been nudged off the default, temperature can act on the idea: under the escaping direction, temperature 0.7 against 1.0 changes the label in 5 of 20 seeds on the shortest path task and 2 of 20 on kth smallest, against 0 of 20 without plan noise.

  **Thinking on.** All 100 shortest path traces completed within the cap (Table 152). Every final program and every first approach named was Dijkstra at every temperature, and every program passed. A repeat at temperature 0.7 diverged byte for byte in all 20 traces (first divergence at token 34 to 653), because this GPU generation lacks batch invariance, yet the final label and the first approach named agreed in 20 of 20; the temperature count of 0 is read against a noise floor of 0. A judge naming the first approach of 20 traces agreed with the lexicon on 20 of 20. In the reduced grid arm (10 seeds) all 40 traces completed (median 5.2k to 6.2k thinking tokens, maximum 9.0k), and every final program and first approach was BFS, a temperature count of 0 of 10 (exact 95% upper rate 0.31). With thinking on, plan noise at alpha 2 and temperature 0.7 (2,048-token cap, the three directions with the highest thinking-off off-default share) moved the first approach named in 1, 0 and 0 of 10 seeds, short of the committed expectation of at least 3 of 10 for some direction. Once the model thinks, the prefill nudge no longer redirects the first idea it names.

  **Checks.** The engine check reran the kth smallest and shortest path cells of the screen with their twins and reproduced 200 of 200 programs token for token (size-k heap 19, quickselect 16, full sort 15; Dijkstra 26, Bellman-Ford/SPFA 24). Filler repeats in other batches were byte-identical in 60 of 60, and the engine-check slots matched the rows of the temperature block at 1.0 in 40 of 40. Under a Gumbel-max replicate the temperature count stays 0 on both tasks, plan noise changes 16.05 of 20 seeds on the shortest path task and 5.8 on kth smallest, and the pooled contrast is 0.546 (p = 1.0e-5). With min-p 0.1 at temperature 2.0, the shortest path task wrote Dijkstra 19 and Bellman-Ford/SPFA 1, kth smallest full sort 19 and quickselect 1, and the grid task BFS 20. The condition-shuffle placebo rejected at p below 0.05 in 2% of 200 runs, and the placebo of the independent rederivation in 10.5%; over 1,440 placebo runs the rejection rate is about 6%. The only correct program labelled other was a naive Dijkstra, a labeller miss; no novel algorithm appeared. The rederivation, sharing no code with the analysis, matched 33 of 33 checks, and the commitment precedes the first decisive row. An 8-bit cross-check of the two engines on the shortest path twin gave Dijkstra 50 of 50 on each, a divergence of 0 bits, which is weak by construction because the cell is all Dijkstra.

  ## 4.6 The plan subspace: does the geometry of forced prompts explain which pushes move the algorithm? (Qwen3-8B)

  **Why.** The site experiment located the choice in the task-specification states at early to middle blocks, but a site is not a representation. The subspace claim gave the internal account the request asks for a testable form: if the algorithm choice is represented along the directions that separate the per-algorithm centroids, a random push should change the algorithm to the extent that it moves the state along them. This experiment  built the subspace from forced prompts alone and asked whether it ranks 40 fresh random directions by their effect, whether removing the in-subspace component of a push removes the effect, and whether a push aimed at the runner-up centroid crosses at the predicted distance.

  **Design.** For each of 15 tasks the plan subspace at blocks 12 to 35 was the span of the centroid differences of the task-specification states (mean over the specification positions) under 30 forced paraphrases per algorithm (10 forced templates by 3 names), and a masked twin used 30 leak-checked descriptions per algorithm. The projection share of a direction is its squared norm in the subspace over its total, averaged over blocks. Forty never-run directions at alpha 1 and 2, with N = 10 each and passers topped up to N = 30, ran on the six movable tasks; 8 directions at both doses ran on the other nine, including cycle detection on its ban-free unit. Every predictor was committed by hash before the first population sample. The run sampled 13,500 programs in 675 batches of 20 over 2.51 GPU hours, labelled by runtime tracer and AST rules with a blind judge on 752 disagreements; 4 disputed and 97 invalid rows were excluded from shares.

  **The subspace is real and reliable.** At block 18 the split-half principal-angle cosine between two halves of the paraphrases is 0.89 to 0.97 on all 15 tasks, against 0.02 to 0.03 for random subspaces of equal dimension, and every centroid difference has a split-half cosine of at least 0.74. Named and masked differences agree only moderately (cosine 0.12 to 1.00 at block 18), so the subspace carries a lexical component. The iteration-3 ban displacement projects strongly onto it (projection share 0.02 to 0.77; 0.08 to 0.39 on the six movable tasks), while a random direction has a share near k/4096, about 0.001. The committed plausibility ratio, the expected in-subspace part of a random push over the distance from the default to the runner-up centroid, is 0.10 to 0.29 on 14 tasks and 0.51 on the grid task: a linear plan account predicted before sampling that random pushes would almost never cross to the runner-up through the subspace.

  **The projection share does not predict which pushes move the algorithm.** The preregistered test, a within-task Spearman correlation of at least 0.4 with p below 0.01 on at least 4 of 6 tasks, failed on all six, and so did the masked variant (Table 153). The pooled within-task correlation is 0.03 [-0.03, 0.09], and the correlation of every task lies inside its random-subspace null. The null is not for want of movers: 34 to 37 of 40 directions moved the algorithm at least once on kth smallest, the shortest path task and connected components. Nor is it noise. Splitting the first 10 samples of each direction by template, the two halves rank the 40 directions alike (Spearman 0.80 on kth smallest, 0.81 on the shortest path task, 0.76 on two sum, 0.90 on connected components; projected to full length by the Spearman-Brown formula, 0.86 to 0.95), and alpha 1 and alpha 2 rank them alike (0.61 to 0.72). Which direction moves the algorithm is a stable property of the direction, with a ceiling near 0.9 for any predictor, and the subspace share explains none of it. The only signal came from the signed component toward the runner-up on connected components (0.32 to 0.33, unadjusted p near 0.02), and the within-class control did as well (0.37).

  **Escape, confirmed on fresh directions.** Random pushes at the plan site buy correct alternative algorithms on four tasks, rarely on the grid task and two sum at alpha 1, and never on the remaining nine (Table 154). Every twin wrote its default in all samples (top-k frequent 90%). The landing is a property of the task, not of the direction, at a given site (qualified in iteration 5: on find duplicate the landing depends on the site; generated-token noise and the energy-matched read position land on Floyd cycle detection, the single plan-site escape of the screen on sort and adjacent check): on every movable task the excess-weighted landing of the 40 fresh directions reproduces the landing of the screen. The single screen escape of find duplicate did not replicate in 40 fresh directions at either dose, so find duplicate is not movable on fresh draws, and cycle detection, pushed on its ban-free unit, did not move in 16 cells. Population programs stayed mostly correct (pass over all population and top-up programs 0.98 on kth smallest, 1.00 on two sum, 0.99 on find duplicate, 0.97 on connected components), with the path tasks the exception (0.84 and 0.79): 255 of 422 pushed Bellman-Ford/SPFA programs and 55 of 123 pushed DFS programs passed.

  **The in-subspace component is not needed.** Up to four confirmed escaping directions per task (20 in all) were resampled on the same slots in three forms: with the subspace component removed, with only that component amplified to the full norm of the push, and with the subspace component of the realised displacement clamped to 0 at every edited block. Table 155 gives the effect ratio of each form against the original push. On every task with clear escapes, removing the subspace component leaves the effect intact (pooled median ratio 1.00 [0.88, 1.08]), and clamping leaves it intact on kth smallest, two sum and connected components while removing about a third of it on the path tasks. The in-subspace component alone, at the same norm, also escapes for 9 of 20 directions, all four on kth smallest. On the most movable tasks a push of this size flips the algorithm along many directions, inside the subspace or outside it. This is the generic-sensitivity account the plan named as the main confound.

  **A targeted push works on one task, and there the geometry is exact.** A push along the direction from the default centroid to the runner-up centroid moved the mean specification state by a fraction s of their distance, with s = 0.5 the predicted midpoint; its control was a random direction with the same per-position magnitude on the same slots. The committed rule (Hill-1 of at least 1.8 within 5 pass points at the midpoint on at least 4 of 6 tasks, at no more than half the median escaping random norm) was met on 1 of 6 tasks, and the targeted push was indistinguishable from the matched random push on 5 of 6 (Table 156). Connected components is the exception. Half the distance to the DFS centroid, 0.15 ban units or a tenth of a random push, turned 48% of programs into correct DFS against 0% for the matched random push (24 slots against 0; McNemar p = 1.2e-7), and the empirical crossing at 0.59 sits at the predicted midpoint. On kth smallest the crossing is at 0.85 of the distance, and the masked axis is stronger than the named one at the midpoint (0.43 against 0.08). On the other four tasks the midpoint does nothing; at 4 ban units the same axis gives 100% brute force on two sum (77% correct), 100% DFS on the grid task (20% correct) and 63% Bellman-Ford/SPFA on the shortest path task (none correct).

  **Knob displacements do not project in proportion to their effect.** Over 270 knob points on 14 tasks (nonce bans, the novelty instruction, modal bans, band patches, iteration-3 bans and random pushes), the pooled within-task Spearman correlation of the projection share of a knob with its recorded off-default share is 0.27, below the committed 0.5, and its advantage over the displacement norm (0.12) has a paired-bootstrap interval of -0.02 to 0.31. Within task it ranges from -0.29 (Fibonacci) to 0.84 (connected components). The class means show the dissociation: modal bans project strongly (mean share 0.23, off-default share 0.40), nonce bans weakly (0.07; 0.00) and the novelty instruction in between (0.15; 0.17), while the iteration-3 random pushes barely project (0.015) yet move the algorithm as often as the novelty instruction (0.17). An exploratory analysis, written after sampling, found that the signed progress of the realised displacement toward the runner-up centroid correlates with the effect on most tasks and blocks (up to 0.57 on connected components at block 31, 0.47 on two sum at block 17, 0.30 on the shortest path task at block 16, 0.26 on kth smallest at block 25, 0.48 on the grid task at block 35), while the unsigned share hovers near 0 (-0.35 to 0.21 at block 18). These are 144 uncorrected correlations, and they point at a direction effect that the committed unsigned predictor cannot see.

  **Push landings forecast ban landings.** On the five gated iteration-3 bench bans, already seen and so scored descriptively, the push-landing forecast of this run was defined on 3 events and scored a mean log score of -0.76, against -3.46 for association and -3.21 for proximity (Table 157). The opening ladder did better than both frozen families (-2.39) and worse than either push forecast. Connected components is the departure: the ban lands on BFS (83%) while pushes land on DFS, which the route landings of Section 4.2.2 explain. Across 14 tasks, the escape fraction of this run correlates with the avoidance of the bench ban at Spearman 0.86: the five movable tasks have avoidance 0.86 to 1.00 and the nine immovable ones 0.00 to 0.79. The opening margin does not track avoidance (0.19). *(Correction, iteration 5: the comparison above sets the push forecast's mean over its 3 defined events against the association mean over 5. On matched events, on the 3 events where the push forecast is defined (kth smallest, two sum, connected components) it scores -0.76 against -3.11 for association and -2.92 for proximity; over all 5 gated events, with an undefined forecast scored as uniform, it scores -1.37 against -3.46. The -1.37 coincides at two decimals with the route replication cell of the screen push in Table 157 (-1.369), a different quantity. Table 171 gives the matched means.)*

  **Geometry at the plan site.** At blocks 18 and 23, metric MDS of the geodesic distances among the forced-prompt states (PCA to 50 dimensions, k = 10) has stress-1 of 0.06 to 0.25 with trustworthiness 0.96 to 0.99; Isomap separates the algorithms into tight clusters (trustworthiness 0.84 to 0.98) but with high stress-1 (0.58 to 0.83), because the neighbour graph is clustered. Persistent loops exceed their coordinate-permutation null only on the shortest path task at block 18 and two sum at blocks 18 and 23, and a planted circle at matched size and noise was detected in every case. The figure below plots the block-18 Isomap of connected components and kth smallest in activation coordinates, with each forced-prompt centroid sized by its implemented count under the push population, and with the mean projected state of the twins, the bans, the targeted pushes and the population pushes grouped by the algorithm they produced. The pushed states stay near the twin region, apart from every forced-prompt centroid, and pushes that changed the algorithm sit among pushes that did not (the group means lie within about one unit of each other on both tasks). Only the targeted push travels toward the runner-up. The two-dimensional geometry of the forced prompts does not separate escaping from non-escaping pushes.

  [FIGURE:fig_plan_geometry]

  **No novel algorithm.** Of 10,651 correct programs from push arms, 4 carried the label other. Two blind judges and a tie-breaker, with a manual pass, classed them as a catalogue variant (a two sum hash map), a labeller miss (a Dijkstra), a plain linear scan for first and last position and a random guess-and-count loop for find duplicate; their nearest known solutions had AST Jaccard of at most 0.22. No novel algorithm appeared (rule-of-three bound 3/10,651, 0.03%).

  **Checks.** Every GPU unit test passed: 20-row decoding is independent of row position, batch-1 prefill is bit-identical on repeat, a zero-magnitude edit reproduces the twin token for token, the realised displacement matched its target within 0.07% over 3,480 prefills, and clamping left at most 6.7e-4 of the displacement in the subspace. The engine reproduced the screen exactly on 180 of 180 slots. Every bench labeller recovered all its references. An independent recomputation matched every headline, and each placebo (projection shares shuffled across directions, among others) behaved as a null should.

  ## 4.7 Movability and compliance in a held-out model family (gemma-3-4b-it)

  **Why.** The movability claim was frozen on Qwen3-8B data that had also produced it: in the screen every movable task obeyed its ban and no immovable task did. Only a family never run in this study could test it. This experiment  froze the screen rule, measured movability in gemma-3-4b-it [76] without any ban text, committed every per-task prediction by hash chain before any ban prompt was built (a grep audit of the 460 prompts fed in the ban-free stage found no ban frame), and then sampled 1,500 modal ban programs.

  **Design.** For each of 15 tasks (the 12 bench tasks, the grid and shortest path tasks, and cycle detection), the model wrote 50 neutral twin programs, and 8 fixed isotropic directions at alpha 1 and 2 were added to the task-specification states of blocks 11 to 22, the middle third of its 34 blocks, during prefill. A direction escaped by the rule of Section 4.1, confirmed at N = 30 by an exact binomial test, and a task predicted to obey its modal ban when its escape fraction was above zero. The ban unit had to change before the commitment. In Gemma the five largest channels carry 99% of the squared residual norm at the specification positions, against 40% in Qwen3-8B, so the committed unit erased the task in a 24-row calibration probe; an outlier-excluded unit was adopted before the first commitment, and after the bans the measured ban displacement turned out to be 1.29 times it (0.92 to 2.1 by block). The rival predictors, the plan noise and temperature arms, the novelty instruction and four landing forecasts ran in the same engine under the same common random numbers.

  **The movability claim is inconclusive in the held-out family.** Movability relates to compliance in the predicted direction but does not separate the tasks well enough (Table 159). The confusion matrix is 3, 3, 1, 8 (predicted obey or fail against observed): balanced accuracy 0.74 [0.40, 0.95], Fisher p = 0.24 (0.71 under the committed three-claim bound), Spearman 0.54 (one-sided permutation p = 0.025) and Kendall 0.47. The rule needed balanced accuracy of at least 0.8, Fisher p below 0.05 and Spearman of at least 0.5. Four tasks broke the prediction: kth smallest obeyed although no direction moved it, and substring search, connected components and longest increasing subsequence were movable but did not obey. A task-permutation placebo has mean balanced accuracy 0.50 (probability 0.13 of reaching the observed value), and leaving one task out gives 0.70 to 0.86.

Under mechanism labels the ban on Dijkstra mostly makes Gemma drop the heap and keep Dijkstra: avoidance falls from 0.96 to 0.11, and the escape fraction from 0.25 to 0.125.   **Other observations and checks.** The fourth template is again the weakest: its avoidance is 0.15 on the grid task against 1.0 for the other templates, and 0.05 on kth smallest. On first and last position the twin writes a linear scan 86% of the time, yet the ban `Do not use a hand-written binary search` makes it write binary search 99% of the time, an ironic rebound of the kind iteration 3 saw on kth smallest. On the shortest path task, 48 of 50 twin slots flip from the default to a survivor under the ban. The 34 correct programs labelled other were 27 degenerate programs from push arms and 7 catalogue variants, with no novel algorithm (rule-of-three bound 0.088). All 13 bench labellers reproduced their gates, the six escape counts of the screen were reproduced, the GPU tests passed, and an independent rederivation from raw samples matched every escape fraction, avoidance, balanced accuracy, Fisher p, Spearman correlation, rival correlation, landing log score and post hoc number with no mismatch; its placebos rejected at 1.7% (Fisher) and 4.9% (Spearman).

  ## 4.8 Positioning: the iteration-3 and iteration-4 claims against published work

  The positioning audit , dated 2026-10-21, checked 112 verbatim quotes from 74 references (101 against full text, 11 against venue abstracts; none mismatched, and an independent pass re-matched all 112). A saturation search over eight query families found 1,729 unique records, scored 63 on an occupancy rubric and found 44 adjacent, 19 irrelevant and none occupying. Two flags it was asked to raise did not fire: no paper measures test-checked, algorithm-level diversity under activation perturbation, and no paper predicts prompt-ban compliance from perturbation sensitivity. Table 92b sets the iteration-3 claims against their nearest neighbours and Table 92c the iteration-4 claims; each finding is paraphrased here and was verified against a quote. Several contemporaneous submissions under review, a workshop poster without an arXiv record and one workshop paper that the bibliography script could not retrieve are adjacent in the audit but are not cited by number.

  ## 4.9 Comparisons across the experiments of this iteration

  **Movability on fresh directions.** Three engines and three direction sets measured whether a task is movable: the frozen screen (fixed directions from iteration 3), the plan subspace experiment (40 fresh fixed directions per dose) and the plan noise experiment (a fresh direction per sample). They agree on five of the six screen-movable tasks and on every immovable one, and they disagree on find duplicate (Table 164). The single escaping direction of the screen on find duplicate at alpha 2 did not replicate in 80 fresh cells, and per-sample plan noise left the hash set in place at alpha 2 or less. On fresh draws the movable set is kth smallest, two sum, connected components and the two path tasks, and the table of the screen against ban compliance (movable and obeying, movable and failing, immovable and obeying, immovable and failing) moves from 6, 0, 0, 8 to 5, 0, 1, 8: find duplicate obeys its ban (catalogue-only avoidance 0.79) without being movable. Across the 14 tasks the escape fraction still ranks ban avoidance at Spearman 0.86.

  The fixed-direction escape fraction and the per-sample off-default share measure different things: a task with a few strong directions (two sum, where 5 of 40 directions escape at alpha 2) can show almost no movement under per-sample noise, which averages over directions. *(Correction, iteration 5: alpha does not mean the same push in every column. The screen uses the displacement of the ban itself; the bench unit of the plan subspace experiment is 9% to 16% smaller (its deviation 'ban_unit_scale'); the kth smallest unit of the same seed experiment is 0.77 of the screen's; the site experiment uses per-position ban units (blocks 0 to 11 at 4.5% to 7.2% of the residual norm against 12.7% to 18.3% for blocks 12 to 23); cycle detection and Gemma use a ban-free unit, which across tasks is 0.30 to 0.97 of the ban unit. Substring search has by far the largest ban unit (58.5 against 11.6 to 19.0 elsewhere) and does not move. Table 174 gives the units.)*

  **Temperature, five times.** Every measurement of temperature in the run says the same thing, now including the thinking-on arm the review asked for. In iteration 1, 797 of 800 grid programs and 797 of 800 shortest path programs kept the default across temperatures 0.3 to 1.3 with thinking off, and all 1,600 with thinking on. In iteration 2, with seeds coupled, the algorithm changed in 0 of 30 seeds in 10 of 12 cells. In this iteration temperature 1.3 and 1.6, top-k 10 and min-p reach a 5-point Hill-1 of at most 1.17 on the six movable tasks; the same seed design changed the algorithm in 0 of 20 seeds on three tasks with thinking off and on the shortest path task with thinking on; and in gemma-3-4b-it temperature reaches 5-point Hill-1 of at most 1.32. A positioning caveat applies: on other problems temperature above 1 does raise algorithmic diversity at a correctness cost [72].

  **Novelty, audited everywhere.** No artifact of this iteration found a correct novel algorithm (Table 165). Together with iterations 1 to 3, every correct program outside the catalogue in the pools audited so far has been read by two blind judges and the executor, and none was new: iterations 1 to 3, the 78 correct programs outside the catalogue among 11,763 unique correct programs (Section 3.2.3, Table 87); iteration 4, the audits of Table 165; iteration 5, its 130 correct programs outside the catalogue, with the 14 over-calls re-adjudicated in iteration 6 (Section 6.2.6); and iteration 6, the pools of Table 278, including the engine control's 3 correct programs labelled other, judged in iteration 7. Two pools were never audited by judges: about 9,000 programs of the forking token experiment, as recorded in Section 3.2.3, and the engine control's nearest-known pass of iteration 6 (up to 237 correct programs per engine and task, compared with known solutions by token overlap only; Table 278). *(Correction, iteration 6: the 14 that judges over-called in iteration 5 were re-adjudicated blind in iteration 6 (judges 14 of 48, manual 0, second adjudication 1 of 14 (Mistral Medium 3.1, three calls at temperature 0, control gate 9 of 10, passed; Kimi (kimi-k2) second view 0 of 14), final count after the executor's full read 0; the contested control, repeated maximum selection for top-k frequent, which the iteration-5 manual pass itself classed as a catalogue variant, was called catalogue variant by Mistral and catalogue variant by Kimi (Mistral gate 10 of 10 under that convention); the final read corrects 1 manual class (CATALOGUE VARIANT to DEGENERATE), none to novel).)* (iteration-7 correction)
