  ## 4.10 What iteration 4 established, what it ruled out, and what it abandoned

  Everything below is one model per claim except the held-out test, which is one family at one size, with labels from labellers that passed their gates (and one, the path labeller on Gemma, that needed a style re-gate). Every Qwen3-8B number in this iteration comes from the 8-bit engine of the screen. (Engine class: Hugging Face with W8A8 linear layers in 8-bit floating point, e4m3 weights per output channel and e4m3 activations per row through the GPU's native 8-bit floating-point matrix multiply . Each item below carries its iteration-6 engine tag, and Section 6.3 decides which of them hold under bf16 at the same absolute dose.)

  **Established.**

  1. *Temperature changes phrasing and not the algorithm, with the seed held fixed, thinking off and on.* Across four temperatures the algorithm changed in 0 of 20 seeds on three tasks with thinking off and on the shortest path task with thinking on, while phrasings per idea grew on the grid task from 3 to 13 clusters. Temperature 1.3 and 1.6, top-k 10 and min-p buy no correct algorithmic diversity on the movable tasks (5-point Hill-1 at most 1.17).
  2. *A random displacement of the task-specification states changes the algorithm, and changing the plan noise draw under a fixed seed changes it often.* One direction at alpha 1 changed the algorithm in 17.25 of 20 seeds on the shortest path task, 4.55 on kth smallest and 2.5 on the grid task (pooled contrast against temperature 0.545 [0.41, 0.67], p = 1.0e-5). *(Engine tag, iteration 6: 8-bit floating-point W8A8; the same-seed contrast itself was not rerun in bf16 . Per-sample plan noise on the shortest path task did not replicate in iteration 5's bf16 cells at the ban-free unit (2 of 47 correct programs off the default at bf16 alpha 2 against 9 of 43 at 8-bit alpha 1, bracket p 0.017), but at iteration 4's own absolute unit and seeds the bf16 engine reproduces it (22 of 50 valid attempts off the default at alpha 2 under both engines; Section 6.3).)*
  3. *The site is the task-specification states at early to middle blocks.* The same displacement at the read position or the condition sentence changed no algorithm at any dose (0 of 526 and 0 of 527 correct programs off the default), the late blocks were almost inert (6 of 521), and at matched downstream displacement the plan site keeps a large advantage (indicator +2.15 [1.79, 2.51]; odds ratio 5.72 [3.94, 8.30]) *(engine tag, iteration 6: 8-bit floating-point W8A8 , not rerun in that form. The bf16 rerun at the ban-free unit of Section 6.4 withdrew the committed site rule, because the condition-span arm never reached the plan site's downstream displacement and alpha 8 broke every plan-site program; a post-hoc model restricted to alpha of 4 or less puts the read position below the task-specification site on both tasks.)*. Blocks 12 to 23 are not distinguished from blocks 0 to 11. *(Correction, iteration 5: two wordings here say more than the experiment supports, that the read position and the condition sentence change nothing at any dose, and that the task-specification states are the site of the choice. Restated: among prefill positions, perturbing the task-specification states changes the algorithm; the read position and the condition sentence are inert at per-position doses up to 4 ban units and far weaker at matched energy (energy-matched read position: +0.23 on find duplicate, Floyd cycle detection 6 of 26 correct programs, and +0.18 on connected components, 5 of 28 off the default); noise in generated tokens 1 to 32 also redirects the choice, more than the plan site on find duplicate (12:0 paired flips at alpha 2 over the 30 pairs, exact McNemar p 0.0005; 6:0 among pairs where both programs are correct). Blocks 0 to 11 against 12 to 23: -0.31 [-0.75, 0.13]. This is a prefill site at which noise is effective, not a locus of the decision, and it is reconciled with the PARTIAL site rule under Inconclusive below.)*
  4. *Plan noise is the cheapest knob on some tasks and not on others.* It wins kth smallest (5-point Hill-1 2.72) and connected components (2.09) at no pass cost *(engine tag, iteration 6: 8-bit floating-point W8A8 at the ban unit; under bf16 and the ban-free unit of iteration 5 the same prices are 1.98 and 1.09, and on connected components 1 of 50 correct programs left the default at bf16 alpha 2 against 30 of 50 at 8-bit alpha 2 (Fisher p 7.2e-11). The engine control of Section 6.3 traces that gap to the unit and the direction seeds, not to the numerics: at iteration 4's absolute unit and seeds, bf16 plan noise moves connected components in 25 of 50 valid attempts.)* and loses find duplicate to the iterated veto and the shortest path task to the semantic seed; the preregistered price claim is PARTIAL.
  5. *Which random directions move the algorithm is a stable property of the direction, and the forced-prompt geometry does not explain it.* Template halves rank 40 directions alike (0.76 to 0.90), the projection share on the plan subspace ranks them at 0.03, and removing the in-subspace component of a push leaves its effect intact (median ratio 1.00). *(Correction, iteration 5: the range 0.76 to 0.90 covers four tasks. On all six: kth smallest 0.80 (34 movers, 27 escaping cells of direction and dose), shortest path 0.81 (37, 14), two sum 0.76 (10, 5), connected components 0.90 (36, 30), find duplicate 0.59 (3, 0) and the grid task 0.39 (22, 6); Table 176.)*
  6. *Where pushes escape, they land on one runner-up per task, and that runner-up forecasts where a ban lands.* The landing replicates across 40 fresh directions and the screen on every movable task, and on the gated bench bans, scored descriptively because they were seen before, the push forecast scores -0.76 against -3.46 for association; in Gemma it hits 4 of 4, on too few disagreeing events for the rule. *(Correction, iteration 5: this item moves from Established to the descriptive results. Where pushes escape, the landing replicates across 40 fresh directions and the screen at the plan site (kth smallest quickselect 0.66 and size-k heap 0.31; connected components DFS 0.83 and BFS 0.17; shortest path Bellman-Ford/SPFA 0.99; two sum brute force; grid DFS). As a forecast of the seen bench ban landings it hits 2 of 3 defined Qwen3-8B events (it misses connected components) and scores -0.76 against -3.11 for association on those events, and -1.37 against -3.46 over all 5 with undefined forecasts scored as uniform; in Gemma it hits 4 of 4, of which 2 disagree with association and 2 are compromised. The landing depends on the site on find duplicate.)*
  7. *Route landings.* On connected components either route of a ban alone lands mostly on DFS, the generic neighbour, and only both routes together choose BFS. On kth smallest the size-k heap share travels by the prompt states. *(Correction, iteration 5: an observation on a single task, with find duplicate as its counterexample: there the direct route alone lands on index marking, 74 of 78, neither the push landing nor the association answer; on two sum pushes and association disagree.)*
  8. *Snap-back replicates in Llama.* On five of six present minor events the modal landing is the default (0.93, 0.73 and 0.72 of attempts not banned on three of them).
  9. *No correct novel algorithm appeared under any push, up to breakage.* Correct-only diversity peaks at alpha 2 to 4, and alpha 8 erases the task; 0 novel among 14,206 correct programs of the site and subspace experiments alone.

  **Ruled out, or not supported.**

  - *A plan subspace read from forced prompts as the channel of push effects.* Disconfirmed by its preregistered rule on 6 of 6 tasks, and the decomposition shows the subspace is not needed.
  - *Targeted pushes as a general cheap knob.* Indistinguishable from a matched random push on 5 of 6 tasks; the exception, connected components, crosses exactly at the predicted midpoint.
  - *Knob displacements projecting in proportion to their effect.* Pooled 0.27, not better than the displacement norm.
  - *The top-five prohibition applied at the plan.* The push never left BFS (avoidance 0.00 at alpha 1 and 2), as the prompt and the token veto had not.
  - *Find duplicate as a movable task.* Its screen escape did not replicate in 80 fresh cells.

  **Inconclusive.**

  - *Movability as a predictor of ban compliance in a held-out family.* Balanced accuracy 0.74 [0.40, 0.95], Fisher p 0.24, Spearman 0.54; the novelty instruction predicts better (0.77), and one correct prediction rests on a labelling failure. *(Correction, iteration 5: INCONCLUSIVE under the primary measure, catalogue-only avoidance, and DISCONFIRMED under the preregistered sensitivity on the drop in the default share (balanced accuracy 0.57, Fisher p 1.0, Spearman 0.39). The grid task (tied twin, BFS 25 and DFS 25; no default under the iteration-5 rule) and find duplicate (38 failing other programs; 0.34 against 0.72) separate the two measures. Without the two compromised true positives, balanced accuracy is 0.61 and Spearman 0.31, one-sided permutation p 0.144.)*
  - *Push landings against association in the held-out family.* Ahead by 2.81 nats, but on 2 disagreeing events, below the 3 the rule needs.
  - *The site claim.* PARTIAL: the plan site is best on 3 of 6 tasks, with every margin but one a bootstrap close call. *(Added in iteration 5: the site rule is PARTIAL, so no site is established as best; what is established is the prefill specificity at matched displacement, odds ratio 5.72 [3.94, 8.30] for the task-specification states against the other prefill sites. The price of 1.5, the pass cost at which a site's randomisation hull first reaches correct-only Hill-1 of 1.5, is 0.12 for generated-token noise against 0.53 for the plan site on two sum.)*

  **Dead ends, with the evidence that closed them.**

  - *The plan subspace as the internal account of the choice.* Closed by Tables 153 and 155: the share does not rank directions, and removing it does not remove the effect.
  - *Verbalized sampling as a diversity knob.* 46 to 49 of 50 programs dispatch at run time to a randomly chosen algorithm, so their labels measure the trace, not the choice.
  - *The frozen counting rule for forecast contests.* It advances some family in 85% of no-information simulations; forecasts are now scored by paired tests and defined-only hit rates.

  ## 4.11 What the next iteration takes from this one

  The iteration answered the first question of the request in its strictest form and narrowed the second. Temperature, at any setting and with the seed fixed, changes how the code is written and not which algorithm it implements, with thinking off and on. The algorithm can be influenced, cheaply on some tasks, by a random displacement of the task-specification states at early to middle blocks, and the read position, the condition sentence and the late blocks are inert. *(Correction, iteration 5: the read position and the condition sentence are inert at per-position doses up to 4 ban units, weaker but not inert at matched energy, and the late blocks almost inert.)* What the iteration did not find is a representation of the choice: the forced-prompt subspace does not explain which displacements work, although which displacements work is reproducible. The open question is therefore what property of a direction makes it move the algorithm. The exploratory signed-progress correlations (up to 0.57) point at direction toward the runner-up rather than share, and the targeted push on connected components shows that one axis can be causally exact. A preregistered test of signed progress on fresh directions, with the reproducible ranking of the directions as the target, is the next step. *(Correction, iteration 5: that step was not taken, and signed progress is closed. Its positive cells concentrate on one task, it is negative on average on two, and on connected components the committed signed component was matched by a within-class control (0.33 against 0.37). Per task over 24 block cells: kth smallest 1 cell with p below 0.05 and a mean of -0.02 over the edited blocks (-0.29 at block 15); shortest path 3 and +0.20; two sum 7 and +0.31; connected components 22 and +0.37; find duplicate 0 and -0.12; grid 2 and +0.05 (Table 177; the record's count of 22 of 35 cells was 22 of 24). The next budget goes to more tasks, not to a further predictor at the level of directions on the same five: new tasks with the base model's repertoire committed before any push, so that which tasks move can be predicted from the base model and tested on units never seen.)*

  The movability claim needs more than one held-out family at one size, a labeller re-gated on the style of each family, and a comparison with the novelty instruction, which predicted compliance better in Gemma. The landing claim needs events on which the push forecast and association disagree: Gemma gave 2 of 4, and the Qwen3-8B bench gave 3 defined events. The contrast set of the price claim lacks the text-level plan samplers that the positioning audit names [73, 74] and a decoding baseline matched to the departure of plan noise from greedy decoding; until both are run, the claim is that plan noise beats the token-level and prompt-seed knobs tested, on the tasks where it moves the model. The route-landing lead from Section 4.2.2 ties these threads together: where one route alone removes the default, the landing is the generic neighbour that pushes reach, and the ban departs from it only when both routes act. *(Correction, iteration 5: this lead rests on connected components alone; find duplicate is the counterexample and two sum has no agreed neighbour, Section 4.2.2. Movability as a forecast of ban compliance and the contest over where a ban lands are closed beyond descriptive reporting; the next test is the narrowed repertoire account, Section 5.1.)*


  # Iteration 5: the base model's repertoire against nudge movability, a transplant of base plan states, text-level plan samplers and a second family

  ## 5.1 Why this iteration ran what it ran

  **The review of the iteration-4 record.** The review was blocking again. It raised five major items, all marked must fix, and three minor ones, and each pointed at a place where the record said more than its own artifacts. The held-out test of the movability claim had been written up as inconclusive under every sensitivity, but one preregistered sensitivity, compliance measured as the drop in the share of the default, disconfirms it, and two of the three true positives behind the positive rank correlation were compromised: the grid task had no default (its Gemma twin wrote BFS 25 and DFS 25), and the shortest path task's compliance rested on array-based Dijkstra read as Bellman-Ford/SPFA. The site conclusions said the read position and condition sentence changed no algorithm *at any dose*, although the energy-matched read position had moved two tasks, and they called the task-specification states the site of the choice, although noise in generated tokens 1 to 32 redirected it as well and beat the plan site on find duplicate. Several landing conclusions generalised from connected components alone or compared forecasts on unmatched event sets. Executed results bearing on the primary claim were missing: plan noise on the plain prompt, the hull deviation restricted to edges, the Llama block of the knob table, the dose unit of each experiment and one artifact's GPU hours. And the closing summary quoted maxima over directions as if they were typical effects, while the lead it chose for the next iteration, signed progress toward the runner-up, rested mostly on one task. The minor items asked for the positioning rows the iteration-4 audit had verified but not carried over, for exposure arms to be declared controls, and for the literal cell of the request (thinking on, top-k 10, same seed). Table 166 maps every item to its answer; the corrections are applied in place in Sections 3.2.5 and 4.2 to 4.11 and marked as iteration-5 corrections.

  **The hypothesis update.** The update kept the plan noise lead of iteration 4 and asked what sets its boundary. Plan noise moved the algorithm on some tasks and on no others, and where it moved it, it landed on one runner-up per task. On the two path tasks those runner-up algorithms were exactly the algorithms the untuned base model writes next to its default: under the chat template Qwen3-8B-Base wrote BFS in 49 of 57 correct grid programs and Dijkstra in 63 of 90 correct shortest path programs, with DFS and Bellman-Ford/SPFA second (Section 1.9). The update therefore proposed what it called the *narrowed repertoire account*: post-training narrowed a choice that the base model makes more evenly, the narrowed choice is set while the model reads the task specification, and a nudge to those states undoes part of the narrowing, reopening the base model's alternatives and only those. A task that no nudge moves would then be one on which the base model itself writes almost one algorithm, and post-training [35, 57, 87] would have narrowed only what pretraining left open.

  We use the following quantities throughout. The *base off-default share* of a task, beta, is the share of the base model's correct programs that use an algorithm other than the instruct model's default, with both models given identical token ids under the chat template; the *base runner-up* is the base model's most frequent correct algorithm other than that default. We call a task *diverse in the base* when beta is at least 0.2 and *collapsed in the base* when beta is below 0.05; between the two it is intermediate. The instruct default comes from a twin of at least 50 samples as the modal correct label with a share of at least 0.6; a task below that has *no default* and enters no movability or landing test. One *ban-free unit* is the residual norm of the task-specification states times the median ratio, in Qwen3-8B at the same relative depth, of a ban's displacement to the residual norm; it replaces the ban's own displacement as the dose unit everywhere, so that a task's dose no longer depends on how far its ban moved it. We call the edit h ← h + lambda (h_base − h_instruct), applied during the instruct prefill at every task-specification position of blocks 12 to 23 with the base states computed on the same prompt, a *transplant of base plan states*, in the spirit of cross-model activation patching [88].

  Eight claims were preregistered, each with its rule committed by sha256 before its first decisive sample.

  - *The movability half: the base repertoire predicts which tasks move* (primary): across new tasks, beta ranks the escape fraction of 8 fixed random directions at Spearman of at least 0.6 with a permutation p within parent clusters below 0.01, at least 80% of tasks collapsed in the base are immovable, and beta is ahead of each rival. Disconfirmed if Spearman is below 0.3 or most tasks diverse in the base are immovable.
  - *The landing half: landings follow the base runner-up* (primary): on movable new tasks the push landing is the base runner-up in at least 70% of events (exact test against per-event chance, p below 0.05), and the base composition beats the association forecast by at least 0.10 nats in log score.
  - *The transplant claim* (primary, causal): on at least two thirds of the tasks diverse in the base among the 15 existing ones, the transplant at its best lambda (with pass of at least 0.8 times the twin's) reaches a correct off-default share of at least half of beta, beats a matched-norm random displacement and what we call a *borrowed shift* (another task's base minus instruct direction at the same norm) on paired flips, and lands on the base runner-up; tasks collapsed in the base and a transplant at the read position stay within 0.05 of the twin.
  - *The plan sampler comparison* (secondary): plan noise prices at least as well as the best of four text-level plan samplers on at least 3 of the 5 tasks movable on fresh draws: intent factored generation [73], plan search [74], a sampler we call *enumerate and pick* (the model lists algorithms and an external random draw picks one) and what we call *base intent* (the base model writes an intent of one sentence and the instruct model writes the code).
  - *The push toward the base*: a push along the base minus instruct direction, which we call a push toward the base, escapes at no more than half the norm a random push needs (secondary).
  - *The Gemma replication* (secondary): both halves in gemma-3-4b-pt against gemma-3-4b-it [76], a replication on fresh samples because Gemma's iteration-4 outcomes were seen.
  - *The literal cell* of the request (descriptive) and *the novelty count* (secondary).

  **The strategy.** Seven artifacts ran (Table 167). One evaluation on CPU only repaired the iteration-4 record from rows on disk and froze eight rival task predictors by hash before reading any outcome. The transplant experiment measured the base repertoire of all 15 existing tasks, committed it, and only then ran the transplant with its controls. Two panels built new coding tasks, committed each task's base repertoire, and only then pushed the instruct model; they split the new tasks between them so that the pooled confirmation would have more units than either could build alone. The knob experiment ran the text-level plan samplers and what we call *decoding at matched departure* (a decoding temperature set so that the output departs from the twin as much as under plan noise) on all 15 existing tasks, and the literal cell. The Gemma experiment repeated both halves and the transplant in a second family, and a research artifact searched the literature for each new claim. The 16 GB card of iteration 4 was replaced by cards of 23 to 24 GB, so every Qwen3-8B experiment of this iteration ran in bf16 rather than with 8-bit linears; this change of engine, together with the change from the ban unit to the ban-free unit, turns out to matter (Section 5.10).

  ## 5.2 The record audit: corrections from rows on disk, and frozen rival predictors

  The record audit  generated no model text. It answered every review item by recomputing the values behind it from the row files of eight earlier artifacts, and wrote each fix as an exact replacement for the record, with every value tagged by provenance and checked against the record within fixed tolerances (counts exact, rates 0.005, Hill-1 and log scores 0.01, intervals 0.02). Of 187 values that had a record value, 186 matched and 1 was corrected: the record's count of *22 of 35 cells* for signed progress on connected components is 22 of 24, because the staged file holds 24 block cells per quantity. A further 15 values were new and 4 were carried from the iteration-4 record because their source was not a declared dependency (the knob table cells, the route landings, the Llama block and the iteration-3 direction counts). All six quotes behind the rows added to Table 92c were verified again live on 2026-10-21. An independent script using only the standard library recomputed 195 values with no failure, and its four placebos failed as they should (balanced accuracy under permuted escape fractions 0.50; the site odds ratio 1.01 when the plan site and read position are swapped, against 101.7 real; a landing shuffle that shrinks the push advantage from 2.35 to 0.46 nats; rejection of permuted escape fractions at 3.5% to 4.8%). Table 168 lists the 35 corrections and the status of the values behind each.

  **The held-out verdict, per compliance measure.** Table 169 restates the Gemma test of iteration 4 under every variant the audit could compute. Under the primary measure, catalogue-only avoidance, the verdict stays INCONCLUSIVE (balanced accuracy 0.74, Fisher p 0.235, Spearman 0.54). Under the preregistered sensitivity that measures compliance as the drop in the default share, which we call the *drop sensitivity*, it is DISCONFIRMED (0.57, Fisher p 1.0, Spearman 0.39). Two tasks separate the measures, and Table 170 shows why. The grid twin is tied, BFS 25 and DFS 25 of 50 attempts, so the default DFS came from a 10-sample pilot (correct BFS 4 and DFS 5, attempts 5 and 5) and the ban's avoidance of 0.83 is measured against a baseline that already left DFS half the time; the default share drops by only 0.33. On find duplicate, 38 failing programs labelled other count as leaving the default under the drop measure (catalogue-only avoidance 0.34, drop 0.72). Under the iteration-5 default rule the grid task is the only one with no default, and the first and last position task's rule default (linear scan, 0.86 of the twin) differs from the frozen one. Removing the grid task leaves the verdict inconclusive (0.70); removing both compromised true positives gives 0.61 and Spearman 0.31 (one-sided p 0.144).

  **Executed results the record had omitted.** Plan noise on the plain prompt, without the prohibition frame of the twin, ran on the same slots and directions as plan noise under the twin frame (Table 173). The frame is not needed on kth smallest, connected components and the shortest path task, and on connected components the plain prompt moved more programs (0.24 against 0.12). The dose units of the experiments differ (Table 174): the ban-free unit is 0.30 to 0.97 of the ban unit across tasks as a ratio of mean norms (Table 174); the knob experiment's mean of per-position ratios is larger (0.83 to 1.39 on the six decisive tasks: kth smallest 1.394, connected components 0.990, shortest path 0.889, two sum 0.995, grid 0.874, find duplicate 0.829), because a mean of ratios is not a ratio of means. By the ratio of means the shortfall is at most about 25% on grid (0.751), shortest path (0.834), kth smallest (0.974), two sum (0.777), connected components (0.745), but 38% on find duplicate (0.620) and first and last position (0.618), 30% on top-k frequent (0.699) and 70% on substring search (0.296) (iteration-6 correction; record audit, Table 227), and substring search, the task that never moves, has by far the largest ban unit. A check made after the rivals were frozen found that the pooled escape fraction does not track the ratio of ban unit to residual norm (Spearman -0.06, AUC 0.49), so movability is not an artefact of the dose unit on the screen tasks.

  **Rival task predictors, frozen before any target was read.** For the movability half to mean anything, beta had to beat simpler explanations of why a task moves. The audit computed eight ban-free predictors for the 15 existing tasks and catalogue size as a covariate, wrote them to a canonical file, and froze them by sha256 in a hash chain before opening any outcome file (frozen at 11:59:44 UTC, first scored at 11:59:50; two later freezes left the values identical). The predictors are the twin's opening margin (the margin in log probability, under teacher forcing, of the opening of the default over that of the runner-up), the forced can rate, association clarity, the off-default excess under the novelty instruction, the diversity of human solutions (Mercury solutions labelled by the frozen rules with a judge on unknowns; audit agreement 0.97, kappa 0.97, 121 programs), the runtime merit gap between the reference programs of the runner-up and of the default (76 references timed on their hidden tests), the twin modal share and the ratio of ban unit to residual norm. Five of them (the opening margin, the novelty excess, the merit gap, the twin modal share and catalogue size) can be computed on new tasks and were frozen for the confirmation panels. Scored against the pooled escape fraction of the screen, none is informative after Holm correction (every adjusted p is 1.0), and 10 of the 15 tasks are tied at an escape fraction of 0 (Tables 179 to 181). These scores are descriptive: the escape fractions generated the hypothesis, so the freeze protects only the confirmation on new tasks.

  ## 5.3 Transplanting the base model's plan states into the instruct model (Qwen3-8B)

  **Why.** If post-training narrowed the choice at the plan site, the narrowing should be undone by giving the instruct model the base model's own task-specification states. No earlier iteration had tried this: iteration 1 subtracted an instruct minus base direction estimated at the read position only, which destroyed the output format (Section 1.9). This experiment  was the first causal test of the transplant claim, and it also measured the base repertoire that every other Qwen3-8B analysis of the iteration needed.

  **Design.** Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-8B-Base (revision 49e3418f, the base revision of iteration 1) ran in bf16 on one RTX 4090 with thinking off, temperature 1.0, top-p 1 and no top-k. The base model sampled 100 programs per task under the instruct chat template on identical token ids (200 on the two path tasks, with top-ups to 200 on connected components, nonoverlapping intervals and cycle detection) and 100 in plain completion. Its labels used the iteration-4 labellers with a blind judge on disagreement, and a 15-program judge audit per task agreed at least 0.86 everywhere. The base repertoire (default, beta with a 95% interval, stratum, base runner-up) was committed by hash before any hooked sample. The transplant set the hooked states to h_instruct + lambda (h_base − h_instruct) at blocks 12 to 23 for lambda in {0.25, 0.5, 1}; the states were set, not added, so nothing compounded, and at lambda 1 the hooked blocks carried the base state exactly. The controls on the same common-random-number slots were a matched-norm random displacement (per block and position), the borrowed shift (another task's mean base minus instruct direction at the same norm), and, where the random control broke the model, a random push matched on pass rate. Site controls transplanted at the read position, at blocks 0 to 11 and at blocks 24 to 35. Lambda was selected on one set of slots and confirmed on fresh slots, both under commits made before the samples.

  **The base model is more diverse than the instruct model on most tasks** (Table 182). Under the same prompt the instruct twin wrote its default in 96% to 100% of programs on all 15 tasks, while 5 tasks were diverse in the base (kth smallest, shortest path, connected components, grid and top-k frequent), 7 intermediate and 3 collapsed in the base (merge intervals, nonoverlapping intervals and topological order). The base model under the chat template is a poor programmer: it wrote 14 to 55 correct programs per 100 to 200 samples, and on the grid task only 14 of 200, so the grid beta rests on attempts. On connected components it writes DFS more often than union find (32 against 19 correct programs), so the instruct default is the base model's second choice there.

  As a screen check, the committed beta ranks the 15 tasks almost exactly as iteration 4's random pushes could move them: Spearman 0.78 against the escape fraction at alpha 1 (one-sided permutation p 0.0002), 0.79 at alpha 2 and 0.79 on their mean, and the base runner-up equals the push's top-1 landing on 5 of 5 movable tasks. This is the observation the hypothesis was built on, measured again; it is not a test, because these tasks generated the hypothesis.

  **Selection and confirmation.** Table 183 gives every arm of the selection stage. The transplant moved two tasks at an intact pass rate on the selection slots, top-k frequent at lambda 1 (0.47 of correct programs off the default, pass 0.98) and connected components at lambda 0.5 (0.12), and it broke the shortest path and grid tasks at lambda of 0.5 or more (pass 0.72 and 0.54, 0.50 and 0.30). On kth smallest the matched random displacement at lambda 1 moved more programs (0.34) than the transplant (0.06). Early-block transplants moved kth smallest (0.30) and connected components (0.28) more than the main band, the transplant at the read position broke the output on 13 of 15 tasks without moving an algorithm, and late-block transplants were inert.

  On fresh slots (Table 184) only top-k frequent passed: the transplant wrote the base runner-up, a heap, in 21 of 49 correct programs against 0 of 39 for the twin, beat all three controls at p of 7e-4 or less after Holm adjustment, and was ahead on 5 of 5 templates. On kth smallest the matched random displacement beat the transplant (2 flips by the transplant alone against 20 by the random displacement alone; exact test, two sided, p 1.2e-4): the base direction disturbs the plan less than an isotropic one of the same size. On connected components the transplant led both controls 3:0, short of significance, and on the shortest path and grid tasks the lambda that survives (0.25) moved nothing. The frozen rule needs a pass on at least 4 of the 5 tasks diverse in the base, so the transplant claim is DISCONFIRMED; the sensitivities restricted to the stable stratum and robust to noise agree. An extension blind to outcomes, to N = 100, on the decisive cells (Table 185) kept top-k frequent (44:0, 35:3 and 49:0 against the three controls) and added only raw significance against the borrowed shift on kth smallest (6:0, p 0.016, Holm 0.11) and connected components (7:0, p 0.0078, Holm 0.06); neither task beat the matched random control. Its verdict reads PARTIAL for a mechanical reason: at N = 100 the grid transplant's pass rate (0.68) fell below 0.8 times the twin's, which removes the precondition for DISCONFIRMED.

  Top-k frequent is the one task on which the base state works and random noise does not: it is diverse in the base (beta 0.35) and iteration 4's random pushes never moved it. Its transplant also raised the pass rate from 0.78 to 0.98, so part of what the transplant restores may be a more correct program rather than a reopened choice; the experiment did not separate the two. Tasks collapsed in the base did not move under the full transplant (change 0.00). The transplant at the read position shifted the off-default share by more than 0.05 on connected components and longest increasing subsequence, but only among the few programs that still passed (5 and 16 correct of 30) and never significantly, so the specificity check on point estimates fails while its version robust to noise holds.

  **The push toward the base and the reverse transplant.** A push along the unit base minus instruct direction never escaped the default on any of the four tasks at doses of 0.5 to 2 ban-free units, while an isotropic push at the same doses escaped on kth smallest at alpha 2 (Table 186). The claim for the push toward the base is DISCONFIRMED. The reverse interchange wrote the instruct model's task-specification states into the base model (Table 187). It raised the base model's correct program counts on all four tasks (kth smallest 20 to 31, shortest path 15 to 20, grid 5 to 11, connected components 18 to 19) and its default share among attempts, while a matched random displacement lowered the counts; the committed prediction (the default share among correct programs rises by at least half the instruct minus base gap) was met only on the grid task (0.80 to 1.00; one-sided p 0.033). Control is asymmetric: instruct states pull the base model toward the instruct default and toward correct code, but base states do not pull the instruct model back.

  **What the base minus instruct difference is.** D = h_base − h_instruct is mostly shared across tasks and templates: the per-task mean D has a cosine across tasks of 0.76 to 0.88 at blocks 12 to 27 and split-half cosine 0.96 to 1.00 between template halves. It is large: at lambda 1, 71% of the hooked cells exceed 4 ban-free units, the dose at which random noise broke programs in iteration 4, and at the read position the difference is as large as the residual itself (Table 188). The transplanted state does not survive downstream: at block 27 the task-specification state stays 88% to 89% of the way to the base twin, but the state at the read position moves only 18% to 31% of the way (Table 189), so blocks 24 and later pull the computation back toward the instruct model.

The novelty audit read every one of 48 correct programs outside the catalogue, base output included: the judges called 14 of them novel, and the manual comparison with the nearest known solution found linear scans, count loops and a threshold binary search, known techniques outside the frozen catalogue; 0 novel (rule-of-three bound 0.062). Ten deviations are logged, among them base sampling and the engine check before the protocol commit (both still before every transplant sample) and the conservative label unknown for the probe of Dijkstra with an array scan.

  ## 5.4 Panel A: does the base repertoire predict which new tasks move? (Qwen3-8B)

  *Three instruct twins of new units are mixed: trapped rain water (default share 0.64), minimum spanning tree weight (default share 0.66) and valid anagram (default share 0.76); on two units the instruct model is more diverse than the base: trapped rain water (twin off-default 0.36 against beta 0.23) and minimum spanning tree weight (twin off-default 0.34 against beta 0.11) (iteration-6 note).*

  **Why.** The screen correlation of 0.78 was measured on the tasks that generated the hypothesis. The movability and landing halves could only be confirmed on tasks never seen, with every forecast committed from base samples before the first push. Panel A  built one half of those tasks.

  **Design.** Nine new units derived from LeetCode problems [12] were frozen up front in new wording (a grep audit found no algorithm word or catalogue name), each with hidden tests from the dataset's input and output pairs plus seeded edge, random and stress cases, one reference per algorithm, mutants that must fail, quadratic baselines and runtime and AST labellers. A labeller passed its gate at a kappa of at least 0.8 between runtime and AST labels, an agreement of at least 0.9 between runtime and adjudicated labels and 100% of references, with one revision round on a holdout. Six of the seven planned units passed; number of islands failed after its revision (holdout kappa 0.74), and the two reserves, jump game and median of two sorted lists, ran as a logged extension. Per unit, the instruct twin drew 50 programs and the base model 100 on identical ids plus 50 in plain completion, the rivals were computed, and the forecast (default, beta with its interval, base runner-up, rivals) was committed by hash; a guard in the GPU worker refused push jobs until then. Only then did 8 isotropic directions at alpha 1 and 2 (N = 10, confirmed at N = 30 by an exact binomial test), plan noise at alpha 1 and 2 (N = 50) and temperature 1.3 (N = 50) run. The 15 existing tasks were remeasured in the same engine on the ban-free unit; we call this the remeasurement arm.

  **The movability half is not supported in panel A** (Table 191). Over the six preregistered units, Spearman between beta and the escape fraction is -0.03 (exact one-sided p 0.56; Kendall 0). The one unit collapsed in the base, maximum block sum (beta 0), is immovable, as the movability half predicts, but 2 of the 5 units diverse in the base are also immovable, among them the most diverse: count primes (beta 0.81) never escapes. A bootstrap over measurement error gives a median of -0.09 (90% interval -0.37 to 0.21). With the two extension units, both diverse in the base (0.47 and 0.71) and both immovable, Spearman falls to -0.33 (p 0.80). Simple rivals tracked movability better than beta (Tables 192 and 193), and so did beta's own variants: Spearman with the escape fraction is -0.09 for beta from plain completion, -0.03 for beta that also counts correct programs labelled other as off-default (identical to beta on these units) and 0.40 for the base Hill-1 (0.16, -0.33 and 0.22 with the extension units). The three units that moved have an alternative at least twice as fast as the default (minimum runtime merit ratio 0.10 to 0.51), the three that did not have ratios of 0.86 to 4.35, and the runtime merit rival reaches -0.88; the extension unit median of two sorted lists breaks this (ratio 0.11, never escapes), and with it the rival falls to -0.66. The twin's own modal share reaches -0.70, ahead of beta by a task-bootstrap interval that excludes zero (-1.90 to -0.09).

  **The landing half is supported in panel A.** On all three movable units (majority element, trapped rain water, longest mirrored substring) the base runner-up is the push landing (Poisson-binomial p 0.019 under chance 1/(K − 1)), and the base composition scores best (Table 194). The committed association forecast was uniform because of a mapping bug: every association answer restates the default named in the question, and the committed mapping took the earliest catalogue mention. With the mapping corrected post hoc on the same answers given before commitment (Table 195), association names the landing on 2 of 3 events and is a strong rival, but the base composition still scores higher on all three (mean margin 0.85 nats; 1.10 against the committed uniform version). Exact Wilcoxon p is 0.25, the smallest attainable with three events. No correct program from plan noise or from an escape cell landed on an algorithm with zero correct and zero valid base programs (Table 198).

  ## 5.5 Panel B: seven more new tasks and disguised variants (Qwen3-8B)

  *Three instruct twins of new units are mixed: trapped rain water (default share 0.64), minimum spanning tree weight (default share 0.66) and valid anagram (default share 0.76); on two units the instruct model is more diverse than the base: trapped rain water (twin off-default 0.36 against beta 0.23) and minimum spanning tree weight (twin off-default 0.34 against beta 0.11) (iteration-6 note).*

  **Why.** Panel B  built the other half of the confirmation units under the same protocol, and added what we call *disguised variants*, eight bench tasks rewritten as narratives, each with a paired remeasurement of its parent, to separate a task's wording from its algorithmic affordances.

  **Design.** Seven units (missing number, single number, minimum spanning tree weight, integer square root, all subsets, valid anagram and count inversions) were built with wording free of algorithm words, hidden tests checked by two independent oracles, three to six references, mutants and excluded brute force methods, and gated labellers; all seven gated, four after one revision round, and the 15-program blind audits of base labels agreed at 0.93 to 1.0. Because the base model was 46% to 61% off task under the chat template, its repertoire was raised to N = 200 per unit before any commit. Each unit's beta, base runner-up, base composition and rivals were hash-chained before its first push; then came 8 directions at alpha 1 and 2, plan noise and temperature 1.3.

  **The movability half is not supported in panel B either** (Table 201). Spearman between beta and the escape fraction is 0.21 (exact one-sided p 0.33, bootstrap interval over units -0.75 to 0.95). Four units moved (single number, count inversions, minimum spanning tree weight and integer square root) and three did not: missing number (beta 0.06), all subsets (0.37) and valid anagram (0.81), the clearest disconfirming case. No unit was collapsed in the base, so the part of the movability half that says collapsed tasks are immovable is untested here. Beta ranks the graded plan noise excess better (0.82, p 0.017), and the runtime and length merit rivals track the escape fraction more closely than beta (0.54 and 0.58; Table 202), all with wide intervals. Under the preregistered sensitivities, beta from attempts gives 0.39 (p 0.18), beta from plain completion -0.45, beta from correct programs 0.04, and excluding the uncertain class or the flagged twins gives -0.03 and 0.06; a placebo with beta shuffled 1,000 times has a mean Spearman of 0.008 and rejects at 0.048.

  ## 5.6 The two panels pooled (computed for this report)

  Neither panel ran the pooled test: both wrote their raw ingredients per unit for a pooled step in the next round. Because the pooled numbers decide how this iteration is read, we computed them here from the two panels' own result files (`work/pooled_a1a2.py`, output `work/pooled_a1a2.json`), with a Monte Carlo permutation test for Spearman and an exact Poisson-binomial tail and exact Wilcoxon signed-rank tests [65] for the landing half.   ## 5.7 Plan noise against text-level plan samplers, decoding at matched departure, and the literal cell (Qwen3-8B)

  **Why.** The positioning audit of iteration 4 found that the price comparison lacked its strongest competitors: text-level plan samplers, which diversify code by sampling a plan before the program [73, 74], and a decoding baseline matched to plan noise's own departure from the twin, the baseline under which an ICLR 2027 submission (OpenReview oag3wgNLRh) found activation steering no better than ordinary decoding. The review also asked for the literal cell of the request. This experiment  ran both.

  **The literal cell never changes the algorithm** (Table 206). On the shortest path task with thinking on, top-k 10 and the same 20 token seeds as the iteration-4 thinking arm, moving the temperature over 0.3, 0.7, 1.0 and 1.3 changed the final program's algorithm in 0 of 20 seeds (one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound 0.14), and the first approach named in the thinking changed in 0 of 20. All 100 traces completed, every final program was heap-based Dijkstra, and every trace named Dijkstra first. Temperature changed the tokens: a repeat at temperature 0.7 was byte-identical on only 4 of 20 traces while the labels agreed on 20 of 20 (median common prefix 309.5 tokens), and paired with the top-p 1 traces of iteration 4 at the same seed and temperature the labels agreed on 100 of 100 pairs although the traces shared a median of only 34 tokens. A judge agreed with the first-approach lexicon on 19 of 19 audited traces. With this cell, question 1a-c of the request is answered under every sampler the run used: with thinking off at top-k 10 (Table 76), with thinking off and on at top-p 1 (Section 4.5), and with thinking on at top-k 10 here.

  At N = 20 with thinking on a rise shows only at T 1.3, and repeat noise is the same size. *(Iteration-6 addition: the two phrasing columns, computed by the knob experiment and missing from the record until now.)*

  **Design of the knob comparison.** Every knob ran in one HF bf16 engine with exact inverse-CDF common random numbers, so all arms of a slot shared the uniform stream of the code stage, on all 15 existing tasks (N = 50 per cell on the five decisive tasks, 30 on the other ten). Plan noise drew a fresh isotropic direction per sample at the task-specification positions of blocks 12 to 23, prefill only, at alpha 1 and 2 ban-free units, under the twin frame and on the plain prompt. The text-level plan samplers used the twin's frame, with the twin's neutral sentence first: intent factored generation at the direction's (1.3, 0.7) and the paper's tuned (0.73, 0.60) temperatures [73]; a lite plan search (five observations, a random pair of them combined into a plan, then code) [74]; enumerate and pick, in which the model lists up to eight algorithms and an external random number picks one; and base intent, in which Qwen3-8B-Base writes the intent sentence and the instruct model the code. Decoding at matched departure applied a temperature to generated tokens 1 to 32, bisected per task so that its mean per-token KL from the twin equalled plan noise's own at each alpha, measured on prefixes used only for calibration. Prices came from a randomisation hull over the full simplex with 2,000 slot bootstraps that select the best mixture again inside every replicate. The committed rule calls the plan sampler comparison supported if the 5-point Hill-1 of plan noise is at least that of the best text sampler on at least 3 of the 5 decisive tasks.

  **The plan sampler comparison is DISCONFIRMED** (Table 207) (ban-free unit and iteration-5 seeds; re-tagged by iteration 7's dose-unit experiment, Section 7.6: at the moving design D* = D1 the plan-sampler rule is still disconfirmed, at 2 of 5) (iteration-8 correction). In Table 207 the margin is the 5-point Hill-1 of plan noise minus that of the best text sampler. Plan noise matched or beat the best text sampler on 1 of the 5 decisive tasks, kth smallest (1.98 against 1.83 for enumerate and pick, P(plan noise at least best) 0.58, unresolved). On connected components, the shortest path task and two sum, base intent won (2.53, 1.45 and 1.61 against 1.09, 1.18 and 1.17), and on the grid task nothing moved much. The mean margin is -0.40 (95% interval -0.70 to -0.24), and only 1.8% of bootstrap replicates reach three wins. Every sensitivity keeps the verdict except one (Table 209): with the multistage samplers dropped (they were padded on the left), intent factored generation is the only text sampler left and plan noise beats it on 4 of 5 tasks, so the disconfirmation rests on base intent and on enumerate and pick. On the ten other tasks (Table 208) plan noise moved only cycle detection and first and last position, while text samplers moved substring search, find duplicate, Fibonacci, longest increasing subsequence, top-k frequent and first and last position. Two prompt knobs outside the text-sampler set also beat plan noise where it was strongest: the novelty instruction on kth smallest (2.03) and the semantic seed on the shortest path task (2.12). (iteration-7 correction)

  Table 210 shows what each arm actually wrote on the decisive tasks. Enumerate and pick buys the most raw diversity (Hill-1 of 2.9 to 4.7 per cell) at a cost of 16 to 62 pass points, and 40% of its grid rows are invalid. Base intent keeps the pass rate high on connected components (0.98) and two sum (0.88) while writing three and four algorithms. Intent factored generation at its cooler code temperature collapsed the grid pass rate to 0.12 and 0.08, with every correct program BFS. Plan noise is much weaker here than in iteration 4: on connected components it wrote union find 49 times in 50 at both alphas, where iteration 4's 8-bit engine at the ban unit had written DFS 29 times at alpha 2 (Section 4.3); Section 5.10 returns to this.

  **Plan noise against decoding at matched departure.** At alpha 2, plan noise moves the algorithm and the matched decoding does not (Table 211): over the decisive tasks 19 slots are correct and off the default under plan noise only and 3 under the matched decoding only (exact p 0.0009), 13 to 0 on kth smallest alone. At alpha 1 there is no difference (4 against 3). The matched decoding's 5-point Hill-1 is at most 1.25 on every decisive task. So plan noise's effect is not its token-level departure from the twin, which answers the objection of the ICLR 2027 submission for these tasks, but as a practical knob it loses to two text samplers. Plan noise on the plain prompt and under the twin frame showed no significant paired difference on any of the 15 tasks (Table 212).

  **Checks and deviations.** The engine check against the 8-bit rows of iteration 4 was sensitive to precision (Table 213): the twins agreed per slot at 0.98 to 1.00 and the pushed cells at 0.74 to 0.86, so no iteration-4 row was reused and temperature 1.3, top-k 10, the novelty instruction and the semantic seed were rerun. Twelve correct programs labelled other were 10 labeller misses, 1 degenerate and 1 unresolved; 0 novel. The style re-gate flagged only top-k frequent (agreement 0.80). An independent recomputation reproduced the literal cell, every McNemar count and the verdict, with the 5-point Hill-1 of the hull within 0.08 of the committed value and a win count of 2 rather than 1 (a near tie on the grid task), still DISCONFIRMED; relabelling plan noise rows as the twin gave margins of 0 or below on all five tasks, and shuffles of the arm labels centred at 1.6 wins (3 or more wins in 3 of 20 shuffles), so the count rule over five tasks is only weakly selective on its own. The plan's one allowed wording revision was used after the first format pilot failed (the model wrote code at once), the committed drop order fired after stage 100 and the dropped cells were restored when the queue finished early, and cells with fewer than 30 (decisive) or 15 (other) programs were excluded from hulls, a rule decided after a dry run that favours plan noise on kth smallest. Post hoc, with iteration-1 base label names harmonised, landing mass outside the base support is 0.11 for enumerate and pick on the grid task (bidirectional BFS) and 0 for every shortest path landing.

  ## 5.8 The second family: gemma-3-4b-pt against gemma-3-4b-it

  **Why.** The Gemma replication asked whether the account replicates in a second family, with the base repertoire of gemma-3-4b-pt committed before a fresh, never-run push population was applied to gemma-3-4b-it [76]. Gemma's iteration-4 push outcomes were seen, so this experiment  is a replication on fresh directions and samples, not a held-out confirmation.

  **Design.** Both models ran in bf16 on one 23 GB NVIDIA GPU, one at a time. A fresh it twin (N = 50 per task) fixed each task's default under the iteration-5 rule; the grid twin now gave DFS on 30 of 40 correct programs, so every one of the 15 tasks had a default. The pt model wrote 100 programs under the it chat template on the same token ids and 50 in plain completion of a `def solve(...)` stub. Under the chat template 91% of its programs had no usable code and only 10 of 1,500 passed, so the preregistered chat validity gate failed, both formats were pooled, and every unit fell under the low-correct rule: beta, the runner-up and the landing forecast come from valid attempts, not correct programs. These were committed by hash before 16 never-run isotropic directions (seeds 52001 to 52016) were applied at alpha 1 and 2 to the task-specification positions of blocks 11 to 22 on the outlier-excluded ban-free unit. A transplant from pt into it at lambda 1 then ran on the seven tasks diverse in the base with a matched random control, a borrowed shift and a transplant at the read position on the same slots, and on three controls collapsed in the base.

  **In Gemma the movability half is inconclusive and the landing half passes** (Table 214). Spearman between beta and the escape fraction is 0.42 (one-sided permutation p 0.060, n = 15), against a bar of 0.5 at p below 0.01; 2 of 3 tasks collapsed in the base are immovable against a bar of 80%; and beta is ahead of no rival, with the twin modal share (0.67) and the novelty instruction (0.64) tracking movability better (Table 215). The direction is the predicted one: 6 of 7 tasks diverse in the base are movable against 2 of 8 others (one-sided Fisher p 0.032, not registered). The partial Spearman given catalogue size and the forced can count is 0.41 (0.45 given catalogue size alone), and the fresh population agrees with iteration 4's movability on 13 of 15 tasks (8 movable now, 6 then). No sensitivity meets the preregistered bar (Table 216); beta from the chat template alone reaches 0.62 (p 0.0095), but that arm is 91% unusable output, and beta from correct programs only reaches 0.27. The pt runner-up equals the modal landing of confirmed escapes in 5 of 7 events (hit rate 0.71 against a mean chance of 0.30; exact Poisson-binomial p 0.025), and the pt composition beats iteration 4's association forecast by 1.50 nats per event (exact Wilcoxon p 0.023) and AST proximity by 0.51 (Table 217). The two misses are kth smallest (landing size-k heap, runner-up quickselect) and connected components (landing union find, pooled runner-up BFS; union find is the runner-up under the chat template alone).

  **The transplant moves two of seven tasks diverse in the base** (Table 218). Every transplanted program stayed valid (pass ratio 0.98 to 1.00). Substring search moved from the naive scan to the built-in find in 40 of 50 programs (twin 6 of 50), and first and last position from the linear scan to binary search in 39 of 50 (twin 4 of 50); both land on the pt runner-up. The other five tasks diverse in the base stayed at their default. The two that moved are exactly the tasks diverse in the base whose it twin already writes the pt runner-up 8% to 12% of the time, so the transplant amplified an existing minority mode and did not install an absent one. The pt-minus-it difference at the task-specification positions is large (median 5.2 ban-free units, 4.7 to 5.8 across blocks), above the dose at which random noise broke programs in iteration 4, and five massive channels carry 86% of its squared norm at block 11, falling to 31% to 36% by blocks 21 and 22. Random controls and borrowed shifts that copy the massive-channel move and match the remaining norm broke most programs (pass ratio 0.16 to 0.50 and 0 to 0.22), so the random comparison is confounded by norm and the borrowed shift is itself broken: what the controls show is that the coherent pt content is benign where an equally large random displacement or borrowed shift is destructive. The transplant at the read position and the three controls collapsed in the base stayed within 0.05 of the twin (Table 219); on nonoverlapping intervals the transplant halved the pass rate without moving the algorithm.

  **Labels and checks.** The base labels are the weakest link: runtime labels agreed with an adjudication by judges from two families on 30 of 30 it programs but on 5 of 30 pt programs (20 of 30 after the inline judge), because the pt code is mostly broken, so the style re-gate failed and its preregistered fallback, judging every disagreement between runtime and AST labels, applied; a 225-program audit of pt labels agreed at 0.64 (0.47 to 0.93 by task). A structural audit of 92 default and runner-up programs agreed at 0.99. The re-gated shortest path rule, which reads array-based Dijkstra correctly, relabels 258 iteration-4 shortest path programs: their escape fraction falls from 0.25 to 0.125 and their ban compliance from 0.96 to 0.34, which confirms the iteration-4 mislabel. The engine check reproduced iteration-4 slots exactly; 0 novel algorithms among 56 correct programs labelled other (35 catalogue variants, 21 degenerate); the commits preceded the first push and transplant rows; two independent recomputations found no mismatch, with placebos failing as required. Seventeen deviations are logged.

  ## 5.9 Positioning: variety in the base model, transplants and base-aligned collaboration in published work

  The positioning audit , dated 2026-10-21, extended the iteration-4 audit to the new claims. It checked 137 verbatim quotes from 93 references (111 against full text, 21 against ICLR 2027 abstracts, 5 against blog posts; no mismatch, and a live second pass re-matched all 137) and ran a saturation search under a protocol frozen before the first call: 169 logged calls, 4,508 raw hits, 3,506 unique records, 49 scored on the occupancy rubric, with the stop rule met after the third round.   Three flags summarise the search. The transplant flag, a paper that writes base-model hidden states into its tuned descendant and reports a change in output diversity, did not fire, narrowly: cross-patching writes base upstream states into a descendant's late stack but measures a next-token margin [91], and earlier patching work measured backdoor removal [89], factual recall [90] or entity tracking [88]; the goal of restoring diversity is published at the weight level, by restoring layer intervals to pretrained weights [92] or merging aligned lower layers with base upper layers [93], and at the token level [94]. The transplant may not be called first. The forecast flag, a forecast from the base model of where post-training narrows, partly fired: forecasts per prompt at training time exist, and one finds that base pass rate and likelihood explain only 0.30 and 0.24 of the explainable variance in post-training gains [99]; inference-time movability and the identity of the landing remain open. The premise flag partly fired: Lee et al. compared DeepSeek Coder base and instruct models with test-checked correctness and found a mixed direction [72], so the premise row reads contradicting in part. The audit recommends further baselines for any later report: weight interpolation between Qwen3-8B-Base and Qwen3-8B [102], layer restoration and splicing at the transplant's block ranges [92, 93], token routing between base and aligned models [94], arithmetic on the logits of base and tuned models, and template control for every base minus instruct contrast [103]. It also lists 27 corrections to earlier citations. Table 92d condenses the neighbour table of the audit; the verbatim quotes are in its `evidence/quotes_iter5.jsonl`.

  ## 5.10 Comparisons across this iteration's experiments

  **The base repertoire against movability: screen, confirmation and second family.** The same quantity, beta against the escape fraction, was measured five ways in this iteration, and the answer depends on which tasks enter. On the 15 existing tasks, with the beta of Step 1 and the escape fractions of iteration 4, Spearman is 0.78 to 0.79; with this iteration's own bf16 escape fractions it is 0.59; on the new tasks it is -0.03 in panel A, 0.21 in panel B and 0.15 pooled; in Gemma it is 0.42. The screen correlation is carried by many tasks with low beta that never move, while on new tasks those diverse in the base that never move are common: count primes and valid anagram (beta 0.81 each), median of two sorted lists (0.71), jump game (0.47), all subsets (0.37) and longest common prefix (0.30). The figure, corrected in iteration 6, plots both sets like for like under bf16: the existing tasks at their bf16 escape fraction under the ban-free unit (filled; the 8-bit screen value as an open ghost marker joined by a segment) and the new units, both at iteration 5's ban-free unit. Existing tasks (n 15): Spearman 0.59, one-sided permutation p 0.010, Bonett-Wright 95% [0.06, 0.86]; with the 8-bit screen E instead 0.79. New units (n 13): 0.15, p 0.315, [-0.44, 0.65]; with the two reserve units 0.01. Pooled bf16 (n 28): 0.48, p 0.005. The existing-task correlation is carried by many tasks with low beta that never move; open markers show the 8-bit screen value of each existing task. Per set, the base runner-up named the push landing 5 of 5 on the 8-bit screen, 1 of 2 on the bf16 remeasurement of existing tasks, 3 of 3 in panel A, 3 of 4 in panel B and 5 of 7 in Gemma (17 of 21, Poisson-binomial p 5.8e-07); the bf16 remeasurement's kth smallest and connected components events were missing from the earlier count of 16 of 19 (kth smallest a miss: landing size-k heap against runner-up quickselect; connected components a hit). On the 8 held-out events where the instruct twin wrote no correct program off the default the base runner-up named 5 (p 0.053; Qwen3-8B 3 of 4, p 0.052; Gemma 2 of 4, p 0.422) (iteration-6 correction).

  **Movability depends on the engine and the unit.** Table 222 sets the existing tasks' movability side by side across the measurements of iterations 4 and 5. Under iteration 4's 8-bit engine and the ban unit, six tasks were movable; under this iteration's bf16 engine and the ban-free unit, only kth smallest and connected components escape with 8 fixed directions, and per-sample plan noise moves more than 10% of programs off the default only on kth smallest (0.28 at alpha 2). On the shortest path task, per-sample plan noise moved 26% of all samples at alpha 1 in iteration 4 (13 of 50 valid attempts off the default; 9 of 43 correct programs) and 0 of 50 correct programs at alpha 1 here (2 of 47 at alpha 2, 1.67 8-bit ban units by the ratio of mean norms and 1.78 by the mean ratio). A dose-bracketed comparison (iteration 6) sets the bf16 alpha-2 cell, which delivers more than the 1.00 ban unit of the 8-bit alpha-1 cell under either dose definition, against the 8-bit alpha-1 cell: a lower bf16 share there cannot be a dose shortfall. By the rule fixed before computing, connected components and shortest path did not replicate in bf16 at the population level (correct-only bracket one-sided Fisher p kth smallest 0.588, connected components 0.056, shortest path 0.017, two sum 1.000, grid 0.732); kth smallest: not established; two sum: not established (no 8-bit effect of at least 10% at alpha of 2 or less to replicate); grid: not established; find duplicate: not established (no 8-bit effect of at least 10% at alpha of 2 or less to replicate). This rules out the dose unit, not the CRN slots, the labels or the kernels (iteration-6 correction; record audit, Table 228). The engine control of Section 6.3 then tested the numerics directly: at iteration 4's own absolute displacement, direction seeds and slots, the bf16 engine reproduces the 8-bit rows (per-sample plan noise at alpha 2: connected components 25 of 50 valid attempts off the default under bf16 against 30 of 50 under the 8-bit engine; shortest path 22 of 50 under both), so the non-replication tagged here belongs to iteration 5's ban-free unit and direction seeds, not to the bf16 numerics. The engine checks pushed two fixed escaping directions at the ban unit in both engines and agreed within or near the resampling null (shortest path: Dijkstra 31 and Bellman-Ford/SPFA 19 in bf16 against 26 and 24 in the 8-bit engine). Those two directions therefore do not explain the difference, and its cause is not established here. *(Correction, iteration 6: the engine control of Section 6.3 establishes that the cause is not the bf16 numerics. At the absolute unit, direction seeds and slots of iteration 4 itself, bf16 escapes on almost the same directions as the 8-bit engine (connected components 26 of 40 against 29 of 40; shortest path 6 of 40 against 8 of 40). The shrinkage belongs to the ban-free unit of iteration 5 or its direction seeds, and the heading should read that movability depends on the unit and the direction draw.)* Movability is therefore a property of a task under a given engine, unit and direction population, and the confirmation panels measured it under bf16 and the ban-free unit only.

  **The transplant in two families.** In Qwen3-8B the transplant passed on 1 of 5 tasks diverse in the base and in Gemma it moved 2 of 7, each time onto the base runner-up. The successes share a feature: in Gemma the instruct twin already wrote the runner-up 8% to 12% of the time, and in Qwen3-8B the transplant raised the pass rate from 0.78 to 0.98 while it moved top-k frequent. Where the instruct model never wrote the base runner-up, the base states did not install it. In both families the base minus instruct difference at the task-specification positions was large (Qwen3-8B 0.39 to 0.53 of the residual norm, 71% of cells above 4 ban-free units at lambda 1; Gemma a median of 5.2 ban-free units), and in both an isotropic displacement or borrowed shift of comparable size did more damage than the coherent base content.
