  ## 5.11 What iteration 5 established, what it ruled out, and what it abandoned

  Everything below is one or two model families at 4B to 8B parameters, memorised tasks in the style of LeetCode, and labels from gated labellers, except the base-model labels of Gemma, which agree with an adjudication at only 0.64. Every Qwen3-8B number of this iteration comes from a bf16 engine.

  **Established.**

  1. *Temperature does not change the algorithm, under every sampler the run used.* With thinking on, top-k 10 and the same seed, the algorithm changed in 0 of 20 seeds across four temperatures on the shortest path task, and the first approach named in the thinking never changed.
  2. *(Moved to the descriptive results, iteration 6.)* *Where a random nudge moves the instruct model, it often lands on the base model's runner-up.* Per set the base runner-up named the push landing 5 of 5 on the 8-bit screen, 1 of 2 on the bf16 remeasurement of existing tasks, 3 of 3 in panel A, 3 of 4 in panel B and 5 of 7 in Gemma (17 of 21, Poisson-binomial p 5.8e-07); on new tasks 6 of 7 events (Poisson-binomial p 0.003). 6 of the 11 held-out hits are also the instruct twin's own minority: on the 8 held-out events where the instruct twin wrote no correct program off the default the base runner-up named 5 (p 0.053; Qwen3-8B 3 of 4, p 0.052; Gemma 2 of 4, p 0.422), and the twin's own most frequent alternative, defined on 7 of 21 events, named 6 of them against 6 for the base runner-up (exact McNemar p 1.000). Where the twin writes an alternative at all, the landing half is therefore the twin's own minority, and the base model adds a forecast only on the events where the twin writes none (iteration-6 correction; record audit, Table 230), with the base composition ahead of association by 0.75 nats (exact Wilcoxon p 0.055 with the corrected association) and of proximity by 0.50. In Gemma it named 5 of 7 (p 0.025; 1.50 nats over association with undefined association forecasts filled uniformly, 1.57 on the 6 defined events, p 0.023), and on the existing Qwen3-8B tasks 5 of 5. In panel A no nudged program landed outside the base repertoire.
  3. *The base model is more diverse than the instruct model on most tasks under identical prompts.* The instruct twin wrote its default in 96% to 100% of programs on all 15 existing tasks, while 5 tasks were diverse in the base and 7 intermediate, and every new unit but one had beta of at least 0.05. The base model's own correct output is thin under the chat template (14 to 55 correct programs per 100 to 200 on the existing tasks). Three instruct twins of new units are mixed (trapped rain water default share 0.64, minimum spanning tree weight default share 0.66, valid anagram default share 0.76). On two new units the instruct twin is more diverse than the base: trapped rain water (twin off-default 0.36 against beta 0.23) and minimum spanning tree weight (0.34 against 0.11), and on both the landing is the twin's own minority (iteration-6 correction).
  4. *Plan noise's effect is not its token-level departure from the twin, on kth smallest.* At alpha 2 it moved 19 slots against 3 for decoding matched to its per-token KL (exact p 8.6e-04), but the discordant counts are kth smallest 13:0, connected components 1:3, shortest path 2:0, two sum 2:0, grid 1:0: without kth smallest the other four tasks give 6:3 (p 0.508); at alpha 1 the pooled count is 4:3 (p 1.000); bf16-conditional (iteration-6 correction; record audit, Table 233).
  5. *The record repairs.* The held-out movability test is inconclusive under catalogue-only avoidance and disconfirmed under the drop sensitivity; the read position and condition sentence are inert only at per-position doses up to 4 ban units; landing comparisons on matched events give push -0.76 against association -3.11 on 3 events and -1.37 against -3.46 on 5.

  **Ruled out, or not supported.**

  - *The movability half: the base repertoire predicts which tasks a nudge moves.* Not supported as a strong predictor, and not disconfirmed (ban-free unit and iteration-5 seeds; re-tagged by iteration 7's dose-unit experiment, Section 7.6: at D* = D1 kth smallest and connected components are movable, and shortest path, two sum and the grid are not) (iteration-8 correction): beta is not a strong predictor of movability (Spearman 0.15 over 13 new units, Bonett-Wright 95% [-0.44, 0.65], bootstrap BCa [-0.50, 0.70], one-sided permutation p 0.317; power of the registered one-sided permutation test about 0.63 at a true 0.6, 0.50 two-sided, and 20 units for 0.8); a moderate relation is not excluded at this n; conditional on the design of iteration 5 (bf16 with the ban-free unit and its direction seeds; the engine control of Section 6.3 shows that the numerics alone do not shrink the escapes). The pooled value rests on the beta of count inversions, 0.75, which the panel committed on the attempt basis because only a few base programs were correct (67% of its attempts fall in the class other); on the correct-only basis used for the other twelve units its beta is 0.13 and the pooled Spearman is 0.035. Per panel Spearman -0.03 (A) and 0.21 (B); 4 of 10 new units diverse in the base never moved. Under one definition of each rival, pooled over the 13 units with signs fixed so that the predicted direction is positive: opening margin 0.08 (Holm p 1.000, delta +0.07 [-0.66, 0.88]); novelty-instruction excess -0.50 (Holm p 1.000, delta +0.65 [-0.06, 1.34]); runtime merit 0.71 (Holm p 0.021, delta -0.57 [-1.26, 0.20]); twin modal share 0.41 (Holm p 0.347, delta -0.26 [-1.05, 0.56]); catalogue size -0.21 (Holm p 1.000, delta +0.35 [-0.57, 1.24]). Under Holm only runtime merit tracks movability, while beta does not; the paired interval for beta minus that rival still includes 0 (iteration-6 correction; record audit, Table 232). The screen correlation of 0.78 did not transfer to new tasks. (iteration-7 correction)
  - *The transplant claim: a transplant of base plan states reopens the base repertoire.* Disconfirmed by the frozen rule (1 of 5 tasks diverse in the base); on kth smallest a matched-norm random displacement moved more programs than the base states (2:20). The narrowing installed by tuning is not carried by the task-specification states of blocks 12 to 23 alone.
  - *The push toward the base.* A push along the base minus instruct direction never escaped at 0.5 to 2 ban-free units, while an isotropic push did on kth smallest.
  - *The plan sampler comparison: plan noise prices at least as well as text-level plan samplers.* Disconfirmed (1 of 5 decisive tasks) (ban-free unit and iteration-5 seeds; re-tagged by iteration 7's dose-unit experiment, Section 7.6: at the moving design D* = D1 the plan-sampler rule is still disconfirmed, at 2 of 5) (iteration-8 correction); base intent won on connected components, the shortest path task and two sum. (iteration-7 correction)

  **Inconclusive.**

  - *The movability half in Gemma.* Spearman 0.42 (p 0.060), with the twin modal share and the novelty instruction ahead of beta; descriptively 6 of 7 tasks diverse in the base moved against 2 of 8 others.
  - *Top-k frequent.* The one Qwen3-8B task where the transplant reopened the base runner-up also gained 20 pass points, so restored correctness and a reopened choice are not separated.

  **Dead ends, with the evidence that closed them.**

  - *The base minus instruct direction as a knob.* Closed by Table 186: it never escapes, and the difference it encodes is mostly shared across tasks (cosine 0.76 to 0.88) and larger than the dose at which random noise breaks programs.
  - *Transplanting at the read position.* The base and instruct states differ there by about the size of the residual, and the transplant broke the output on 13 of 15 tasks without moving an algorithm.
  - *Plan noise as the practical knob for algorithmic diversity.* On the decisive tasks two text-level samplers price better, and under the bf16 engine and ban-free unit plan noise moves more than 10% of programs only on kth smallest (conditional on the design of iteration 5, bf16 with the ban-free unit and its direction seeds: at the absolute unit and seeds of iteration 4 the bf16 engine reproduces the 8-bit effects on connected components and the shortest path task, Section 6.3; iteration-6 correction).
  - *Signed progress toward the runner-up as the next predictor.* Closed in the record audit (Table 177): concentrated on one task, negative on two, matched by a within-class control.

  ## 5.12 What the next iteration takes from this one

  The narrowed repertoire account split in two. Its landing half held descriptively in both families and on unseen tasks (5 of 5 on the 8-bit screen, 1 of 2 on the bf16 remeasurement of existing tasks, 3 of 3 in panel A, 3 of 4 in panel B and 5 of 7 in Gemma (17 of 21, Poisson-binomial p 5.8e-07)), but it is not yet separated from the instruct twin's own minority (on the 8 held-out events where the instruct twin wrote no correct program off the default the base runner-up named 5 (p 0.053; Qwen3-8B 3 of 4, p 0.052; Gemma 2 of 4, p 0.422); iteration-6 correction): when a nudge moves the instruct model, it moves it to the algorithm the base model writes next, and a forecast built from base samples, before any push, names that landing better than the model's stated alternative. Its movability half failed on unseen tasks: a base model that writes many algorithms does not mark a task the instruct model can be nudged off, and its states, written into the instruct prefill, reopen the choice on one task in five. The base repertoire marks where a nudge can lead, not whether it can lead anywhere.

  The open question is therefore what makes a task diverse in the base immovable. Count primes and valid anagram (beta 0.81 each) never moved, while trapped rain water (0.23) did. Two leads came out of this iteration's data. In panel A the three units that moved had an alternative at least twice as fast as the default and the three that did not had none, although median of two sorted lists broke the pattern. And in the transplant experiment early blocks 0 to 11 moved kth smallest and connected components more than the main band, which suggests the narrowing sits at least partly upstream of blocks 12 to 23. The positioning audit names the baselines a further test needs: weight interpolation between the base and instruct models, layer restoration at the transplant's block ranges, and token-level base and aligned collaboration [92, 93, 94, 102]. Base intent, which beat plan noise on three of five tasks, is the strongest practical knob the run has priced, and it is itself a form of that collaboration at the level of sentences. Finally, movability has to be measured under the engine and unit at which it will be used: the six screen-movable tasks of iteration 4 shrank to two under bf16 and the ban-free unit, for reasons this iteration did not establish. *(Iteration-6 correction: a dose-bracketed contrast rules out a scalar dose shortfall on connected components and shortest path, and the engine control rules out the bf16 numerics, since at iteration 4's absolute unit and seeds bf16 reproduces the 8-bit escapes (Section 6.3). What remains is the per-position and per-block profile of the ban-free unit, or the direction seeds; every verdict that rests on bf16 plan noise or escape fractions at the ban-free unit is conditional on that design.)*

  # Iteration 6: an engine control, where a ban and an instruction are carried, a one-token fork in Gemma, and the plan in words

  ## 6.1 Why this iteration ran what it ran

  **The review of the iteration-5 record.** The review was blocking again. It raised five major items, all marked must fix, and four minor ones. The first went to the run's main internal result. Every plan-noise positive of iteration 4 had come from an 8-bit engine whose W8A8 linear layers compute in 8-bit floating point (e4m3 weights per output channel, e4m3 activations with a per-token scale), while iteration 5's bf16 knob experiment found per-sample plan noise nearly inert: connected components moved in 1 of 50 programs at alpha 2 against 30 of 50 under the 8-bit engine. The record had left the cause open, had not reported the knob experiment's own measurement of the dose it delivered, and still listed iteration-4 items 2 to 4 as established. The review asked for a decisive control: the same directions and slots at the same absolute displacement under the 8-bit engine, under 8-bit floating-point weights with bf16 activations and under bf16. The second item found the landing half of the narrowed repertoire account overstated. Its tally of 16 of 19 omitted the bf16 remeasurement made in that same iteration, and it never scored the minority algorithm of the instruct twin itself as a rival, although that rival explained half the hits. The third item asked for the power and interval behind the claim that the movability half was ruled out, and for the frozen rivals on the pooled set. The fourth listed executed outputs missing from the record: the phrasing columns of the literal cell, the prices at Hill-1 1.5 and 2, the dose file of the knob experiment, the knob rows of panel B and three Llama rows of Table 126c. The fifth said that after five iterations the record still had no internal account of how the choice manifests, which is the request's central question, and that its one internal positive rested on the 8-bit engine. The minor items asked for the per-task counts behind item 4 of Section 5.11, the fill rule for undefined Gemma forecasts, a sentence on the three new tasks whose instruct twins are already mixed, and a second blind adjudication of the 14 transplant programs that two of three judges had called novel. Table 224 maps every item to its answer.

  **The hypothesis update.** The update turned from the outside of the model to its inside. Five iterations had mapped what moves the algorithm from outside: a ban, a meaningful hint, a plan sentence written by the base model, a list-then-pick step. None had located where the model holds its choice. The update proposed one concrete answer, which it called the plan-variable account. While the model reads the task, it computes a small hidden variable that says which algorithm to write. We call this variable the *plan*. On tasks where a ban acts through the prompt states (shortest path, kth smallest, connected components) the plan sits in the residual stream at the task-specification positions; on tasks where generated tokens read the ban directly (two sum, find duplicate) it sits at the first generated tokens. Exchanging a few of its dimensions between two prompts should switch the algorithm the model writes, with correct code. Random noise should change the algorithm only through the part of it that falls inside the plan, which would explain why most random directions do nothing; temperature should never touch it.

  The update tested the account with the instruments the request names and the run had not yet used. An *interchange intervention* replaces a component's activations under one input with those under another and measures the change in output. *Distributed alignment search* (DAS) fits an orthonormal low-rank subspace in which such an exchange reproduces a counterfactual behaviour [110, 111]. A *natural language autoencoder* (NLA) pairs an activation verbalizer, which writes a text explanation of a residual-stream state, with an activation reconstructor, which maps text back to a state; released checkpoints exist for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct [124] at layer 20, not for Qwen3-8B. Gemma Scope 2, released in December 2025, provides JumpReLU sparse autoencoders [114] and transcoders trained on gemma-3-4b-it itself, the successor of the Gemma Scope release for Gemma 2 [113], so no transfer test from a base model is needed.

  Eleven claims were preregistered, each with a rule committed by sha256 before its first decisive sample. We call them by their content rather than by their codes: the engine claim, the localization claim, the mediation claim, the discreteness claim, the token claim, the resampling claim, the verbal readout claim, the feature claim, the site rerun, the landing contest and the novelty count.

  - *The engine claim* (primary): on connected components and shortest path, the same 40 directions and common-random-number slots at the same absolute displacement under four numerics. Activation rounding is the cause if the escape fraction under bf16 weights with 8-bit floating-point activations (W16A8) exceeds bf16 by at least 0.2, the full 8-bit engine (W8A8) matches W16A8 within 0.1 and 8-bit floating-point weights with bf16 activations (W8A16) match bf16 within 0.1, on both tasks. The result is called not reproduced if W8A8 minus bf16 is below 0.1.
  - *The localization claim* (primary). Stage A, with no training: exchanging the full residual states of the ban prompt into the neutral twin transfers the ban's substitute at a transfer share of at least 0.5 on at least two of shortest path, kth smallest and connected components, at a pass rate of at least 0.8 times the twin's, and at most 0.2 on two sum and find duplicate. Stage B: DAS at one layer recovers at least 0.8 of the full-state transfer at a rank of 16 or less on held-out templates.
  - *The mediation claim* (primary): the energy that a random direction puts into the fitted plan subspace predicts which directions switch the algorithm (Spearman at least 0.5).
  - *The discreteness claim*, *the token claim* (temperature leaves the plan coordinate flat while state noise at generated tokens beats temperature at matched per-token KL) and *the resampling claim* (resampling the plan as a diversity knob) (secondary).
  - *The verbal readout claim* (secondary): the NLA names the substitute of a ban before any code is written at a rate at least 0.3 above a judge reading the visible text; editing the explanation's algorithm phrase and reconstructing transfers the algorithm by at least 0.2.
  - *The feature claim* (secondary): in Gemma's natural BFS against DFS split on the grid task, Gemma Scope 2 features decode the upcoming algorithm at least 0.10 balanced accuracy above a classifier on the visible text, and steer at least as well as a difference-in-means direction at matched pass.
  - *The site rerun* (secondary): the iteration-4 noise-site comparison in bf16; the prefill-site claim survives if the task-specification site beats the read position and the condition sentence at matched downstream displacement on at least one task, and is withdrawn otherwise.
  - *The landing contest* (secondary): the base runner-up against the instruct twin's own teacher-forced ranking of algorithm openings, on every recorded push-landing event.
  - *The novelty count* (secondary).

  **The strategy.** Seven artifacts were planned (Table 225). One evaluation on CPU, which we call the record audit, repaired the record from rows on disk and ran the second novelty adjudication. An experiment we call the engine control ran the four numerics on a 16 GB RTX 2000 Ada, an Ada-generation card with the 8-bit floating-point tensor cores that the 8-bit engine needs. A bf16 experiment, which we call the exchange and site experiment, ran the Stage A exchanges, the site rerun, state noise against matched temperature, the top-five push and the landing contest. Gemma and the NLA each received their own experiment, which we call the Gemma feature experiment and the NLA experiment, and a research artifact, which we call the positioning audit, searched the literature for each claim. The seventh artifact, which was to fit the DAS subspaces of Stage B and run the mediation, discreteness, resampling and temperature-coordinate tests together with a manifold of plan coordinates, was lost before it existed: the planning agent returned no plan. Section 6.8 records it as planned and not run. Every Qwen3-8B number of this iteration except those of the engine control comes from a bf16 engine.

  ## 6.2 The record audit: corrections, engine tags and a second novelty adjudication

  The record audit  generated no model text. It recomputed from the row files of the earlier artifacts every number the review touched, tagged each internal result with the numerics that produced it, and wrote each change as a verbatim replacement keyed to the report. Of the values behind its corrections, 78 matched the record, 18 were new, 2 were carried from earlier evaluations and 1 was corrected: the power of the movability test, recorded as 0.46, is 0.63 for the registered one-sided test and 0.50 two-sided. A standard-library re-derivation passed 277 of 277 checks, its five placebos failed as they should, and a second script reproduced 7 of 7 headline numbers from the rawest files. Judge spend was USD 0.29 over four passes.

  ### 6.2.1 The corrections

  Twenty-nine of the 36 corrections are applied in place in Sections 4 and 5 and marked as iteration-6 corrections. The seven that target the closing section are folded into the closing section, which is rewritten at the end of this iteration. The audit ran in parallel with the engine control, so its engine tags were written before the control's result existed; where the control supersedes them, the in-place text adds a pointer to Section 6.3. Three further notes of the same kind mark the frozen screen of Section 4.2.6, the movability paragraph of Section 5.10 and the caption of Table 222. Table 226 lists every correction.

  ### 6.2.2 Engine and dose

  The two artifacts that the review compared recorded off-default shares on different definitions: the bf16 knob experiment counted correct programs off the default over all samples, the 8-bit plan-noise experiment valid attempts off the default over all samples. The dose definitions differ as well. Table 174 gave the ban-free unit as a ratio of mean norms, while the knob experiment measured a mean of per-position ratios, which is larger because a mean of ratios is not a ratio of means (Table 227). On the six decisive tasks, by either definition, the bf16 alpha-2 cell of iteration 5 delivered at least 1.24 ban units, so a dose-bracketed contrast sets it against the 8-bit alpha-1 cell, which delivered 1.00. A lower bf16 share in that comparison cannot come from a shortfall of the scalar dose.

  ### 6.2.3 Landings

  Table 230 restates every recorded push-landing event with its base support and the instruct twin's own composition. Per set, the base runner-up named the landing 5 of 5 times on the 8-bit screen, 1 of 2 on the bf16 remeasurement of existing tasks, 3 of 3 in panel A, 3 of 4 in panel B and 5 of 7 in Gemma, 17 of 21 in all (Poisson-binomial p 5.8e-7). On 6 of the 11 held-out hits the landing is also an algorithm the instruct twin already writes. Restricted to the 8 held-out events where the twin wrote no correct program off the default, the base runner-up named 5 (p 0.053; Qwen3-8B 3 of 4, p 0.052; Gemma 2 of 4, p 0.42). On the 7 events where the twin wrote any alternative, the twin's own most frequent alternative named the landing 6 times, as often as the base runner-up (exact McNemar p 1.0). The landing half therefore moves to the descriptive results: where the twin writes an alternative, the landing is that alternative, and the base model adds a forecast only where the twin writes none.

  ### 6.2.4 Movability

  The movability verdict is restated with its interval and power (correction in Section 5.11) (ban-free unit and iteration-5 seeds; re-tagged by iteration 7's dose-unit experiment, Section 7.6: at D* = D1 kth smallest and connected components are movable, and shortest path, two sum and the grid are not) (iteration-8 correction). Over the 13 new units, Spearman between the base off-default share and the escape fraction is 0.15, with a Bonett-Wright 95% interval from -0.44 to 0.65, a Fieller interval from -0.46 to 0.66, a BCa bootstrap interval from -0.50 to 0.70 and a one-sided permutation p of 0.317. At a true correlation of 0.6, the registered one-sided permutation test has power 0.63 (0.50 two-sided, the figure the record had quoted as 0.46), and 20 units would give 0.8. The data exclude a strong relation, not a moderate one. The pooled value also leans on one unit: count inversions' committed base share of 0.75 came from attempts, because only 15 base programs were correct and 58 of its 87 attempts are labelled other; on the correct-only basis of the other twelve units its share is 0.13 and the pooled Spearman falls to 0.035. Table 231 lists every unit with its share on both bases and each rival under one definition. (iteration-7 correction)

  ### 6.2.6 A second blind adjudication of the 14 disputed programs

  In iteration 5 two of three judges had called 14 of the 48 correct transplant programs outside the catalogue novel, and the zero count rested on a manual read by the executor. The audit stress-tested each program in a sandbox at the maximum size of the specification and on adversarial cases, retrieved its three nearest known solutions by Zhang-Shasha tree edit distance [64], and had two judges from model families the run had never used classify it blind: Mistral Medium 3.1 (three calls at temperature 0, Fleiss kappa [128] 1.00 across the calls) and Kimi (kimi-k2, Moonshot AI). Ten controls of known class were mixed in, and both judges passed the control gate at 9 of 10. All 14 programs pass their hidden tests; one, a repeated maximum selection on top-k frequent, times out at the maximum size. Mistral called 1 of 14 novel and Kimi 0 of 14 (Table 234). The one program called novel, a first-and-last-position solution, is range guards plus a linear scan to the first match and over its run; it passes 56 of 56 hidden tests and every stress group, and a full read by the executor classes it as a linear search. The final count is 0 novel of 14. Agreement with the manual verdict on the 14 is 0.86 raw (95% interval 0.57 to 0.98), Gwet's AC1 [127] 0.83 and a Cohen kappa of 0.71; with the controls included (24 items) kappa is 0.80 [0.57, 1.00]. The final read corrected one manual class: one first-and-last-position program, a linear scan plus a count of each element, is degenerate rather than a catalogue variant.

  ## 6.3 The engine control: are the random-push escapes a property of the model or of 8-bit rounding?

  **Why.** The engine claim was the primary test of the iteration, because its answer decides which internal results of iteration 4 belong to Qwen3-8B. The review had pointed at a plausible mechanism without establishing it: a displacement changes the per-token absmax of each linear input, so under dynamic per-token 8-bit floating-point scaling it changes the rounding of every downstream activation, and the engine adds its own perturbation to the push. The 8-bit floating-point format in question is e4m3, with a maximum of 448 [115]. The engine control  separated weight rounding from activation rounding by running iteration 4's own design under four numerics, all built from one bf16 snapshot of Qwen3-8B (Table 235).

  **Table 235.** The four numerics of the engine control.

  | Engine | Weights | Activations | Role |
  |-|-|-|-|
  | W8A8 | e4m3, per-output-channel absmax / 448 | e4m3, per-token absmax / 448 | iteration 4's engine (native 8-bit floating-point matrix multiply) |
  | W8A16 | e4m3, the same codes | bf16 | weight rounding only |
  | W16A8 | bf16 | e4m3, fake-quantised per token | activation rounding only |
  | bf16 | bf16 | bf16 | full-precision reference |

  **Design.** Everything except the numerics was held fixed: the 40 direction files of iteration 4 (seeds 9101 to 9140, checked bitwise), the absolute displacement per block and position at blocks 12 to 23 and the task-specification positions (the bench unit of iteration 4), the twin prompts, the common-random-number slots and uniforms, the stop rule, a 1,024-token cap, one labeller version (that of iteration 4 plus the iteration-5 re-gate that reads array-based Dijkstra correctly) applied to every row, and the two-stage escape rule of iteration 4, with each engine scored against its own twin. The W8A8 engine first regenerated the rows of iteration 4 on the same GPU model, driver and library versions: 400 of 400 programs of the plan-subspace experiment and 40 of 40 per-sample plan-noise programs came out byte-identical, the realised downstream displacement had ratio 1.000, and per-slot label agreement was 1.0. Under the reuse rule committed before sampling, the rows of iteration 4 therefore stand in for the W8A8 engine on every other cell. The bf16 twins reproduce the bf16 twin composition of iteration 5 (connected components union find 50 of 50; shortest path Dijkstra 49, Bellman-Ford/SPFA 1). The direction screen ran at alpha 2 on connected components and shortest path, and per-sample plan noise at alpha 1 and 2; the alpha-1 direction arms of the two single-factor engines, a Gaussian mimic of the 8-bit noise and kth smallest were dropped by the committed drop order, and the W8A16 engine ran on a slower cast path because the fused kernel could not be compiled.

  **bf16 escapes on almost the same directions.** At the same absolute displacement the bf16 engine escapes on 26 of 40 directions on connected components and 6 of 40 on shortest path, against 29 and 8 under W8A8 (Table 236). The direction-level discordance is 3:0 and 4:2 (exact McNemar p 0.25 and 0.69), the per-direction off-default shares rank alike (Spearman 0.96 and 0.87; kappa on escape 0.83 and 0.48), and permuting the pairing of directions drops kappa to about 0. The committed verdict on both tasks is the rule's outcome for a high escape fraction that 8-bit rounding does not explain: W8A8 minus bf16 is below 0.1 and bf16 is within 0.15 of iteration 4's escape fraction, so bf16 escapes too and the account specific to 8-bit rounding is not reproduced. Table 237 pairs every two engines direction by direction. The low escape fraction on shortest path is a pass-rate effect common to both engines: in each, 17 of 40 directions reach the +0.20 off-default excess but fail the pass clause, because the pushed Bellman-Ford/SPFA programs often fail the hidden tests. At the screen level the shortest path verdict is MIXED (the artifact's `screen_level_verdict`), beside the literal NOT_REPRODUCED_HIGH: W8A8 passes the screen on 15 of 40 directions against 8 to 9 for the other engines, and 17 (W8A8) and 17 (bf16) of 40 directions reach the +0.20 excess but fail the pass clause. (iteration-7 correction)

  **The 8-bit engine adds a small boost on connected components, and activation rounding is not its source.** Pairing every pushed sample with the same slot (direction, template, slot index and uniforms) in the other engine, on the 400 screen slots of the first two samples of all 40 directions, W8A8 is off the default in 58.3% of slots against 53.2% under bf16 on connected components (discordant 30:10, exact McNemar p 0.0022), and 43.2% against 40.7% on shortest path (55:45, p 0.37) (Table 239). The factorial locates the boost. Activation rounding alone (W16A8) sits slightly below bf16 on connected components (49.7% against 53.2%, 9:23, p 0.02); weight rounding alone (W8A16) sits between bf16 and W8A8 (55.6%; 17:7 against bf16, p 0.06). The small boost therefore comes from the e4m3 weights, from the native kernel's reduced-precision accumulation (it matches an exact fp64 reference on 94.2% of outputs, against 99.96% for an exact emulation), or from their interaction. The landing algorithms do not change: correct off-default programs are DFS, then BFS, on connected components and Bellman-Ford/SPFA on shortest path under every engine, with compositions compatible across engines (permutation chi-squared p 0.22 and 0.94; Table 240).

  **Mechanism diagnostics.** Per-token e4m3 rounding perturbs every linear input by about 2.5% RMS. Under an alpha-2 push, the push-induced difference in rounding error is 6% to 12% of the push-induced change in activation (median over blocks 13 to 35 per site, peaking at 34% at the block-14 attention input), and 70% to 100% of the rows the push moves receive a new per-token scale. Linear inputs at blocks 0 to 12 are bitwise identical in the pushed and the twin pass in every engine, as the edit site requires. The extra rounding barely changes how the push propagates: relative to bf16, the non-nominal part of the perturbation is 1.01 at the task-specification positions, 1.04 to 1.05 at the read position and 1.03 to 1.12 at generated tokens 1 to 32 under W16A8, and 0.995 to 1.006 under W8A16. Teacher-forced on 40 iteration-4 twin programs, every engine is very close to bf16 (Table 241). One preregistered fidelity check failed uninformatively: teacher forcing runs one long prefill instead of 20-row decode steps, which itself changes the numerics, so log probabilities of iteration 4's programs could not be matched closely enough to resolve engines at that level; the engine was validated instead by byte identity.

  ## 6.4 Where a ban and an instruction are carried, and where noise acts, in bf16 (Qwen3-8B)

  **Why.** The localization claim predicted, from the route classes of iterations 2 and 3, where the substitute of a ban is carried: in the task-specification states on the prompt-route tasks, at the condition span on the direct-route tasks. Stage A tests that prediction without any training, by moving the states themselves. The same experiment  reran the iteration-4 noise-site comparison in bf16, set state noise at generated tokens against a temperature matched on per-token KL, applied the top-five plan push, and ran the landing contest. Everything ran in one bf16 engine with exact common random numbers on a 16 GB card, with the input embedding table kept in CPU memory; per-slot twin labels agreed with iteration 5's bf16 engine on 0.975 of slots for kth smallest and shortest path and 1.00 for the other tasks. Seven commitments formed an unbroken sha256 chain, and a standard-library script re-derived every headline from raw rows (295 checks, 0 mismatches) while a placebo version of each test failed.

  ### 6.4.1 Stage A: full-state exchange of the ban

  We call a *full-state exchange* the replacement, in the forward pass of the neutral twin, of the residual states at a set of positions and blocks by the states the full ban prompt produces at the same positions; because the twin and the ban have identical token ids from the task text on, every task-specification position aligns. The exchanges covered four block bands at the task-specification positions (0 to 11, 12 to 23, 24 to 35, 0 to 35), a splice of the key-value cache of the condition span (the direct route), and the read position at all 36 blocks. The controls were the twin, a matched-norm random exchange (the state of the twin plus a fresh random direction scaled to the displacement that the ban itself causes per slot, block and position), a placebo that takes a second neutral twin as the source, and an identity exchange. The outcome, as committed before sampling (the first commitment: "share(label == Y | cell) - share(label == Y | TWIN), all samples (invalid rows count as not-Y)"), is the *Y share*: the share of all attempted programs labelled Y, invalid rows counting as not-Y; the *transfer* of a cell is that share minus the share under the twin; a cell counts only if its pass rate is at least 0.8 times that of the twin (the validity gate of the first commitment); and its *recovery* is the transfer divided by that of the full ban. The *correct Y* column added to Tables 244 to 250 counts programs labelled Y that pass every hidden test, because an attempted share counts broken programs as Y: on the grid task the exchange at blocks 0-35 has 14 attempts labelled DFS but 3 correct DFS programs. Each cell has N = 30 on paired slots. Tables 244 to 249 give every cell on the six tasks. (iteration-7 correction)

  The prediction held where the route data said it should, and failed at one task where they said it should not. On shortest path, exchanging the full ban's task-specification states at all blocks into the twin turns 24 of 30 slots from Dijkstra to Bellman-Ford/SPFA (24 of 30 attempts, 21 of 30 correct programs; transfer 0.80, McNemar 24:0, Holm p 7e-7, pass ratio 0.90), while the condition-span splice and the read-position exchange transfer nothing. Blocks 12 to 23 alone carry 0.60 (18 of 30 attempts, 11 of 30 correct programs, at a pass ratio of 0.73, below the 0.8 gate) and blocks 24 to 35 alone 0.37 (11 of 30 attempts, 11 of 30 correct programs); blocks 0 to 11 carry none. On kth smallest the same exchange transfers 0.57 to quickselect (17 of 30 attempts, 16 of 30 correct programs) with every slot leaving the full sort, blocks 0 to 11 alone already transfer 0.40 (12 of 30 attempts, 12 of 30 correct programs), and here the condition span also carries the ban (0.93; 28 of 30 attempts, 25 of 30 correct programs). On connected components every slot leaves union find under the exchange at blocks 12 to 23 or 0 to 35 (off-default transfer 1.00), but only 0.37 to 0.47 land on the ban's BFS (11 and 14 of 30 attempts, 11 and 14 of 30 correct programs) and the rest on DFS. On the grid task, whose route was carried by the prompt states in likelihood and mixed in behaviour, the exchange at all blocks transfers 0.47 toward DFS (14 of 30 attempts, 3 of 30 correct programs, pass ratio 0.59, below the 0.8 gate) and the condition-span splice 0.33 (10 of 30 attempts, 7 of 30 correct programs, pass ratio 0.89), so each carries part of the ban in attempts and only the splice passes the committed validity gate. On the direct-route tasks the condition-span splice alone reproduces the ban (two sum 1.00, 30 of 30 attempts, 30 of 30 correct programs; find duplicate 0.90, 27 of 30 attempts, 26 of 30 correct programs), as predicted, but on two sum the task-specification states also transfer brute force at 0.43 (13 of 30 attempts, 13 of 30 correct programs), above the predicted ceiling of 0.2. The committed verdict is therefore not supported. The secondary predictions hold: the condition span carries at least 0.5 on the direct-route tasks and at most 0.2 on shortest path, the read position carries at most 0.2 everywhere (it carries 0.00 on all six tasks), the placebo moves at most 0.03, and the exchange beats the matched-norm random exchange where it transfers (shortest path 23:0, kth smallest 16:2, connected components 11:0, on attempted Y as preregistered); counted on correct Y instead, a post-hoc contrast added in iteration 7, the same pairs give 21:0 (exact p 9.5e-07), 15:2 (p 2.3e-03) and 11:0 (p 9.8e-04). The ban's information, not the size of the perturbation, is what moves the algorithm. (iteration-7 correction)

  ### 6.4.2 Where noise acts, in bf16

  The site rerun repeated iteration 4's grid on kth smallest and connected components in bf16, at the ban-free unit, with a fresh direction per sample, N = 30 per cell and alpha 1, 2, 4 and 8 (Tables 251 and 252). Noise at the task-specification positions moves the algorithm in bf16: on kth smallest blocks 12 to 23 reach a correct off-default share of 0.37 at alpha 2, and on connected components blocks 0 to 11 reach 0.33 at alpha 4. The read position, the condition span and the late blocks barely move it below alpha 8. On kth smallest the plan site (the task-specification states at blocks 12 to 23, as in iteration 4) beats the read position in paired slots 24:5 (exact p 5.5e-4) and the condition span 22:0, and a Mantel-Haenszel odds ratio [129] within quintiles of the downstream displacement is 4.6 [1.9, 11.3]. Connected components shows a weaker picture: its plan site moves only 0.07 at alpha 2 and 0.17 at alpha 4, the early blocks beat it (4:18, p 0.004), and the read position starts moving at alpha 8 (0.30).

  The committed rule fitted a Firth logistic regression [125] of a correct off-default program on site indicators and the log displacements, so that sites are compared at matched downstream displacement (Tables 253 and 254). It returned the verdict withdrawn, for two reasons. The raw condition-span arm never reaches the plan site's downstream displacement, so it has no common support and its energy-matched arm stood in; and at alpha 8 every plan-site program failed (pass 0.00) while the read position began to move, which erases the read-position contrast in the preregistered model. A post-hoc sensitivity restricted to alpha of 4 or less (before breakage) puts the read position clearly below the plan site on both tasks: beta -3.76 (profile interval [-7.29, -0.47], cluster bootstrap [-8.18, -1.40]) on kth smallest and -4.98 ([-9.77, -0.89]; [-11.48, -1.53]) on connected components. The prefill-site claim is therefore withdrawn as preregistered. Post hoc (alpha of at most 4) the read position is below the task-specification site on both tasks; the condition-span clause fails post hoc as well (beta -1.70 [-3.96, 0.42] on kth smallest; -0.56 [-4.93, 2.91] on connected components, cluster bootstrap; profile intervals [-6.82, 1.16] and [-6.15, 3.41]), so the site of the choice remains open, as the artifact concludes; its rule label withdraws the site claim as specific to 8-bit floating point and states that the site of the choice is open. The half of that label about 8-bit floating point cannot apply: Section 6.3 shows that bf16 reproduces the escapes direction by direction (Spearman 0.96 and 0.87) and that activation rounding adds nothing, so the withdrawal comes from the missing common support and the breakage at alpha 8 in bf16, not from the engine. Noise sites and Stage A agree on the band on kth smallest and disagree on connected components (Table 254b): there noise moves the algorithm most at blocks 0 to 11 (mean 0.19 over alpha 1 to 4 against 0.08 at blocks 12 to 23; 0.33 correct off-default at alpha 4; coefficient +2.51 [1.39, 3.80] against the plan site; paired flips 4:18, p 0.004, between the plan site and blocks 0-11), while the exchange transfers BFS at blocks 12 to 23. The removal of the default there is depth-redundant: the exchange at blocks 0-11 alone takes 0.87 of attempts off union find and at blocks 24-35 alone 0.63. (iteration-7 correction)

  ### 6.4.3 State noise at generated tokens against matched temperature

  The token claim's second half set noise on the residual states of generated tokens 1 to 32 against a temperature applied to the same tokens and bisected to the same per-token KL, which we call decoding at matched departure (Table 255). At alpha 2 the state noise leads on discordant correct off-default flips, 12:6 on kth smallest and 7:3 on connected components, but neither is significant (p 0.24 and 0.34). At alpha 4 the lead on connected components reaches 8:1 (p 0.039), at a pass rate of 0.38 against 0.70. The rule (p below 0.05 on both tasks at alpha 2) is not met: state noise against token temperature is not established in bf16.

  ### 6.4.4 The top-five push in bf16

  On the grid task, iteration 4's top-five direction (from the mean of the five banned centroids toward the mean of the survivors) was applied at the plan site at alpha 1, 2, 4 and 8 (Table 256). At doses of 1 to 8 ban units, which overshoot the forced-prompt manifold, the push breaks programs before it moves the algorithm; an in-manifold dose was not tried: the pass rate falls from 0.67 at alpha 1 to 0.30, 0.03 and 0.00, with at most one correct program other than BFS per cell, so the landing test could not be computed. Projected onto the plane of the first two principal components of the ten forced-prompt centroids (36% and 25% of their variance), the push leaves the forced-prompt manifold: already at alpha 1 it moves farther along the first component than the whole spread of the ten centroids (the four alpha-1 points move from a twin mean of +0.09 to -0.44 on that component, against centroids spread from -0.098 to +0.144). The prompt version of the top-five ban moves the task-specification states from below the centroid cloud into it, between the banned DFS and greedy best-first centroids and the three surviving centroids (bidirectional BFS and two variants of A*), and its behaviour stays inside the banned set (BFS 25, DFS 23 of 50; avoidance 0.00). (iteration-7 correction)

  ### 6.4.5 Who forecasts the landing

  The landing contest scored, on the 21 recorded push-landing events, three forecasts: the base runner-up, the most frequent algorithm other than the default in the instruct twin itself (defined on 7 events), and a teacher-forced ranking of the openings of the catalogue algorithms by the instruct twin, the log-mean-exp likelihood of the first 48 tokens of each algorithm over its reference and forced programs, which we call the opening ranking (Table 257). The base runner-up named 17 of 21 landings and the opening ranking 10. On the 9 events where they disagree the base runner-up wins 8:1 (exact one-sided sign test p 0.020), and its mean log score is higher by 1.62 nats (Wilcoxon p 0.032). Where the twin wrote an alternative, its own minority does as well as the base runner-up (6 of 7; log-score difference 0.02, p 0.69). The comparison is retrospective, because the landings were known when the rule was frozen, and the opening ranking rests on 1 to 6 programs per algorithm. The base model adds information beyond the ranking of openings by the instruct model itself; it does not add information beyond the minority algorithm of the twin where one exists.

  ## 6.5 Gemma: a one-token fork, and Gemma Scope 2 features against difference in means

  **Why Gemma.** Asked one and the same grid-path prompt, gemma-3-4b-it [76] writes DFS about 70% of the time and BFS about 30%, so it offers what Qwen3-8B never does: the request's BFS-against-DFS contrast inside one prompt, with no ban or instruction to confound it. Gemma Scope 2 provides sparse autoencoders on the residual stream after each block, trained on this instruct model, so the feature claim needs no transfer test. Qwen-3 transcoders for circuit tracing exist as well [123], but they would have to study a choice Qwen3-8B does not make naturally. The experiment  asked where the choice forks, whether it can be read from the internals beyond what the visible text already says, and whether the SAE features steer it better than plain baselines: a difference-in-means direction, the raw residual, random features, isotropic directions, DAS and prompting. It used the residual-stream SAEs at layers 9, 17, 22 and 29 (16k latents, at the release's medium sparsity), one 16 GB card and exact common random numbers, under two hash-chained commitments.

  **Natural splits.** Over 200 samples per task, the grid prompt gave DFS 139 and BFS 61 (Wilson interval for DFS 0.63 to 0.75), with DFS on 134 of 172 correct programs (Table 258). The choice depends on the template: BFS takes 6 to 18 of 40 attempts per template. Substring search (naive 173, built-in find 27) and first and last position (linear scan 170, binary search 29) split as well. Labels agreed with iteration 5's Gemma rows on 0.94 of the grid slots and 1.00 of the substring slots.

  **The instrument gate.** Each SAE was spliced into the forward pass on three corpora: the model's own programs, generic text and LeetCode prompts. A layer passed if its increase in cross-entropy and its fraction of variance unexplained on the model's programs were at most 1.5 times those on generic text (Table 259). Layers 22 and 29 passed; layer 9 failed the cross-entropy ratio and layer 17 the variance ratio by 0.0001, so their results are descriptive. On generic text the mean number of active latents per token was 57 to 64, slightly above the quoted medium band of 30 to 60.

  **The plan is a single-token fork.** Prefix resampling with change-point detection, the method of forking-path analyses [30, 31], located the fork: 24 base paths, 16 prefix lengths, 8 continuations each and a refinement, 3,712 continuations in all, scored by a partial-code labeller that agreed with the full labeller on 200 of 200 programs. Every one of 12 BFS base paths had a significant change point with a rise of at least 0.4, at prefix lengths 16 to 36. In 177 of 200 programs the first 32 tokens are identical (the code fence, `def solve(grid, start, goal):`, `rows = len(grid)`, `cols = len(grid[0])` and an indent), and the next token decides (Table 260): ` visited` leads to DFS (BFS probability 0.011 over 1,409 continuations), while a blank line, `if`, `queue` or `q` lead to BFS (0.95 to 1.00). The first token that identifies the algorithm in code comes a median of 138 tokens after the fork (10th to 90th percentile 80 to 181). The fork index was chosen by the token class with the most mutual information with the outcome (0.62 bits at index 32), after the first median rule landed on a deterministic indentation token; the change was made before the second commitment.

  *Executed but not reported until iteration 7.* The empty-prefix unit test of the fork failed mildly: continuations from the empty prefix give BFS 0.38 (73 of 192) against the natural 0.305 [0.245, 0.372] (outside the interval; exact binomial p 0.028 against 0.305), so the resampled continuations are slightly richer in BFS than the natural samples. The deviation log records what did not run: the clamp read-back and matched-norm realisation tests as separate unit tests (the matched norm is imposed by construction in the clamp code, `src/clamp.py` (file name restored, iteration-8 correction), and the realised norm of each edit is logged per row); the clamp-cell overlay on the generated-position panel; the fork and the cross-prompt readouts of two further bench tasks (dropped in order); and per-sample displacement at generated tokens 1-32 (prefill displacement at blocks 11-33 is logged). (iteration-7 correction)

  **Readable beyond the text, at the fork, but not specifically through the SAE.** Within one prompt, decodability before the first identifying token is at ceiling for every method, the visible-text control included (balanced accuracy 1.00 at all four layers), so the SAE has no advantage there; at the fork itself the test is undefined, because 185 of 200 samples share their prefix with a sample of the other class. Across prompts, the experiment built 120 neutral prompt variants by changing nouns and measured each variant's fork log-odds of BFS, which we write y (mean -0.92 nats, SD 0.67; the sampled BFS share tracks it at Spearman 0.65 over 60 variants of 10 samples). A Lasso on layer-29 SAE codes at the fork position predicts held-out y with R-squared 0.66, against 0.18 for a text-only model (difference 0.49, 95% interval 0.26 to 0.65, permutation p 0.003), above the difference-in-means readout (0.34) and a 16-component PCA of the raw residual (0.56) (Table 261). That meets the preregistered bar. Two checks outside the preregistration qualify it: a tuned ridge on the raw layer-29 residual reaches 0.72, and ridge on the same SAE codes reaches at most 0.09. Beside the Lasso, the standardised ridge on the same layer-29 SAE codes reaches R-squared 0.15 against 0.086 for a template-plus-noun-norm control (delta 0.064, below the preregistered 0.10 bar); the unstandardised SAE ridge ranges from -0.76 to 0.06 across penalties while the raw ridge stays at 0.70 to 0.72, which is why the SAE advantage depends on the estimator. Moreover, a linear readout of the fork log-odds from the residual at the fork position is close to a next-token readout, so the raw-residual 0.72 shows that the next-token distribution is linearly encoded there, not that a plan is; no logit-lens control of matched capacity was run. At the task-specification positions, before any response token, the SAE codes do no better than the text (0.18). (iteration-7 correction)

  **Steering: the features move the fork, difference in means moves it more, and edits toward BFS cost correctness.** We call an *SAE clamp* setting the k latents that best separate forced-BFS from forced-DFS prompts (input-selected) to their BFS-class mean at the fork position; output-scored latents are chosen instead by their attribution to the fork's logit difference, and the two sets of 20 share 2 latents. At the fork position of layer 22, edits at matched norm moved y by +4.04 nats for the difference-in-means direction, +1.78 for the SAE clamp of the top 20 input-selected latents, +0.51 for 20 random latents and +0.12 for an isotropic direction. Table 261b gives the whole dose-response sweep over the 120 prompt variants (11,280 measurements), at the fork and at the task-specification positions. In generation (N = 50 paired slots), the twin wrote BFS in 13 programs; the SAE clamp raised this to 30 (top 20 latents) and 36 (top 50), the difference-in-means edit at the same norm to 46 and 49, and random latents to 21 (Table 262). Edits toward BFS at the fork lowered the pass rate from 0.84 for the twin to 0.58 and 0.48 for the top-20 and top-50 SAE clamps and 0.32 and 0.16 for difference in means (0.60 to 0.78 for the other BFS-ward fork edits, 0.00 for the DAS interchange), except the SAE top-5 clamp (18 BFS of 50, pass 0.84), so the preregistered outcome, correct BFS programs, shows no significant effect anywhere after Holm correction, and no feature claim is made. The preregistered feature rule (SAE target-correct count at least the difference-in-means count, at a pass rate of at least 0.8 times the twin's) is also met by random latents at k = 50 (9 against 7, pass 0.76), so it cannot discriminate here. The informative comparisons are on attempted BFS, and they are descriptive: the SAE clamp beats the twin (17:0 and 23:0 discordant slots, p 1.5e-5 and 2.4e-7) and random latents (15:0, p 6.1e-5), and difference in means beats the SAE clamp at matched norm (16:0, p 3.1e-5). At matched effect on y rather than matched norm, difference in means and the SAE clamp shift the plan equally (32 against 30 BFS, p 0.50; 34 against 36, p 0.63) and difference in means keeps slightly more programs correct (13 against 9, 14 against 10). Edits at the task-specification positions do nothing (12 to 19 BFS against 13). Steering toward DFS works cleanly for both (SAE 47 of 50, difference in means 50 of 50, against 37 for the twin; pass 0.98 to 1.00). Difference-in-means steering of a code model's choice of language and library has shown the same trade-off, with overly strong interventions reducing output quality [130]. AxBench found simple baselines ahead of SAE steering [34], and a 2026 reanalysis puts SAEs close to AxBench's reference when latents are selected and labelled by a supervised pipeline [131]; here, at comparable norms, neither the input-selected nor the output-scored clamp reached the difference-in-means edit (Table 261b). (iteration-7 correction)

  **DAS moves the fork log-odds within the controls it had, and forcing it breaks the program.** DAS at the fork position of layer 22, with forced-BFS prompts as sources, moved held-out y by +8.8, +9.5 and +9.8 nats at ranks 1, 2 and 4, against -0.08 to +0.05 for random subspaces of the same rank (Table 263). The shuffled-source control was uninformative as built, because every source was a forced-BFS prompt. In generation the rank-4 interchange made 50 of 50 programs BFS and 0 of 50 passed. Stated within its controls, a rank-1 DAS subspace fitted on forced-BFS sources moves the held-out fork log-odds by 8.8 nats (random subspaces of the same rank -0.08 to +0.05); because every source was forced-BFS, the shuffled-source control is uninformative by construction (10.1 nats); no random-initialisation or target-shuffled control was run; and the rank-4 interchange gives BFS in 50 of 50 attempts with 0 of 50 programs passing, so this does not show that the choice is one-dimensional. With unrestricted alignment maps interchange accuracy reaches 100% even on randomly initialised language models (Sutter et al., Table 277 row 14), so the fit stays uninterpretable until those controls run; pushing hard costs correctness, as subspace interventions can when they leave the model's natural range [122]. (iteration-7 correction)

  **The top-five prohibition in a model that writes two algorithms.** Banning the five most common grid algorithms (BFS, DFS, IDDFS, A* and greedy best-first, which share one catalogue label here) left no program outside the banned set: avoidance 0.00, as in Qwen3-8B in iteration 2 (Table 265). The ban pushed Gemma from its default DFS to BFS (10 to 41 of 50; McNemar 32:1, p 7.9e-9) and cut the pass rate from 0.86 to 0.38. In actual activation coordinates (PCA, Isomap with k = 10 and classical MDS of layers 17 and 22, raw and SAE codes), the top-five prompt states sit next to the banned A* and greedy cluster (Table 266); among all 15 ways of splitting the six catalogue centroids into four banned and two survivors, the observed split ranks first in three of the four spaces (rank share 0.067) and third in the fourth (0.20). The prohibition lands inside the banned region, not at its edge or on the opposite side. The single-name bans of BFS and DFS left the banned algorithm in 11 and 8 of 50 programs, and the forced prompts gave BFS 50 of 50 (38 correct) and DFS 50 of 50 (45 correct).

  ## 6.6 The plan in words: a natural language autoencoder on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct

  **Why.** The request names NLA as an instrument, and the release of NLA checkpoints for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct [124] made it possible to ask, in words, whether the residual stream states before the first code token say which algorithm will be written. The experiment  read layer-20 states with the released verbalizer and reconstructor pair, judged the explanations blind, and tested an edit of the explanation as a steering vector. Published verbalizers of the same kind include LatentQA [117] and SelfIE [118], and a 2026 analysis of a released Qwen-2.5-7B verbalizer found that only a small share of an explanation's specific claims are ones the reconstruction depends on [119]. Pre-registration was a sha256 chain of four commitments, each preceding its samples; the parts added after the committed nulls are marked exploratory.

  **Behaviour.** Over eight tasks, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct defaults to BFS, Dijkstra (0.88), a hash map (0.98), a hash set (0.71), DFS for connected components (0.62, where Qwen3-8B writes union find), the naive scan and binary search; kth smallest has no default (quickselect 0.40, size-k heap 0.34) and failed the style re-gate. The model mostly ignores bans (Table 267). Only two sum gave a substitute (brute force in 32 of 46 correct programs). On connected components a ban of DFS raised DFS from 29 to 43 correct programs, with 15 paired slots flipping from union find to DFS, the rebound that naming a forbidden concept can cause [7, 53]. Every one of the 70 programs written under the fourth template attempted the banned default. The shortest path semantic seed barely moved the model (Dijkstra 28, Bellman-Ford 6, against 38 and 5 for the twin). The labellers recognised 51 of 51 references, and the style re-gate passed on 7 of 8 tasks against two blind code judges.

  **The instrument gate.** The extraction convention that matches the training code reads the output of block 20; it reaches a fraction of variance explained of 0.695 on the reference set against 0.580 for the convention in the release's example, and 0.695 is within 0.06 of the released 0.752. Generic web text and chat give 0.78 and 0.79. Code is out of distribution for this NLA: LeetCode prompts 0.45, HumanEval+ prompts 0.39, CLRS traces 0.33. On the task states the fraction of variance explained, with the reference-set variance as denominator, is 0.512, so the gate's verdict is partial (Table 268).

  **Table 268.** Fraction of variance explained of the layer-20 reconstructions on the task states, by position (reference-set denominator). Source: NLA experiment `results/gate.json`.

  **The NLA never names the planned algorithm before the code.** Two blind judges from different families (Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite and Mistral Small 3.2, both scoring 1.00 on calibration; a third model resolved 1,064 disagreements) mapped each of 6,180 explanations to a catalogue algorithm or to none named (Table 269). Every preregistered readout at the end-of-prompt positions is exactly zero (Table 270). On ban prompts, explanations named the substitute in 0 of 16 states (only two sum had a substitute, so this test is underpowered); on twin prompts they named the default in 0 of 112, as did the text-only reader; on ban failures they named the default the model still writes in 0 of 96. The positive control failed too: on forced `Implement Y` prompts the explanations called Y planned in 0 of 7 tasks, while the text-only reader did so on all of them, and they mentioned the algorithm named in the prompt in 0.7% of cases. The explanations describe the local format line, such as a request for no explanation or a Python code block to follow, and confabulate the task (Fibonacci, medians, prime numbers); 4,733 of 5,700 judged explanations name no algorithm at all. At generated tokens the NLA sometimes names the realised algorithm before the visible text identifies it (up to 0.28 at token 8 under the ban), but an outside reader who sees only the prompt and prefix predicts the realised algorithm better, per sample (0.25 against 0.07; exact McNemar 20:88, p 2e-11 when the 364 units are treated as independent). The units are nested in 104 samples and 5 task clusters: the task-cluster bootstrap interval of the difference is [-0.35, 0.02], with one unit per sample (the first in position order, 104 samples) the contrast is 0:25 (exact p 6.0e-08), a median over 2,000 draws of one random unit per sample of 4:29 (p 1.9e-05; 1.00 of draws below 0.05), a sign test on the per-sample differences 12:38 (p 3.1e-04) and a Durkalski-adjusted McNemar with samples as clusters p 6.5e-05. The samples share 5 task clusters, and with 5 clusters no cluster-level test can reach a two-sided p below 0.0625, so the evidence at the task level is inconclusive whatever the sample-level p. (iteration-7 correction)

  **The information is local and fades within a sentence (exploratory).** To tell an instrument limit from information that fades along the prompt, the same NLA and judges read states at the token that names the algorithm inside the condition sentence and at the final period of that sentence (220 states, 660 explanations; Table 271). At the name token the explanations mention the algorithm in 80% of forced and 89% of ban states, and they respect the negation: they call it planned in 48% of forced states and in 6% of ban states. Two to eight tokens later, at the end of the sentence, the mention rates fall to 27% and 6%, and about 170 tokens later, at the end of the prompt, to 0.7%. The null therefore says that the pre-code positions do not carry the algorithm choice in a form this NLA puts into words, not that the instrument is blind.

  **The preregistered verbal edit fails at the prefill site.** The causal arm replaced the default's name in a twin explanation by an algorithm Y the model writes on request, reconstructed both versions, and patched the difference into the layer-20 states at the last four prompt positions at doses of 1, 2 and 4 (N = 30 paired slots per cell). It failed on all four tasks (Table 272). The edits barely move the reconstruction (cosine 0.9992 between the edited and unedited reconstructions; 0.04 of the state norm per position; Table 273), the unedited round trip at 0.8 of the norm propagates downstream but moves nothing, and all 15 prefill cells per task stay within 0 to 3 slots of the unedited control. The edit direction is nearly orthogonal to the forced-state difference in means (median cosine 0.09).

  **At the generated-token site and large doses, the verbal edit steers two of four tasks (exploratory).** After the committed nulls, the experiment extended the doses and moved the edit to the read position plus generated tokens 1 to 64 (Tables 274 and 275). On find duplicate the edit at dose 8 (about 0.3 of the state norm at each position) raised Floyd cycle detection from 0.28 to 0.76 (25:1 over 50 paired slots), replicated on fresh slots (15 of 20, 13:0, p 2e-4), and beat a matched random push (28:1), an unrelated-word edit built the same way (12:1, p 0.003) and a norm-matched round trip (13:1, p 0.002); at dose 16 the programs broke (pass 0.37). On two sum brute force rose from 0 to 10 of 50 at dose 8 and to 23 of 30 at dose 16 with a pass rate of 0.90, while the random push never moved it. On connected components only the forced-state difference in means steered (union find 0.80 at dose 16, 15:1); on substring search nothing steered short of breaking the program. The prefill site stayed inert even at dose 16 or at the natural norm of the difference in means. Asking for the algorithm in the prompt remained the ceiling (forced adherence 0.90 to 1.00 on all four tasks), as the AxBench comparison of prompting and steering predicts [34]. The NLA paper itself reports that editing a plan explanation and steering at one token succeeds roughly half the time; this run's success on two of four tasks is of the same kind and is not a reliable control knob.

  In activation space (exploratory), read-position states projected on the plane of the forced-prompt states show every forced algorithm in its own region, with twin and ban prompts apart from all of them. Relative to the algorithm-specific directions of the forced prompts, the ban moves the state toward the banned default's own direction on two sum (+0.13), find duplicate (+0.26) and first and last position (+0.15), as the ban sentence names the default, and toward an alternative on shortest path (Bellman-Ford +0.13), connected components (BFS +0.23), substring search and the grid task (DFS +0.18). The novelty audit found 10 correct programs labelled other in every arm: 8 labeller misses (six kth smallest counting sorts built on a counter, two boolean seen-arrays) and 2 degenerate programs, 0 novel. Spend was about USD 2.0 on OpenRouter (NLA judges with calibration, two interrupted passes, the local control and the novelty audit USD 1.82; code judges for the bench tasks USD 0.11 and for the path tasks USD 0.10) and about 2.0 GPU hours on one 24 GB NVIDIA Ada GPU (68 minutes of generation for behaviour and the committed causal arm, about 27 for the exploratory causal cells, 16 for 6,180 explanations and about 8 for reconstruction passes and the state cache).

  ## 6.7 Positioning against published work

  The positioning audit , dated 2026-10-22, extended the audits of iterations 4 and 5 to this iteration's claims. A protocol frozen and stamped before the first call drove 126 logged searches over seven lanes, from 2,191 raw hits to 1,820 unique records, 1,401 in the window, and 75 claim rows scored on the occupancy rubric for 67 papers: 3 occupying, 66 adjacent and 6 irrelevant. Its 123 new quotes from 94 sources matched the cached source text and were re-matched by an independent live pass. Table 276 gives the verdict per claim, and Table 277 condenses the 65 rows of its neighbour table; the verbatim quotes are in the audit's evidence files.

  **Table 276.** Lane verdicts for the iteration-6 claims as of 2026-10-22. Source: positioning audit `research_report.md`.

  | Claim | Lane verdict | Deciding neighbours |
  |-|-|-|
  | Localization: a low-rank causal plan variable, found by interchange or DAS, decides which algorithm Qwen3-8B writes, validated by generation | partly occupied: the method is occupied, the object is open; the flag for a published localization of algorithm choice did not fire, narrowly | DAS and Boundless DAS [110, 111]; MIB [52]; CDAS, DAS steering validated by generation on refusal and a backdoor [112]; prompt cues only for algorithm choice in code [1] |
  | Mediation: the plan subspace mediates which random pushes switch the algorithm | adjacent only | pre-generation planning subspaces; output-sensitive steering components |

  Three of the audit's flags bear on what this run may claim. No source localizes which algorithm a code model will write by interchange or DAS and validates it by scoring the generated programs, so that combination is open; the method itself is DAS. Editing an NLA explanation of a plan and steering with the reconstruction is published, so the NLA arm is a replication on a new object. Steering under quantization has been compared with full precision only for weight-only 8-bit integer and 4-bit NormalFloat quantization, with activations kept in 16-bit floating point [116]; no source found measures how dynamic per-token activation rounding changes the effect of random perturbations, which is the question the engine control answered, in the negative. The audit also recorded that community NLAs exist for Qwen3-8B at layer 24, that circuit-tracer ships Qwen-3 transcoders including 8B [123] (so the choice of Gemma for the feature claim needs its reason, which is the natural within-prompt split), and that Gemma Scope 2 dates from 22 December 2025 with instruct SAEs initialised from the pretrained ones.

  ## 6.8 Planned but not run

  The seventh artifact of the strategy never existed. It was to fit DAS subspaces of rank 1 to 16 at one layer of the task-specification positions in bf16 Qwen3-8B on three training templates and confirm them on two held-out templates (Stage B of the localization claim), test whether a fresh random direction's energy in that subspace predicts its effect (the mediation claim), interpolate and extrapolate the plan coordinate between algorithms (the discreteness claim), measure the plan coordinate's variance across temperatures (the first half of the token claim), resample the plan per generation as a diversity knob (the resampling claim), and draw the request's manifold of algorithms in the fitted plan subspace, with the top-five prohibition placed on it. It was lost at the planning stage: the planning agent returned no plan, so no experiment ran. These claims are untested and open; nothing in this report is a result for them, null or otherwise. The only DAS result of the iteration is Gemma's, at the fork position (Section 6.5). The deviation log of the Gemma experiment adds what it did not run: the clamp read-back and matched-norm realisation tests as separate unit tests (the matched norm is imposed by construction in the clamp code, `src/clamp.py` (file name restored, iteration-8 correction), and the realised norm of each edit is logged per row); the clamp-cell overlay on the generated-position panel; the fork and the cross-prompt readouts of two further bench tasks (dropped in order); and per-sample displacement at generated tokens 1-32 (prefill displacement at blocks 11-33 is logged). (iteration-7 correction)

  ## 6.9 Comparisons across this iteration's experiments

  **Where the choice is held, model by model.** The three internal experiments measured different quantities at different sites, so their results are stated per model and per quantity (Table 279) rather than as one map. In Qwen3-8B what was measured is where an external ban or instruction is carried: exchanging the task-specification states alone reproduces the substitute of the ban on shortest path (Bellman-Ford/SPFA in 24 of 30 attempts, 21 of 30 correct programs) and a forced instruction on shortest path (30 of 30 attempts, 30 of 30 correct) and connected components (BFS in 28 of 30 attempts, 24 of 30 correct), while on the direct-route tasks the condition span carries it; Qwen3-8B's natural choice was not measured, because it writes one algorithm per prompt. In gemma-3-4b-it, which writes two algorithms for one prompt, the natural choice is made at one generated token after a shared opening; task-specification edits and readouts barely reach it, and the read position was never read or edited (Gemma's SPEC site is a mean over the task-specification positions, which exclude the read position). In Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct no verbalisable plan was found at pre-code positions: the NLA names the algorithm at the token where the prompt names it and not 170 tokens later, and edits work only at the generated-token site. The read position is inert as a carrier in Qwen3-8B (its exchange transfers nothing on six tasks) and reads only the format line in the NLA; Gemma's read position was not measured. The finding of iteration 3 that a ban gives way at the opening of the program body and the fork of Gemma at response index 32 point at the same moment from two models: the first statement of the body that is specific to an algorithm, after an opening shared by every algorithm.
