  **Established.** Temperature applied at the fork moves the algorithm mix exactly as the fork's logits and token map predict (mean absolute error 0.010 to 0.047 on five units in two families), and a law composed over one or two forks found blind predicts global temperature sweeps on held-out Gemma units (0.033 and 0.014) as well as on Qwen3-8B (0.029 to 0.054): on 5 of 6 units the fork tokens predict temperature's effect on the algorithm mix, but the flat law is better on valid anagram (0.030 against 0.054), algorithm-level tempering is better on substring search (0.023 against 0.033), the law beats the flat law on only 4 of 6 units (sign test p 0.34), and on Llama's grid task every predictor fails (0.142) (iteration-9 correction). The fork's entropy lies above the 90th percentile of the twin's per-token entropies in all 209 twin samples that reach it, though it can be small in absolute terms (median 0.13 nats on connected components); it is the single highest-entropy position among the first 64 tokens on 44 of 44 (Gemma), 32 of 39 (minimum spanning tree) and 21 of 39 (valid anagram) slots, but on 2 of 50 (connected components) and 0 of 37 (trapped rain water), the two units where a highest-entropy rule misses it (iteration-9 correction). Post-training widens the fork margin by 2 to 13 nats on the collapsed tasks and leaves phrasing positions almost unchanged, so the instruct default is a sharpened second or third choice of the base model, not its mean; the concentration of post-training shifts at base-entropy forks is prior work (Cantarero et al. [142]; Sparse but Critical [143]), and the contribution here is the algorithm-level reading on code (iteration-9 correction). A rank-4 edit at the fork moves the written algorithm in both families. Under the committed rule it is a sufficient handle in Gemma and NO HANDLE at Qwen3-8B's fork, where the edit toward BFS writes BFS in 29 of 30 programs but 24 fail (pass 0.20 against 0.83; 5:0 against random, p 0.063). Neither passes the specificity controls: permuted labels, an untrained network or matched random components reproduce most of each effect (iteration-9 correction). Late fork-position components of Qwen3-8B (validated MLPs at layers 26, 27, 28, 30 and 32, and heads such as head 14 of layer 33 and head 28 of layer 34) carry the fork logit; the committed motif test reads different motif from Gemma's circuit (condition share 0.01 against Gemma's band [0.21, 0.51]; fork-stack depth 0.86 against [0.45, 0.80]), and the layer-0 MLP at the condition span rests on the 20 pair prompts because its held-out edit was never applied (iteration-9 correction). In Gemma, prompting with the dial's prefill fails because the prefill is off-policy for the forced prompt and selects a BFS implementation that skips the wall check; in free generation the dial and prompting are within each other's range. Among ten open configurations, only a 32B model with thinking on obeys a five-name ban often, and its catalogue survivors are all the algorithm farthest from the banned five on its alias-named manifold, where its alias analysis (Section 8.8) finds that g follows alias overlap across algorithms (rho -0.61, exact p 0.009) but not clearly within them (stratified p 0.46 on content words; 0.057 on the model's BPE tokens): names and mechanisms are confounded there, and the name-free manifolds of TP-G decide (iteration-9 correction).

  **Ruled out.** A certified low-rank variable for the algorithm at the fork under the committed controls, in either family. Temperature at the fork as a route to two ideas on a collapsed task without breakage. The edge prediction for the survivors of the top-five prohibition on the model that obeys, on the alias-named manifold (iteration-9 correction). The explanation of iteration 7 that ' queue' programs in Gemma fail by slowness (they fail a wall case). Iteration 7's lean of the minimum spanning tree sweep (a property of its streams). Fitted subspaces as the channel of iteration 4's random pushes (clamping removes nothing; the prospective association is 0.09).

  **Dead ends.** The blind locator at T 1 cannot find the fork of a collapsed task, because resampling never leaves the default. The window of 16 tokens at the boundary units breaks the programs before it can test anything. Steering at dose 2 saturates both the circuit and its random control. The transcoder attribution graph was dropped again, now because Qwen3-8B's transcoders need about 96.5 GB. The two Llama bench units of the temperature law and the band and minimum spanning tree sites of the DAS experiment were dropped under time boxes.

  **Not run.** The task band of Gemma and DAS at minimum spanning tree weight; a ban-against-twin contrast for the Qwen3-8B circuit; the engine check of the DAS experiment against iterations 6 and 7; a feature-level account at either fork; plan resampling and the placement of top-five survivors in DAS coordinates on the grid task, carried from iteration 7.

Sparse but Critical is an ICLR 2026 paper, MIB an ICML 2025 paper (arXiv v2), and Many Circuits, One Mechanism carries the journal reference Transactions on Machine Learning Research, 2026 (arXiv v2), which confirms the venue Table 92c gives it. The arXiv pages of Manifold Steering, The Invisible Lottery and the denial-prompting study state no venue, so the venues that earlier sections give them (an ICML 2026 workshop spotlight, ICML 2026, and NAACL, which reference [23] dates 2024) are carried, not verified (3 venue statements left unverified, none contradicted). No iteration-8 result is called first.

  ## 8.11 What the next iteration takes from this one

  Four leads remain. First, the controls show that a large enough push at a late fork-position site flips a collapsed fork whatever its direction, so a variable, if there is one, has to be sought where the full state carries the class and with doses below saturation: the block-24 fit of Qwen3-8B passes every off-manifold control and fails only specificity, and the circuit separates from random components at dose 0.5. Second, the composed temperature law passed on held-out Gemma units but scored only three held-out units, and it fails where a family reaches its fork through many openings (Llama); more held-out units, and a law that sums over openings, are what would settle it. Third, the top-five prohibition placed survivors on one model with one landing algorithm, which cannot reach significance at the level of algorithms; tasks where an obeying model writes several catalogue survivors are needed for the edge-against-opposite question, on a manifold whose prompts do not name the algorithm (TP-G), because on the alias-named manifold names and mechanisms are confounded (iteration-9 correction). Fourth, no route has produced a correct novel algorithm. The forced branches show that the known ideas a model does not write sit at deep ranks of the fork. Evolutionary search on a task whose catalogue already covers the known techniques remains the only route left untried.

  # Iteration 9: names against mechanisms under a prohibition, the top-five landing with and without names, where post-training sharpened the fork, and the record repaired

  ## 9.1 Why this iteration ran what it ran

  **The review of the iteration-8 record.** The review was blocking. It raised five items that had to be fixed before any new claim and two minor items. The first concerned the circuit of Section 8.5. Three passages said that Qwen3-8B's fork circuit has the same shape as Gemma's, although the committed motif test read different motif (condition-span share 0.01 against Gemma's band [0.21, 0.51], fork-stack depth 0.86 against [0.45, 0.80]). The layer-0 condition-span MLP, the node behind the injection story, scored exactly zero on all ten held-out prompts, because the cache of span means only accepted pair prompts of the same template and so never applied the edit. The second item found that the DAS verdict of Section 8.4 called the rank-4 edit a steering handle in both families, while the committed rule reads NO HANDLE at Qwen3-8B's fork: the edit toward BFS writes BFS in 29 of 30 programs and 24 of them fail. The third found a superlative in the closing. The fork is above the 90th percentile of per-token entropy in every sample, but it is the single highest-entropy position on three of five units only; two neighbouring sentences also overreached, on Llama's 0.63 bits and on the scope of the temperature law. The fourth was about novelty. The base sub-arm of Section 8.7 parallels Cantarero et al. [142] and Sparse but Critical [143], which the record did not cite, and only two iteration-8 sections set their claims against published work. The fifth questioned the method behind the answer to the request's top-five question. The manifold of Section 8.8 is built from prompts that name each algorithm by an alias, and its classes follow the words the aliases share with the banned names, so "opposite" may be a distance between names. The minor items asked for the Gemma comparator sentence to say that min-p and block-start temperature were never run on Gemma, and for figure markers with six-field captions for the iteration-8 geometry figures that had none.

  **The hypothesis update.** Eight iterations had narrowed what a code model's "idea" is to a small known repertoire, decided at one or two tokens and sharpened by post-training. The iteration-9 hypothesis states this as a *repertoire account* in seven parts. Four restate what is measured: where the algorithm is decided (the fork), what writes the fork's odds (a late stack of fork-position components, with no certified variable), how sampling acts (only through the fork) and how post-training acts (it sharpens the fork). The other three are the repertoire bound (no route has produced a correct novel algorithm), lexical compliance at exhaustion, and discovery with an evaluator. The sixth part is new and is the iteration's main claim. When a ban leaves a known alternative, the model changes mechanism (BFS to DFS). When a ban names the whole repertoire, the model complies on names and keeps a banned mechanism under another name or container. The survivors of an exhaustive ban should then sit opposite the banned set on a manifold of names and at its edge, or inside it, on a manifold of mechanisms. The expectation had concrete grounds. Across ten configurations, 55% to 100% of programs that use a banned mechanism under a five-name ban carry no banned name (Section 8.8). Unit-weight Dijkstra and FIFO SPFA expand a unit grid in BFS order by construction, and wavefront propagation is BFS, so 14 of the 17 screen survivors of iteration 8 were candidates for BFS under a non-banned name before any trace was read.

  The claims were preregistered in four groups, each with a sha256 commitment before its first decisive sample. We call them by their content. Four *names-against-mechanisms claims* are primary:

  - the *rename gap*: over every program written under a five-name ban in earlier artifacts, lexical compliance minus mechanistic compliance is at least 0.3 pooled and positive in at least 7 of 10 configurations;
  - the *survivor reading*: at least 0.6 of Qwen3-32B's correct survivors are in a banned expansion class;
  - the *exhaustion curve*: under cumulative bans of k = 1 to 5 names, mechanistic compliance falls with k while lexical compliance stays at or above 0.7, with a gap of at least 0.4 at k = 5;
  - the *name-free landing*: unit-weight Dijkstra lands at the edge on a manifold of programs and on a manifold of name-free descriptions, and stays opposite on the named and name-only manifolds.

  The secondary family holds rotated ban sets, a second task (weighted shortest path), the discovery claims (an evaluator-guided search on online bin packing and constructive TSP) and the record repair. It also holds the *sharpening claims*: base against instruct at the fork in Gemma and Llama, the components that carry the sharpening in Qwen3-8B, and the held-out rerun of the circuit's layer-0 node.

  **The strategy.** Seven artifacts were planned and four ran (Table 418). The record audit answered every review item in place and tested on CPU whether the named manifold's distances follow the aliases. A rename experiment built a name-blind runtime tracer of expansion order, retraced every earlier five-name-ban program, and sampled cumulative, rotated and described bans. A geometry experiment rebuilt the ten-algorithm manifold four ways, with and without names, and placed the survivors on each. A base-model experiment measured the fork's sharpening in Gemma and Llama, patched base outputs into Qwen3-8B at the fork, and reran the circuit's held-out arm. The second-task experiment, the bin-packing search and the TSP replication were planned but not run (Section 9.6).

  **The circuit's held-out arm.** Recomputed from the stored rows, the layer-0 condition-span MLP has a held-out effect of exactly 0.00 under ablation and under steering, and all 20 stored held-out rows of that node and its 50 random comparators are exactly zero. The edit was never applied. The cache that supplies the condition-span means takes them only from pair prompts of the same template. The held-out prompts use five templates that no pair prompt uses, so none of the ten held-out prompts found a mean, and the edit function returned nothing.   **Positioning.** The new Section 8.10b sets the seven iteration-8 claims against their nearest published neighbours (Table 416b), with every venue checked live: Cantarero et al. [142] appear as two NeurIPS 2026 workshop posters, Sparse but Critical [143] is an ICLR 2026 paper, MIB an ICML 2025 paper, Position-aware Automatic Circuit Discovery [145] an ACL 2025 long paper, and Many Circuits, One Mechanism [146] a TMLR 2026 paper. The base sub-arm is narrowed to what is new: the algorithm-level outcome on code at a counterfactually located fork, and the reading that the default is the base model's second or third choice, sharpened.

  **The alias test.** The audit computed, on CPU from iteration 8's stored states and geodesics, how the geodesic distance g of each non-banned alias to the banned five relates to the number of content words the alias shares with a banned alias. Its four gates passed; the last recomputed the k-nearest-neighbour geodesics independently from the stored states and matched the stored k = 15 matrix at Spearman 1.000. Across the 15 aliases, g falls as overlap rises (Spearman -0.61 at k 15, exact p 0.0093 over 360,360 assignments; -0.77 at k 10, p 0.0007). Within algorithms the relation is not detected (three algorithms; underpowered) (iteration-10 correction): the stratified test, which permutes overlap only among the three aliases of one algorithm, gives -0.12 (p 0.46 over 216 effective relabelings), and the slope of a fixed-effects fit has the wrong sign (+2.36, p 0.78). With only five algorithm centroids, the centroid-level Spearman of -0.63 cannot reach significance (p 0.133; the attainable floor is 0.033). The committed reading is that g follows alias overlap across algorithms, but the pattern is carried by algorithm identity: on this manifold names and mechanisms are confounded. A sensitivity on the model's own BPE tokens gives a borderline within-algorithm statistic (-0.50, p 0.057; -0.40, p 0.11 at k 10), so a small name effect inside algorithms is not excluded. The placebos fail as required and a planted name effect is recovered (Table 424). The figure of Section 8.8 plots the alias-level points and the classical MDS of the stored k = 15 geodesics.

They differ from the artifact files in small ways that each caption states: the fork-dose states are coloured by the frozen labeller's program label with the arms pooled, and the DAS figure shows the stored group centroids of its MDS embedding, because the per-prompt coordinates of that figure are stored only in the artifact's tensor caches.   ## 9.3 Do banned models rename their default? Compliance by name and by expansion order

  The rename experiment  read every program written under a ban of path algorithms three ways. *Lexical compliance* means that no banned alias appears in the code or its comments. The *name-level label* is the algorithm the program is called or judged to be, from iteration 8's labeller and gated judges. *Mechanistic compliance* means that the program's expansion order, measured at runtime on 40 probe grids without reading any name, is not the order of a banned algorithm. The five banned names (BFS, DFS, IDDFS, A* and greedy best-first) map to four banned order classes: BFS order, DFS order, iterative deepening and heuristic order. The task was iteration 1's grid path task with the frozen 48-case hidden suite and the 41-case suite of iteration 1. Every prompt, cell, seed, rule and threshold was committed in a sha256 chain before the rows it governs: three commitments and seven amendments, each logged before the rows it touched.

  **The tracer failed its gate, so the names-against-mechanisms numbers are descriptive.** A new expansion-order tracer instruments the grid accessor and every frontier container and records the sequence of cells whose neighbours are read. It classified 14 of 15 reference implementations correctly (bidirectional A* is the unverified class) and all 9 planted controls by class (8 of 9 counting the requirement that the control itself pass the suite). On 260 gold programs from conditions without a ban, it agreed with the adjudicated label on 182 (0.70) after the two allowed revision rounds, against a committed bar of 0.90 (Table 426). The failures are concentrated in programs that the model writes as iterative deepening, IDA* or jump point search, which enumerate paths exponentially or prune in ways the order statistics do not capture. Under the committed fallback, logged before any ban row was traced, the primary mechanism label is iteration 8's name-free runtime label (heap priorities, FIFO and LIFO evidence, restarts), and the tracer's class is a second column. Neither instrument passed everything: the runtime label classifies only 6 of 9 planted controls, reading grid Bellman-Ford rounds as iterative deepening. Every number in this section is therefore a measurement without an inferential verdict, and where the two instruments disagree both are given.

  **Table 426.** The expansion-order tracer's gate (round 2, the last allowed) and its other checks.

  | Gold programs from conditions without a ban | 163 of 249 (0.65) in round 0, 162 of 248 (0.65) in round 1, 182 of 260 (0.70) in round 2; committed bar 0.90 |

  **The rename gap.** We retraced 580 rows written under a five-name ban in iterations 2, 6 and 8, 546 of them with a program. Lexical compliance exceeds mechanistic compliance by 0.70 with the runtime label (configuration-cluster bootstrap 95% interval 0.57 to 0.82; program-weighted 0.67) and by 0.61 with the tracer (0.45 to 0.76). The gap is positive in all ten configurations under either instrument (Table 427 and the figure below). It does not depend much on the lexical rule (0.73 when only self-naming counts) or on how untraceable programs are scored (0.70 either way). Most of these programs are BFS or DFS written without the banned words; the covert share, the fraction of programs that are lexically compliant but use a banned mechanism, ranges from 0.41 to 1.00. In the three configurations with reasoning, the reasoning of nearly every covert program names a banned algorithm: 20 of 20 for Qwen3-8B, 32 of 35 for Qwen3-14B and 47 of 47 for Qwen3-32B. The model writes the banned mechanism while its reasoning discusses the ban.

  **What Qwen3-32B's survivors run.** The survivor reading pooled the 91 correct programs of Qwen3-32B with thinking that the name-level label calls non-banned: the 17 screen and 21 held-out survivors of iteration 8 and 53 new survivors of the five-name ban (Table 428). The runtime label puts 72 of them (0.79) in a banned order class, the tracer 39 (0.43). Unit-weight Dijkstra and FIFO SPFA are BFS order on a unit grid by construction, so the committed reading (b) leaves out those identities: there the runtime label gives 30 of 40 and the tracer 4 of 40. Under the coarse classes three of the five non-banned catalogue algorithms already fall into a banned class, so 0.6 is also what a choice blind to mechanism would give; against that null the runtime label is 0.19 above and the tracer 0.17 below. Exactly FIFO BFS order is found in 29 of the 91 survivors.

  The two instruments disagree on two families of program, so the executor read all 76 survivors of the full five-name ban for Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-14B (every name-level or mechanism-level survivor at k = 5, on the committed and the held-out templates; Table 429). By these reads, 23 of 76 (0.30) are in a banned order class, and all 23 are unit-weight Dijkstra, a heap on path cost that expands a unit grid in BFS order. The other 53 are known algorithms with a different expansion discipline. The largest families are heaps keyed by a coordinate that does not depend on the goal (18), grid Bellman-Ford programs that relax the whole grid in raster rounds (17) and frontiers with random priorities (8); four smaller families make up the rest. The reads agree with the tracer on 0.88 of these programs and with the runtime label on 0.64; the runtime label reads the Bellman-Ford rounds as iterative deepening. The judges' names are least reliable on exactly these programs. Across every new cell, heaps keyed by a goal-independent coordinate were called greedy best-first 45 times and unit-weight Dijkstra 27 times (Table 430).

  **The exhaustion curve.** Cumulative bans of the first k names in Qwen3-32B's frequency order (BFS; then DFS, IDDFS, A* and greedy best-first) were sampled 50 times per k on three templates, with the full ban also sampled on four held-out templates, for Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-14B with thinking (Table 431 and the figure below). At k = 1 both models comply by name and by mechanism in every completed program: banning BFS changes the mechanism. Lexical compliance stays at or above 0.86 at every k on the committed templates. Mechanistic compliance by the runtime label falls with k, from 1.00 to 0.22 for Qwen3-32B and from 1.00 to 0.10 for Qwen3-14B (Jonckheere-Terpstra [149] Monte-Carlo p 0.00001 for each model; Cochran-Armitage [150] one-sided p below 0.00001). At k = 5 the gap is 0.67 (0.50 to 0.78) and 0.76 (0.59 to 0.85), and on the held-out templates 0.56 and 0.68. Whether the committed bars are met depends on the reading (iteration-10 correction). By the runtime label both models meet every committed criterion, descriptively. The registered fine-class sensitivity was a no-op for the runtime label in the executed code: results/n3.json repeats the primary in all 12 cells, because analysis_v9.py applies fine classes only when the mechanism field is the tracer's; it was applied for the tracer (results/n3_tracer.json). Computed for the runtime label, it changes one step: from k = 3 to k = 4 Qwen3-32B falls from 0.84 to 0.24 by the coarse runtime label, but 11 of the 35 coarse violations at k = 4 are greedy best-first programs, a name not yet banned, and with fine classes compliance is 22 of 46 = 0.48 (tracer 0.47 coarse and 0.82 fine); at k = 5 the fine runtime value equals the coarse one (10 of 46 = 0.22). By the runtime label mechanistic compliance falls to 0.22 (Qwen3-32B) and 0.10 (Qwen3-14B) at five names; by hand reads to 0.59 and 0.12; by the tracer to 0.67 and 0.24 (fine classes 0.74 and 0.37; Table 431b). Qwen3-14B meets the k = 5 bar of a 0.4 gap under every reading (runtime label 0.76, hand reads 0.73, tracer 0.61, tracer fine 0.49) and the held-out bar under every reading except the tracer's fine classes, where its held-out gap is 0.38 (lexical 0.78 against 20 of 50 = 0.40). Qwen3-32B meets both bars only by the runtime label (0.67 at k = 5, 0.56 held out): at k = 5 the hand reads (0.30), the coarse tracer (0.22) and the fine tracer (0.15) fall below 0.4, and on the held-out templates the hand reads give 0.396, just below the bar, and the coarse tracer 0.42; counting unit-weight Dijkstra, IDA* and jump point search as compliant gives 0.57 at k = 5 and 0.31 held out. Its tracer curve is not monotone (1.00, 0.86, 0.91, 0.47, 0.67), because the tracer reads the coordinate-key heaps and Bellman-Ford rounds of the late cells as compliant. The hand reads adjudicate between the instruments on exactly these programs: they agree with the tracer on 0.88 of the 76 read programs and with the runtime label on 0.64; coordinate-key heaps and grid Bellman-Ford rounds are other known disciplines, and the runtime label reads the Bellman-Ford rounds as iterative deepening. Correctness does not follow compliance: at k = 1 only 9 of 50 Qwen3-32B programs and 14 of 50 Qwen3-14B programs pass the hidden tests, against 33 to 40 and 17 to 27 of 50 at the larger k.

  **A ban described without names (exploratory).** The described ban lists the five banned mechanisms in words, with no algorithm name (each description first named correctly by the model). Its effect on mechanistic compliance is instrument-dependent (iteration-10 correction): +0.58 by the runtime label (39 of 49 = 0.80 under the described ban against 10 of 46 = 0.22 under the named five-name ban; 0.39 to 0.71), -0.07 by the tracer (29 of 48 = 0.60 against 31 of 46 = 0.67; -0.25 to 0.12), +0.05 by the tracer's fine classes (-0.12 to 0.22), and about +0.21 (0.02 to 0.38) under the per-cell reading the record argues for, the runtime label for the described cell and hand reads substituted for the named cell (27 of 46 = 0.59). The described cell was not hand-read, and its denominators differ because the tracer cannot trace one described program (49 against 48). At about 50 programs per cell the unpaired Newcombe half-width of these differences is 0.16 to 0.19, so differences below about 0.2 between readings are not resolvable and the record does not rank them; NOV-R's single-instrument retest in iteration 10 addresses this. By the runtime label the share of samples that are correct mechanism-level survivors rose from 0.16 to 0.68 (Table 433). The committed direction was that mechanistic compliance or violation rises; by the runtime label compliance rose and violation fell. Under the described ban the model mostly writes heaps keyed by goal-independent coordinates (19 called greedy best-first and 8 unit-weight Dijkstra by the judges). The runtime label calls them other and the tracer weak heuristic order. Since their keys do not depend on the goal, they are by mechanism neither a heuristic search nor BFS order, so for this cell the runtime reading is the closer one; the 11 FIFO BFS programs are its real violations.

  **Rotated ban sets (secondary).** Six further five-name sets, each containing BFS, were drawn by the committed tercile rule; the planned name distance was degenerate (most alias pairs share no term, so it equals 1 in 72 of 100 cells and no set of the planned lexical type exists). The account predicted Dm below zero and Dn above zero in at least 5 of 7 sets; the joint sign holds in 3 of 7 (binomial p 0.24 against a chance rate of 0.25), and the claim is disconfirmed (Table 434). The distances use the tracer, which failed its gate.

  **A larger reasoning model (exploratory).** gpt-oss-120b [152] at medium reasoning effort writes BFS 45 and DFS 5 of 50 at baseline, all passing. Under a ban of its own top five (BFS, DFS, greedy best-first, IDDFS and A*) it complies by name in 0.80 of programs and by mechanism (runtime label) in 0.22, a gap of 0.58 (0.40 to 0.70); 0.60 of programs are named survivors but only 0.06 are mechanism-level survivors, at a pass rate of 0.68. The name-level labels are other 24, unit-weight Dijkstra 21, DFS 4 and BFS 1. The planned Qwen3-235B-A22B cell was dropped before the first commitment because only one provider served it, at five times the planned price.

  **Novelty, audits and cost.** Of 568 correct programs, 73 were labelled other or flagged; two judges and the executor called all 73 known (Bellman-Ford on a grid, random-priority and coordinate-key searches among them), so no correct novel program was found (rule-of-three 95% upper bound 0.0053). A separate standard-library script recomputed the 2-by-2 tables, gaps, intervals, trend statistics, survivor counts and sign counts with 0 mismatches, and a second short script re-derived the headline numbers from raw rows. The placebos behave as required: swapping the lexical and mechanistic flags at random gives a pooled gap of -0.002 against 0.70; permuting k labels gives Jonckheere-Terpstra p below 0.05 in 0.07 and 0.06 of draws; random survivors of the rotated sets give a mean joint count of 1.80 against 1.75 by chance. OpenRouter spend was USD 3.889. The committed cap of 3.5 was raised to 4.0 at USD 3.21, before the last six cells were labelled, so that every cell is labelled by one judge protocol. Seven of 350 rotated and described samples were lost to rate limits and not resampled (293 of 300 rotated and 50 of 50 described samples are present) (iteration-10 correction), and the manual reads cover only the k = 5 survivors.

  **Positioning.** The experiment's dated search (2026-10-23) found no work that audits whether a banned technique returns under another name, read by the runtime label (heap priorities, frontier evidence, restarts) and by the expansion-order tracer (iteration-10 correction). Denial prompting [23] imposes technique-level bans to elicit new strategies and scores them behaviourally. Compact constraint encoding [38] reports that constraints opposing a model's defaults fail at 10% to 100%. The Invisible Lottery [1] steers algorithm choice by incidental cues. Semantic Gravity Wells [7] and the white-bear study [53] show that naming a forbidden word primes it. IFEvalCode [151] checks code constraints, including naming, with programmatic checkers, which cannot see a renamed mechanism. The measurement here is new only as a measurement: with the tracer's gate failed, no inferential claim is made.

  ## 9.4 The top-five landing on manifolds with and without names

  The geometry experiment  rebuilt Qwen3-32B's map of the ten grid algorithms four ways, holding the model, the readout, the block rule, k and the landing code of iteration 8 fixed. The *named manifold* (M-name in the artifact) reproduces iteration 8's 300 forced prompts, ten algorithms by ten templates by three aliases. The *described manifold* (M-desc) replaces each name by a name-free description of the mechanism that Qwen3-32B itself names correctly in at least 16 of 20 queries. The *name-only manifold* (M-lex) uses sentences in which an alias only appears as a word in an unrelated context, such as a line of a changelog, minus neutral-noun twins matched in token length. The *program manifold* (M-code) is the mean state over the code tokens of name-scrubbed, verified programs of each algorithm, teacher-forced under the neutral prompt. On each, g is the geodesic distance of a non-banned algorithm to the banned five on the k-nearest-neighbour graph (Isomap [25]), and unit-weight Dijkstra, the algorithm of all 15 catalogue survivors of iteration 8, is classed edge if its g is below the median g of the non-banned algorithms used and opposite if above. The geometry is correlational: it shows where representations and survivors sit, not whether the model uses this geometry to choose (iteration 7's pushes inside the manifold moved 0 of 300 programs).

  **Stimulus gates.** The reproduction of the named manifold matched iteration 8's cached states at cosine 0.99998 or higher per prompt at every block from 17 to 47, with identical classes and g within 0.030. The committed rank gate, the Spearman of the 45 between-class geodesic entries at k 15 and block 31, gave 0.894 against a bar of 0.95 (0.997 at k 10), because near-tied neighbour edges among the banned clusters flip at k 15; under the committed fallback the new states are used throughout and iteration 8's verdict is reported beside them. Jump point search has no name-free description that the model names reliably (0.70, 0.60 and 0.45 of namings for its three candidates), so the described manifold classes the other four non-banned algorithms. Program sets needed at least 10 verified programs per algorithm. Under the committed acceptance (both hidden suites) four of the five non-banned classes fell short, mostly through iterative-deepening timeouts on the 30-by-30 hidden cases, so the sets use a second tier: mechanism labels, the committed syntax rules, a trace check, and valid paths on at least 38 of 40 probe grids, applied to every source and algorithm alike. The primary program set holds BFS 20, DFS 20, bidirectional BFS 8, IDDFS 2, A* 20, greedy best-first 20, unit-weight Dijkstra 20, IDA* 17, jump point search 0 and bidirectional A* 2 programs. Below the floor, bidirectional BFS, IDDFS, jump point search and bidirectional A* are excluded, so the program manifold classes unit-weight Dijkstra against IDA* alone. Name scrubbing preserved the syntax tree modulo names, the expansion sequences, the labels and the suite outcomes for 449 of 470 programs, and a planted 'def bfs' was removed. The expansion tracer reproduced the expected properties of 13 of 15 references (bidirectional A* shows no second frontier; IDA* rarely restarts because the Manhattan bound is tight).

  **Where unit-weight Dijkstra lands.** On the three manifolds built from language it lands opposite; on the program manifold it lands at the edge, as the nearest of the non-banned algorithms to the banned five (Table 435 and the two figures below Table 436). The named outcome committed for this split is MIXED. On the named manifold unit-weight Dijkstra is the farthest non-banned algorithm (rank 5 of 5, g 1.63 times the median; bootstrap probability of edge 0.00). On the name-only manifold it is opposite at 1.20, and on the described manifold at 1.08 (rank 3 of 4; bootstrap probability of edge 0.01; opposite in all 15 cells of the robustness grid). On the program manifold it is the nearest (0.67 times the median; bootstrap probability of edge 1.00), and the class holds at block 21 (0.32) and on the frame built from Qwen3-32B's own programs only (0.79), so the program-manifold result is robust to the source of the programs. Qwen3-8B gives the same split: opposite on its named manifold (1.17), edge on its program manifold (0.63); its described manifold is opposite at k 15 by a hair (1.01) and unstable (bootstrap probability of edge 0.50; edge in 10 of 15 robustness cells). The class of unit-weight Dijkstra is the same at k 10 and k 15 on every manifold (Table 436); the committed landing verdict, which also scores the survivors against iteration 8's nulls, reads neither at k 10 and opposite at k 15 on Qwen3-32B's described manifold. The crossnobis, z-scored and centroid-distance variants agree with the class on every Qwen3-32B manifold.

  **Names drive the alias-level geometry, across algorithms.** On the named manifold, g of the 15 aliases falls with the number of banned algorithms whose alias pattern an alias matches. For Qwen3-32B the Spearman is -0.74 at k 10 (permutation p 0.0010) and -0.65 at k 15 (p 0.0052), and -0.67 after partialling out alias length; for Qwen3-8B it is -0.70 and -0.78. Within algorithms the relation is not significant (exact p 0.157 and 0.551 over 7,776 permutations), which matches the record audit's stratified test (Section 9.2). On the name-only manifold the same Spearman is -0.59 at k 10 and -0.65 at k 15, just short of the committed -0.6 at both k. The prediction that names drive the alias-level geometry on the named manifold holds; the geometry cannot separate a name effect from algorithm identity inside it.

  **What each manifold tracks.** Representational similarity analysis [147] compares each manifold's class-by-class distances with four model matrices: lexical distance between the aliases, behavioural distance from expansion-order traces of the reference implementations, surface distance between the programs' token sets, and length (Table 437; exact label-permutation p-values; noise ceilings from split halves [148]). The named, described and name-only manifolds track the lexical matrix (0.46, 0.57 and 0.47) and textbook data-structure attributes, not measured expansion order (iteration-10 correction): on the named Qwen3-32B manifold the data-structure matrix gives 0.65 (exact p 0.001) against 0.46 for the lexical matrix, and the expansion-order matrix gives -0.03 to 0.16 on the five language manifolds. The two model matrices are nearly unrelated there (Spearman 0.13, variance inflation 1.02), and each survives partialling out the other: lexical given data structure 0.50 and data structure given lexical 0.67, exact relabeling p 0.002 and 0.001 when the tested matrix is relabeled and 0.003 and 0.001 under Freedman-Lane residual relabeling (Table 437b). With ten classes and a contested partial Mantel test these p-values are descriptive. The program manifolds track behaviour (0.64 on Qwen3-32B and 0.88 on Qwen3-8B), but they track surface and length as strongly (0.67 and 0.78; 0.87 and 0.88), so with six classes the program manifold cannot tell an edge in mechanism from an edge in how the code looks. The described manifold also evokes the names: a classifier trained on the named manifold's block-31 states labels the described prompts at balanced accuracy 0.69 (chance 0.11) and the programs at 0.17, which is chance for six classes (0.167) (iteration-10 correction). The behavioural anchor holds by construction: in expansion order, unit-weight Dijkstra is the nearest non-banned algorithm to BFS (distance 0.31, against 0.72 for bidirectional BFS and 0.86 to 1.12 for the rest).

  **The survivors themselves.** Each of the 15 unit-weight Dijkstra survivors of iteration 8 was teacher-forced, name-scrubbed, and placed on the program manifold by its nearest algorithm and its own g (Table 438). On the primary frame, where leave-one-out placement of the frame's own programs is right 0.85 of the time (gate 0.70), all 15 survivors are classed edge (Wilson interval 0.80 to 1.00) and 13 are nearest to the unit-weight Dijkstra programs, 2 to greedy best-first. They sit farther from the banned five than the frame's own unit-weight Dijkstra programs (median g 20.2 against 16.5, Mann-Whitney p 0.00009), but still on the edge side of the non-banned median.

  **Audits, cost and positioning.** A standard-library script re-derived the classes and the alias rows with 0 mismatches. An independent script recomputed the neighbour graphs and geodesics from the raw state files with scikit-learn and networkx and matched every class (largest difference in g 4e-13). Random survivor labels give a landing verdict of neither in 0.93 of draws, and shuffled algorithm labels give unit-weight Dijkstra the opposite class in 0.37. OpenRouter spend was USD 0.094 for 1,440 calls (naming gate and 600 forced programs). For time, the Qwen3-8B name-only manifold, the Qwen3-8B-only program frame and two further readouts were not analysed; their states are kept. Labeller disagreements excluded several first-source program pools without manual adjudication. The experiment's dated search found no work that rebuilds a model's algorithm manifold with and without the algorithms' names; the nearest neighbours treat lexical identity as a confound of interpretability metrics [154] and compare behavioural with hidden-state semantic geometry [155].

  ## 9.5 Where post-training sharpened the fork: base against instruct in three families

  The base-model experiment  compared base and instruction-tuned models on identical token ids at the fork, the decision token where a code model picks its algorithm. The question is the request's hypothesis that a model gives "the mean answer". Iteration 8 found, in Qwen3-8B only, that post-training widened the fork margin by 2 to 13 nats while phrasing positions barely moved. Three parts were preregistered. The *sharpening measurement* repeats that comparison in two new families with the controls of Cantarero et al. [142]: Jensen-Shannon divergence at base-entropy-matched positions and at rate-matched random positions. The *patching test* uses cross-model activation patching [88]: it writes the base model's outputs of chosen components into the instruct run at the fork and measures the share of the instruct-minus-base margin gap that closes. The *held-out rerun* repairs the circuit's held-out arm. Everything decisive was committed in a sha256 chain, and a standard-library script re-derived every headline with placebos (0 mismatches).

  **The sharpening measurement (verdict partial).** The margin is log P(default class) minus log P(alternative class) at the fork, under the chat template for Gemma. Llama was switched to template-free prompts by the committed rule, because the Llama-3.1-8B base model's embedding rows of its chat-header and end-of-turn tokens have about 3e-21 of the median row norm, which means they are untrained. On Gemma's grid fork the instruct model puts 0.671 on its default class and the base model 0.089, a gain of 1.78 nats [1.59, 2.00], and the argmax differs on all 20 prompts: post-training reversed and concentrated the choice (base P(BFS) 0.25 against P(DFS) 0.09, with 0.663 of the base model's mass on tokens mapped to no class) (iteration-10 correction) (Table 440). On the two first-and-last-position forks the gains are 3.07 and 1.68 nats with the same argmax. On substring search the gain is 1.75 nats with an interval that crosses zero (5 prompts). Phrasing positions barely move (entropy change 0.44 to 0.50 nats; the instruct token is the base model's top choice at 91% to 97% of phrasing positions, the URIAL pattern [100]). The divergence at the fork is 4.7 to 6.6 times the mean phrasing divergence, but only 0.75 to 1.18 times the divergence at positions matched for base entropy: at these forks, "fork" and "high base entropy" coincide. Cantarero et al.'s own pattern reproduces: divergence 11 to 15 times higher inside their base-entropy fork set than outside, a rate-matched random set near 1.0, and every Gemma fork inside their set. Of the committed predictions, the phrasing prediction holds; the gain of at least 2 nats on every near-collapsed fork fails (1.68 at the second first-and-last fork); divergence at least 1.3 times the entropy-matched positions fails; and a different argmax on at least half the units holds only on the grid. Llama's grid fork fails the committed on-policy rule (the instruct model's log probability of the shared opening is about -13.6, below -5), so its two forks are descriptive.

  **The patching test (verdict partial; localisation distributed).** In Qwen3-8B against Qwen3-8B-Base, on minimum spanning tree weight (Kruskal against Prim) and connected components (`find` against `dfs` or `bfs`), base outputs of components were patched into the instruct run at the fork, 20 prompts per unit with fixed batch shapes (Table 441 and the figure below it). The ten validated fork-stack nodes of iteration 8's circuit close 1.00 [0.96, 1.04] of the 2.06-nat gap on minimum spanning tree. That is not specific: 50 sets of random late-layer components, matched in write norm, close a median 0.81 (95th percentile 1.41; empirical p 0.45), and random sets that exclude the circuit's top 15 components close a median 0.66, below the fork stack at p 0.039. On connected components the fork stack closes 0.45 [0.28, 0.57] of a 4.52-nat gap, above random sets (median -0.22, p 0.020), but short of the committed 0.5. (iteration-10 correction) Most matched random sets repeat a component, because the draw falls back to the whole candidate pool once an MLP pool is used up: an MLP repeats in 1 of 50 random sets and 47 of 50 sets without the circuit's top 15 on minimum spanning tree, and in 36 of 50 and 50 of 50 on connected components. Restricted to sets of ten distinct components, the minimum spanning tree null keeps a median 0.80 (49 sets; p 0.44) and the sets without the top 15 keep 3 (median 0.65; p 0.25, the floor at that N); random sets scaled to the fork stack's write norm give a median 0.64 (p 0.098), beside 0.66 (p 0.039) and 0.81 (p 0.45). On connected components the 14 full-size random sets give a median -0.33 (p 0.067, at its floor) and no set without the top 15 is full-size. The fork stack's 0.45 there is a ratio of means; per prompt its share has mean 0.13, median 0.43 and interquartile range -0.02 to 0.61, negative on 6 of 20 prompts (the five fork MLPs: ratio of means 0.41, mean of per-prompt shares 0.07; Table 441b). On minimum spanning tree specificity stays unresolved in this record; BASE-W redraws the sets without reuse. The task-specification nodes close nothing (-0.02 and -0.17), so the sharpening is not written upstream. It is carried at the fork by late MLPs, redundantly: several single MLPs between layers 26 and 35 each close about half the minimum spanning tree gap (layer 35 alone 0.98), and the fork stack's joint share is about half the sum of its singles. A large part of the gap is not in the residual stream at all. The instruct model's unembedding, reading the base model's own final residual, accounts for 0.43 of the gap on minimum spanning tree and 0.85 on connected components, which is why swapping the whole residual at the fork in layer 36 does not reach 1. Weight differences agree: every module moved by 5% to 11% in relative Frobenius norm, the unembedding by 9%, while the unembedding rows of ' dfs' (12.0%, 91st percentile) and ' bfs' (14.4%, 96th) moved more than almost any other row and ' find' (6.6%, 27th) little. Per-layer weight change does not track the per-layer patching shares (r at most 0.2). Along the first principal component of the block-30 output at the fork (98.5% and 94.6% of the variance of the instruct and base states on the two units), the patched states move most of the way from the instruct states toward the base states, and the median random and residual-swap states move less.

  **Does a one-token patch change the written program?** On 30 slots of common random numbers per arm (five templates, six seeds each; T 1; the instruct model's own opening prefilled), the arms differ only at the fork token, and every later token is sampled from the unpatched instruct model (Table 442). On minimum spanning tree, patching the fork stack turns 19 of 30 programs into correct Prim against 0 of 30 for the twin (19:0 discordant, exact McNemar p 3.8e-6, Holm 1.1e-5). The median matched random set does exactly as well (19 of 30; 2:2, p 1). Splicing the base model's whole fork distribution (Fork-Patched Decoding [142]) gives 18 Prim, 17 of them correct. On connected components the fork stack changes nothing (29 union-find and 1 DFS, as committed for a 0.45 share of a 4.5-nat gap), and only Fork-Patched Decoding brings back the base model's alternative (18 DFS against 1; 18:1, p 7.6e-5). The algorithm shares observed in each arm match the shares predicted from the patched fork distribution within a mean absolute error of 0.005 to 0.069; pass rates are 29 or 30 of 30 in every arm, and no correct program is labelled other (none novel; rule-of-three bound 3 of 237).

  The twin shows 0 of 30 Prim against a predicted 0.19 because only 2 of the 30 shared fork uniforms exceed 0.81 (5.7 expected) and the instruct model's cumulative distribution lists ' Kr' before ' Prim'; since the uniforms are shared across arms, every contrast is paired on the same draws.

  **The held-out rerun.** The rerun confirmed the cache bug: the original lookup returns nothing for every condition-span node on every held-out prompt of the forced-Prim contrast, so iteration 8's held-out arm applied no edit. With span means interpolated to the target span length, the layer-0 condition-span MLP has a held-out effect of about 7.9 nats on the five forced prompts (7.90 under ablation, 7.65 under steering at dose 2), close to its pair-prompt values (8.14 and 7.41, each the mean over both sides of the 20 pair prompts), and about 0 on the five padded twins (-0.19 and 0.05), unlike the pair prompts, where both sides carry the effect (ablation 8.68 forced and 7.61 padded); the means of 3.86 (sign-flip p 0.0625) and 3.85 (p 0.023) over the 10 held-out prompts average the two sides (iteration-10 correction). Taken as five contrasts, the exact sign-flip test has 32 equally likely patterns, so its smallest attainable p is 0.031 one-sided and 0.0625 two-sided; all five contrasts are positive under both modes, which gives exactly those values, so five contrasts cannot reach two-sided 0.05. On the F11 and F15 rows 153 of the 765 edit jobs of each row (612 of 3,060) were empty, all in the exact-length sensitivity variant, whose ablation mean is 3.50 with those rows and 5.83 without them; the primary interpolated variant applied every edit. The matched random set holds 10 distinct components among its 50 draws. Holm-adjusted within the six-test family the p-values are 0.22 and 0.12. The layer-5 condition MLP reverses sign (-1.50, p 0.008), and dose 0.5 shows nothing (post hoc). The engine reproduces iteration 8's pair-prompt value only to 0.096 nats (8.387 against 8.291), because the circuit artifact's engine was modified after its validation rows were written; its clean margins reproduce exactly, so token ids and positions are right. Matched in kind between the families, the committed motif statistic still differs on the condition share: on natural contrasts Qwen3-8B gives condition 0.08 and fork 0.34 against Gemma's 0.37 and 0.51, and on forced contrasts 0.01 and 0.62 against 0.34 and 0.54.

  **Deviations, not run and positioning.** An engine check against iteration 8 misses by 0.05 on some templates, because iteration 8 ran on a different GPU. The first patching pass used variable batch shapes and was replaced by a fixed-shape rerun, kept as a sensitivity. The self-patch placebo reaches 0.15 nats (head writes cached in bf16) against a 0.02 target. Llama's shortest-path unit, the optional grid and shortest-path patching units, patching in Gemma and token maps for unmapped base fork tokens were not run. That post-training shifts concentrate at forks of high base entropy is shown by Cantarero et al. [142] and by Sparse but Critical [143], and sharpening of what the base model already ranks high is the mechanism Huang et al. formalise [153]. What this experiment adds is the algorithm-level outcome on code at counterfactually located forks, and which validated components carry the sharpening: late MLPs and the unembedding, not the task-specification nodes.

  ## 9.6 Planned but not run

  Three directions of the iteration-9 strategy never produced an artifact. Each was lost at the execution step (gen_art), which returned no artifact for its plan, so none says anything about the hypothesis: each is untested and still open, and this report records no result, null or dead end for any of them.

  - *The second task* (TP-W): the names-against-mechanisms test on weighted shortest path, the inspiration repository's task, with a ban of each model's own top five (filled from Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford/SPFA, bidirectional Dijkstra, Floyd-Warshall, Dial's buckets and A* with a zero heuristic) on Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-14B with thinking and Qwen3-8B without, a relaxation-order tracer gated like the grid tracer, and a name-free program manifold of the shortest path catalogue. Lost at gen_art; no artifact.
  - *Discovery on online bin packing* (NOV-B): an evaluator-guided island search with Qwen3-8B as mutator in FunSearch's priority-function setting, comparing at matched calls temperature 1.0, temperature 1.6, branching at the decision token, the same branching at a random position and an instruction to differ from both parents, scored on held-out instances against best fit and published discovered heuristics. Lost at gen_art; no artifact. Before the failure the harness was built and passed its gate (iteration-10 correction): G-HARNESS PASS, with best fit at 5.37% excess on OR3 and 3.98% on Weibull 5k reproduced, FunSearch's published heuristics at 3.11% and 0.68%, and the priority-form first, best and worst fit equal to the hand-coded packers; iteration 10's evaluator search reuses it, and no search ran in iteration 9.
  - *The replication on constructive TSP* (NOV-T): the same arms on a next-city heuristic, fixed in advance so that the operator contrast is not chosen after seeing bin packing. Lost at gen_art; no artifact.

  ## 9.7 Comparisons across this iteration's experiments

  **The top-five question, read by mechanism and by geometry.** The rename experiment and the geometry experiment answer the request's edge-or-opposite question from two sides (Table 443). By expansion order, the survivors of the full five-name ban are a mixture. Unit-weight Dijkstra, 0.30 of the hand-read survivors and all of iteration 8's catalogue survivors, is BFS order under a non-banned name and container. The other 0.70 are known algorithms with a different expansion discipline. By geometry, unit-weight Dijkstra sits opposite the banned five on every manifold built from language, including the one that avoids names and still evokes them, and at the edge on the manifold built from the programs. For that one algorithm the account's prediction, opposite in names and at the edge in mechanisms, holds. Two limits apply. The program manifold tracks surface and length as strongly as behaviour, and the geometry experiment's verdict placed only the 15 unit-weight Dijkstra survivors. Its placement file also places 23 further iteration-8 survivors (iteration-10 correction): the 15 Bellman-Ford/SPFA programs land opposite on both gate-passing Qwen3-32B frames (15 of 15 and 15 of 15) and 10 edge, 5 opposite on Qwen3-8B, while the 3 BFS variants and the 5 other known programs place at the edge on the primary frames; 'opposite' there means farther than the median of two reference classes, and the placement was not preregistered (Table 438). The coordinate-key heaps have no landing yet.

Specificity fails at the same place under three methods: steering, DAS and now patching.   **Established.** A ban of five path-algorithm names is obeyed by name far more often than by expansion order. The gap is 0.70 pooled over ten configurations with the runtime label and 0.61 with the tracer, positive in every configuration, and in the three configurations with reasoning nearly every covert program comes with reasoning that names a banned algorithm (descriptive, because the tracer failed its gold gate). Under cumulative bans lexical compliance stays at or above 0.86, and mechanistic compliance at five names depends on the reading (iteration-10 correction): by the runtime label it falls from 1.00 at one name to 0.22 (Qwen3-32B) and 0.10 (Qwen3-14B); by hand reads to 0.59 and 0.12; by the tracer to 0.67 and 0.24 (fine classes 0.74 and 0.37). Banning one name changes the mechanism; banning the whole repertoire is answered by renaming in Qwen3-14B under every reading except the fine tracer on held-out templates, while Qwen3-32B moves mostly to other known disciplines. A ban described without names changes mechanistic compliance by an instrument-dependent amount (+0.58 by the runtime label, -0.07 by the tracer, about +0.21 under the per-cell reading; exploratory). By hand reads the survivors of the obeying models are mostly not renamed BFS: 0.30 are unit-weight Dijkstra (BFS order under another name) and 0.70 are known algorithms with other expansion disciplines (grid Bellman-Ford, coordinate-key heaps, random frontiers); judges' names are unreliable for exactly these programs, and the instruments disagree on them (by the runtime label 0.79 and by the tracer 0.43 of Qwen3-32B's 91 name-level survivors are in a banned class). On manifolds built from text, unit-weight Dijkstra lies opposite the banned five, and on the manifold built from its name-scrubbed programs it lies at the edge, robust to the program source and the readout; its 15 survivors place at the edge on the primary frames (15 of 15) and 10 of 15 on the Qwen3-32B programs-only frame, while the 15 Bellman-Ford/SPFA survivors place opposite on both gate-passing Qwen3-32B frames ('opposite' relative to the median of two reference classes; not preregistered). The language manifolds track lexical distance and textbook data-structure attributes, not measured expansion order; the program manifold tracks behaviour, surface and length together. Post-training sharpened Gemma's grid fork by 1.78 nats and reversed and concentrated the base model's preference there (20 of 20 prompts; base P(BFS) 0.25, 0.663 of base mass unmapped); in Qwen3-8B the sharpening is not written upstream of the fork but by late MLPs and, for most of the connected-components gap, by the unembedding.

  **Ruled out.** The prediction that unit-weight Dijkstra lands at the edge on a name-free manifold of descriptions: the described manifold reads opposite, and it evokes the names (balanced accuracy 0.69 from a probe trained on named prompts). The robust-opposite outcome, in which the survivors land opposite on both name-free manifolds: the program manifold reads edge. The rotated-set prediction (3 of 7). A fork-stack specificity for the sharpening on minimum spanning tree (random late-layer sets close 0.81).

  **Dead ends.** The expansion-order tracer, after two revision rounds, cannot classify LLM-written iterative deepening, IDA* and jump point search (0 of 34, 1 of 22 and 1 of 7 gold programs), so any order-based test on those classes needs a different instrument. A name distance between aliases is degenerate on this catalogue (1 for 72 of 100 cells), so rotated sets cannot be chosen to separate name from mechanism. Llama-3.1-8B's base model cannot be compared under the chat template, whose special-token embeddings are untrained.

  **Not run.** The second task, discovery with an evaluator on bin packing, and its TSP replication (Section 9.6); within the run artifacts, the Qwen3-235B scale cell, the Qwen3-8B name-only manifold and the patching of Gemma.

  ## 9.9 What the last iteration takes from this one

  Iteration 10 is the last. Three leads remain from this one. First, the edge-or-opposite answer is now split by the kind of map: opposite on every manifold built from language, at the edge on the manifold built from programs, for the one survivor algorithm that is a banned mechanism under another name. Two steps would make it decisive. One is a program manifold whose classes can be separated from surface and length, with more non-banned algorithms above the floor. The other is placing the remaining survivor families (iteration-10 correction): the record's placement file already places iteration 8's grid Bellman-Ford/SPFA survivors, which land opposite on both gate-passing Qwen3-32B frames (15 of 15; 'opposite' is relative to the median of the two non-banned reference classes, and the placement was not preregistered), while the unit-weight Dijkstra survivors place at the edge (15 of 15 on the primary frames, 10 of 15 on the programs-only frame); the coordinate-key heaps have no landing yet, and TP-G2's preregistered placements address both. Second, the names-against-mechanisms numbers are descriptive because the tracer failed on iterative deepening; an instrument that reads those programs would turn the strongest behavioural finding of this iteration into a test. Third, the request's "truly novel" question has still not met the one route left untried, an evaluator-guided search on a task with a measurable score; the bin-packing and TSP plans were lost before they ran, so the question stays open, not answered; the bin-packing harness had been built and had passed its gate before the loss (best fit 5.37% and 3.98% excess reproduced; FunSearch's heuristics 3.11% and 0.68%), iteration 10's evaluator search reuses it, and no search ran in iteration 9 (iteration-10 correction). The sharpening reading can be stated for Qwen3-8B and Gemma at the fork, with Llama descriptive and the base-entropy confound of Cantarero et al. carried, and does not need another experiment to be written up.

  # Iteration 10: an evaluator-guided search for new bin-packing and TSP heuristics, prohibition with an exact instrument, discipline against container on the program map, the weights that hold the default, and the record repaired

  ## 10.1 Why this iteration ran what it ran

  **The review of the iteration-9 record.** The review was blocking. It raised five items that had to be fixed before any new claim, and five minor items. The first found that the exhaustion curve of Section 9.3 contradicted the record's own hand reads. For Qwen3-32B the runtime label put mechanistic compliance at five banned names at 0.22, but 17 of the 22 hand-read violations in that cell were other known disciplines (grid Bellman-Ford rounds read as iterative deepening, raster sweeps, set frontiers, random frontiers), and with the reads substituted the cell reads 0.59. The second found that greedy best-first programs were counted as violations at four names, where greedy best-first was not yet banned, and that the registered fine-class sensitivity for exactly this case was a silent no-op in the executed code. The third found that the described-ban comparison mixed instruments and left out the artifact's own tracer result, which reverses its sign. The fourth found that the geometry artifact had placed all 38 iteration-8 survivors, of which the report used only the 15 unit-weight Dijkstra programs. The 15 Bellman-Ford/SPFA survivors land opposite on both gate-passing Qwen3-32B frames, and the report had listed those placements as future work. The fifth found that the table of representational similarity analysis (RSA) left out the best-fitting model matrix of the named manifold, the textbook data-structure matrix. The minor items concerned a bimodal held-out mean, random patching sets that repeat components, the instrument range of the one obeying configuration, four reporting slips and the bin-packing harness that had passed its gate before the iteration-9 search was lost.

  **The hypothesis update.** Nine iterations had narrowed what a code model's idea amounts to: a small known repertoire. The model writes BFS on the grid; temperature, seeds, top-k and thinking change the wording and not the algorithm; where the model is undecided one or two generated tokens decide the algorithm; post-training sharpened those tokens; and no knob, internal edit, forced branch or prohibition had produced a correct novel algorithm among more than 20,000 audited correct programs. The iteration-10 hypothesis keeps this as a *repertoire account* in seven parts. The first four restate what is measured: where the algorithm is decided, what writes the odds there, how sampling acts, and how post-training sharpened the choice. The fifth is the repertoire bound. The sixth restates prohibition on the corrected evidence: a ban that leaves a known alternative changes the mechanism, a ban that names the whole repertoire is answered by renaming in most configurations, and where reasoning lets a model obey, it moves to other known disciplines. The seventh is the main claim of the iteration. Because the repertoire is bounded and decoding spends its randomness on phrasing, a correct new idea needs an executable evaluator that keeps rare improvements and composes them across generations; and exploration should buy more distinct ideas per call when it is spent at the decision token (branching there) than when it is spent on every token (temperature) or requested in words (an instruction to differ).

  The run had never done the one thing the field's discovery systems do: let an evaluator select among the model's samples on a task where a new heuristic is measurable [81, 82]. The two artifacts that would have done it in iteration 9, on online bin packing and on constructive heuristics for the travelling salesman problem (TSP), were lost to stalled sessions after the bin-packing harness had passed its gate (Section 9.6). Iteration 10, the last, therefore made the request's question about truly novel solutions its main object. Online bin packing was chosen because a priority function with new terms is new behaviour by construction, and bin choices on fixed probe states measure behaviour exactly, with no tracer gate to fail. Constructive TSP was fixed in advance as the replication task, so the operator contrast could not be chosen after the bin-packing result.

  **The claims.** The primary family (Holm correction at 0.05) holds three claims on online bin packing, each preregistered with a sha256 commitment before the first search call. We call them by their content:

  - the *held-out claim*: the best program of every core arm (temperature 1.0, temperature 1.6, decision-token branching and its random-position placebo), chosen on selection instances only, beats best fit on the two primary held-out sets by the 0.8 rule (excess at most 0.8 of best fit's, that is at most 3.19% on the Weibull 5k test set of FunSearch, the evaluator-guided program search whose bin-packing setup the run reuses, and at most 4.29% on OR-Library binpack3), in both bin-packing searches;
  - the *operator claim*: decision-token branching yields at least 1.5 times the behaviour clusters per 1,000 calls of each temperature arm in each seed set, with a held-out best at least as good, and at least 1.2 times its random-position placebo;
  - the *novelty claim*: at least one program, selected without held-out data, beats best fit by the 0.8 rule and agrees on fewer than 0.9 of probe decisions with every heuristic of the known corpus, and is judged not known by gated judges and a manual read.

  The secondary family holds the TSP replication of the first two claims, the rename rate of instruction offspring, three prohibition claims on bin packing with an exact instrument, two geometry claims on a factorial program set, two weight claims, and the record repair. The analysis of where new heuristics are born inside the model and the Gemma row test are descriptive.

  **The strategy.** Seven artifacts ran, and none was lost (Table 445). Each copied and verified its inputs first, hash-committed its predictions before any long run, checkpointed every stage and wrote partial results as it went, because iteration 9 lost three artifacts to stalled sessions. The record repair answered the review on CPU. Two bin-packing searches ran the same frozen protocol independently, on seeds 0 and 1 and on seeds 2 and 3, and the second added two exploratory seeds. A TSP search ran the same arms on the constructive interface of ReEvo and Evolution of Heuristics (EoH). A prohibition experiment asked three Qwen3 models for one-shot bin-packing heuristics under cumulative name bans and scored each program by name and by behaviour. A geometry experiment built a factorial program set that crosses expansion discipline with storage container and placed every survivor family on it. A weights experiment asked which weights of Qwen3-8B hold the default at the fork token.

  The proofs were mechanical. The apply test passed: every old text occurs once, no spans overlap, the edits apply back to front, every new text occurs once, and the corrected copy is byte-identical outside the edited spans. A residual-claim lint with 15 rules hit 20 sentences in the original and none in the corrected copy; the two rules with no instance in the original were shown firing on planted sentences. Seventy-six attainability checks on reported fractions found no impossible value. An independent standard-library re-derivation ran 861 checks with 0 mismatches, and its six placebos failed as required. A second spot-check that reads the raw sample file instead of the labelled cell files recomputed 45 headline values with 0 mismatches; random within-program swaps of the lexical and mechanistic flags gave an exact McNemar p below 0.05 in 0.010 of 200 draws and moved the pooled gap to -0.006 on average. Of the values the corrections quote, 10 were corrected, 44 matched and 90 are new.

The random patching sets were not redrawn without reuse; the weights experiment (Section 10.9) draws its nulls independently instead. The partial-RSA p-values are descriptive, the per-family placement was not preregistered, and opposite there means farther than the median of two reference classes. The averaging rule behind the 8.14 and 7.41 pair values was recovered from the iteration-8 rows vendored in the base-model artifact.

  ## 10.3 The first evaluator-guided search on online bin packing (seeds 0 and 1)

  **Setup.** The first bin-packing search  copied the iteration-9 harness, verified every file and instance set by sha256 and reran its gate before any call. The harness has FunSearch's exact semantics [81]: a priority function scores every bin that can hold the item, the item goes to the highest score with ties broken by the first index, and the score of a program is the percentage of bins it uses above the lower bound of Martello and Toth [173], the total item size divided by the bin capacity and rounded up. The gate passed again: best fit [172] uses 212.0 bins on binpack3 (5.37% excess) and 2,067.0 on the Weibull 5k set (3.98%), FunSearch's published heuristic for the OR-Library instances 207.45 (3.11%) and its Weibull heuristic 2,001.4 (0.68%), and the priority forms of first, best and worst fit equal the hand-coded packers. Selection used two sets only, 20 OR instances of 120 items and 5 Weibull instances of 5,000 items, through one fitness F, the mean of the two excesses normalised by best fit's (best fit has F = 1, lower is better). Eight held-out sets were never touched by selection: FunSearch's Weibull 5k test set and OR-Library binpack3 as the primary pair [163, 164], binpack1, binpack2 and binpack4, fresh Weibull sets of 5,000 and 10,000 items, and a shifted Weibull set.

  The search was a FunSearch-style island search with Qwen3-8B as the mutator: five islands per arm and seed, a prompt with two parents sorted by score, rounds of 25 calls with a one-round lag between generation and registration, and best fit as the seed program. Five arms ran in lockstep at matched calls, 2,000 per arm and seed:

  - *temperature 1.0* (top-p 1);
  - *temperature 1.6* with top-p 0.95;
  - *decision-token branching* (DTB, or branching for short): sample at temperature 1.0 while recording the top-20 log probabilities of the first 48 generated body tokens, force a token drawn uniformly from ranks 2 to 8 at the highest-entropy code position among them, and continue at temperature 1.0;
  - *random-position branching* (RPB, called the placebo below): the same forcing at a uniformly random eligible position;
  - *IDEA* (called the instruction arm below): temperature 1.0 with one added sentence asking for an idea different from both parents.

  A sixth arm without selection (NS) ran afterwards: 1,000 calls per seed from fixed first-fit and best-fit parents, the analogue of the random-sampling baseline of Zhang et al. [161]. The known corpus held 86 priority-form programs: the textbook rules, a sum-of-squares rule, FunSearch's two heuristics, 60 programs from the three published EoH runs [156], the ReEvo [157], HSEvo [158], MCTS-AHD (Monte Carlo tree search for automatic heuristic design) [159] and LLM4AD [160] programs, and members of the ab family of Herrmann and Pallez [162] (a best-fit or first-fit base with a preferred near-exact fit and an avoided residual band), including a member tuned on the selection sets. The full ab grid of 3,843 members served as a strict sensitivity. Behaviour is the bin chosen on 2,000 committed probe states, agreement is the share of identical choices, and behaviour clusters are complete-linkage clusters with within-cluster agreement of at least 0.95. Six hash-chained commits fixed every rule, threshold and code file before the samples they govern.

  **Validity, clusters and tokens.** Table 447 lists each stream. Validity ranged from 0.59 to 0.85, and the arms generated similar numbers of tokens per call (259 for temperature 1.0, 265, 293 for branching, 264 and 277 for the instruction). The arm without selection, which always prompts with the fixed first-fit and best-fit parents, generated about 15 tokens per call and found five and six behaviours.

  **The novelty claim was supported, with a flag.** The novelty funnel took the 20 best programs by selection fitness from each stream (211 candidates). Of these, 70 beat both bars on held-out data, and all 70 also agreed on fewer than 0.9 of probe decisions with every corpus program. By arm they came from temperature 1.0 (2), temperature 1.6 (5), branching (27), the placebo (7) and the instruction arm (29), and none from the arm without selection. They formed 53 joint clusters; 30 representatives were read (2, 4, 10, 5 and 9 by arm) and 23 were left unread. Three judge models were gated on 10 control programs each, and only one reached the required 9 of 10: Mistral's medium model, version 3.1 (9 of 10), DeepSeek's chat model, version 3.1 (5 of 10) and Kimi (6 of 10). By the committed fallback the judges were advisory and an arm-blind manual read decided. The reader classed 22 representatives as known families with new parameters, all reducing to the ab principle, and 8 as novel. The 8 share one idea: prefer a bin whose leftover after packing is a whole multiple of the item size (0, one item or two items of room), even over a tighter non-exact fit, and avoid leftovers smaller than the item. They came from temperature 1.0 (2), branching (4) and the instruction arm (2) (Table 451). The passing judge agreed on 8 of 8, and a majority of the three judges on 5 of 8.

  Four facts weaken this result, and the artifact states each. The probe-agreement filter did no work: permuting the corpus's decision vectors left the 70 novel-and-better programs at 70, because every program that passed both held-out bars already sat below 0.9 against the whole corpus. The verdict therefore rests on one reader's classification. One of the eight programs, the branching arm's best, adds uniform random noise to its scores, so its decisions are stochastic. No ablation of the multiple-of-item term was run, so it is not shown that the term carries the improvement. And none of the eight beats the published ab members or FunSearch's heuristics on the primary sets (Table 448).

  **Where new heuristics are born, and renaming under the instruction.** The birth-token analysis teacher-forced 40 founders of new better clusters, forced the argmax back at up to three of their high-entropy non-argmax positions and resampled 20 continuations each. Reversion to a parent's cluster was 0.40 at birth positions against 0.36 at control positions, and births beat controls on 19 founders against 14 (sign test p 0.49): no evidence that single decision tokens carry the new heuristics in this search. By arm, the share of founders whose birth positions revert at least half of their continuations was 0.67 (temperature 1.0, 3 founders), 0.86 (temperature 1.6, 7), 0.45 (branching, 11), 0.80 (placebo, 5) and 0.43 (instruction, 14). We call an offspring a rename when it agrees with one of its parents on at least 0.95 of probe decisions, and the rename rate is the share of renames among valid offspring. The rename-rate claim predicted a rename rate of at least 0.4 for instruction offspring, at most 0.1 below temperature 1.0's, and it was partial. The instruction arm's rename rate is 0.44, against 0.86 for temperature 1.0 offspring (difference -0.45 to -0.40), so the instruction lowers renaming instead of producing it. The other arms sit between: 0.73 at temperature 1.6, 0.58 under branching, 0.74 under the placebo and 0.99 without selection. Offspring that claim a new idea in a comment are 0.16 of the instruction arm and 0.03 of temperature 1.0.

  **The evaluator effect.** Without selection the search never left best fit: the best program of each seed has F = 1.0 and the held-out excess of best fit, from five and six behaviours in 1,000 calls. Temperature 1.0 with selection had programs better than best fit on the selection sets by its 1,000th call in both seeds (F 0.974 and 0.978, from 29 and 77 clusters), although those early bests did not yet beat best fit on held-out data (3.75% and 4.13% on the Weibull test set).

  **Checks and departures.** Thirty unit tests passed. The standard-library audit re-derived the held-out verdict, the cluster counts, the novelty counts, the rename rates, the placebos and the commitment chain. A random priority function fails the held-out bars (71.0% and 71.8% excess), and FunSearch's Weibull heuristic disguised under new names is found at agreement 1.0. The artifact lists its departures. The hard stop moved to fit the session and never bound. Ten evaluation workers ran instead of five. FunSearch's OR heuristic times out on the 10,000-item set, so its vectorised equivalent, with identical decisions, supplies its scores, and the MCTS-AHD loop program times out on the Weibull selection set. The first birth-token run crashed the engine and reran at lower memory. The bfloat16 replay check was dropped first by the drop order, and the judge gate was unmet as described.

  ## 10.4 The replication search on seeds 2 and 3, and two exploratory seeds

  **Setup.** The replication search  implemented the same shared specification independently: the same harness (copied, verified and re-gated with the same values), the same selection and held-out sets, the same arms at 2,000 calls per arm and seed, 1,000 calls per seed without selection, and its own committed probe set of 2,000 states. Its corpus held 82 published, textbook and dependency programs (FunSearch, the three EoH runs, HSEvo, MCTS-AHD, ReEvo, LLM4AD and one further published method, plus a scan of the run's own dependency datasets) plus all 3,843 ab members. The budget rule chose 2,000 calls per arm and seed (commit 2); a later commit added two exploratory seeds and the corpus additions, before any novelty comparison. An optional arm that would draw the forced token from Qwen3-8B-Base's distribution was dropped, because two engines would not fit on the GPU (two engines with 8-bit floating-point weights need 21.8 of the 21.9 GiB budget, with no room for activations).

  The two implementations differ in one instruction sentence. The first asked the model to write priority_v2 as an improved version of priority_v1 and to return only its code; the replication asked it to complete the module by writing the body of priority_v2 and to reply with code only. Both prefilled the function header and a docstring. Under the replication's wording the temperature arms almost always copied a parent. Temperature 1.0 generated 17 and 10 tokens per call and repeated an earlier program in 91% and 94% of its calls. Temperature 1.6 with top-p 0.95 generated exactly 8 tokens per call and produced one behaviour in each seed (Table 452). The model's top token carries more than 0.95 of the mass at every position of a copied body, so top-p 0.95 is greedy there. Branching, the placebo and the instruction arm do not copy: the forced token breaks the copy, and the instruction asks for a change. We did not test which difference between the two prompts causes the gap.

  **Table 452.** The replication search, one row per arm and seed. The duplicate share is the share of calls whose program repeats one already generated in the same stream.
