  **The manual read.** The 40 read programs fell into six groups, all recombining principles already in the corpus: a first-fit base with an avoided residual band (2), a best-fit base with near-exact fits first and an avoided band (4), quadratic scores (3), an item-proportional target residual (14), sinusoidal terms in the bin-to-item ratio (12) and logarithmic terms (5). The reader placed the item-proportional target residual, a residual of about c times the item, in the published EoH run-3 and MCTS-AHD programs. No judge model passed its gate (DeepSeek 5 of 10, Mistral 5 of 10 as the one-time replacement, Kimi 4 of 10), because the judges call even the executor's planted novel compositions known; their advisory labels agree with the manual read.

  **The exploratory seeds.** The same frozen rules on seeds 4 and 5 gave the operator claim as supported: branching against temperature 1.0 34.4, against temperature 1.6 310, against the placebo 1.47 (Table 455). The held-out claim stayed partial; only the instruction arm's best passed both bars, and the bests of branching and the placebo failed on binpack3 (5.19% and 6.01%). Pooled over the four seeds of this artifact, branching found 25.5 times the clusters of temperature 1.0, 248 times those of temperature 1.6 and 1.08 times those of the placebo. The per-seed ratios of branching to placebo were 0.86, 0.61, 1.92 and 1.11, so the entropy-targeting effect is within seed-to-seed noise, while forcing over temperature is robust in this implementation.

  **Engine check and audit.** A bfloat16 replay of 20 branching calls matched the 8-bit engine's top-1 token at every position, chose the same forced position in 20 of 20 and placed the forced token within bfloat16 ranks 2 to 8 in 20 of 20. Forty offline unit tests passed, and the standard-library audit re-derived every headline number with its placebos failing. The search programs cannot be regenerated byte for byte, because batched inference with 8-bit floating-point weights is not deterministic; every raw row is kept.

  ## 10.5 The constructive TSP replication

  **Setup.** The TSP search  ran the same arms on the constructive interface of ReEvo and EoH [157, 156], `select_next_node(current_node, destination_node, unvisited_nodes, distance_matrix)`: a tour is built greedily from city 0 and closed, and each call gets fresh copies of its inputs. Selection used 64 instances (32 with 50 cities, 32 with 100) scored against LKH-3 tours [166, 167]. The fitness F averages, over the 50-city and the 100-city sets, a program's mean optimality gap divided by the mean gap of the nearest neighbour heuristic on the same set, so nearest neighbour has F = 1. The held-out sets were 32 random instances of 200 cities (primary), 96 more (extended) and 13 TSPLIB instances [165] with published optima, all 13 of which the reference solver reached. Each arm and seed had five islands seeded with nearest neighbour, prompts with two parents, and FunSearch's cluster sampling, with the two worst islands reset every 400 calls. The arms ran interleaved, 32 calls per arm and seed per round, so calls stayed matched at any stop. The behaviour instrument is the next-city decision on 2,000 frozen probe states, with the same complete-linkage clusters at agreement 0.95. An arm without selection ran on seed 0 from a prompt with nearest neighbour only.

  The search stopped at its hard stop after 33 rounds, with 1,056 calls per arm and seed instead of the 2,000 that commit 2 had projected: programs lengthened from about 140 to about 400 tokens and rounds slowed from 60 s to about 300 s. The arm without selection reached 252 calls.

  **Novelty and renaming on TSP.** Thirty-two pooled programs were better than 0.8 of nearest neighbour's gap and agreed on fewer than 0.90 of probe decisions with every admitted corpus member (temperature 1.0 5, temperature 1.6 8, branching 6, placebo 7, instruction 6). Neither judge passed its gate (DeepSeek 8 of 10, Kimi 5 of 10), so the written manual-read rule decided: the 12 read candidates are all known families with new parameters, weighted sums of the distance to the current city, terms in the destination and statistics of the distances to the unvisited set (0 of 12 novel; rule-of-three upper bound 25%). The instruction arm renamed a parent in 0.06 of its valid offspring, against 0.18 and 0.22 for temperature 1.0, so the rename-rate prediction failed in the other direction here too.

  Three further committed predictions failed. Branching's forced tokens fell on identifiers, operators and keywords in 50% and 62% of branched calls, not in at least 60% of both; numeric literals took 44% and 35%. The instruction arm's rename rate was predicted at 0.4 or more and came out at 0.06. Nearest neighbour's held-out gap, 23.94%, fell just under the predicted range of 24% to 28%. The standard-library audit re-derived every cluster count exactly (10 of 10 arm-seeds), the ratios, the held-out means and both verdicts, and re-derived 50 of 50 logged forcings from their top-20 log probabilities and seeds; its placebos failed as required (shuffled arm labels give ratios of 1.03 to 1.10).

  ## 10.6 The three searches compared

  The three searches answer the iteration's main question from three implementations and two tasks (Table 459 and the figure below). An executable evaluator turned the 8B model's samples into heuristics better than the textbook rule on held-out data on both tasks. With selection, the bests of five of five arms in the first search and three of five in the replication beat best fit by the 0.8 rule; on the exploratory seeds only the instruction arm's did. Every arm closed at least 30% of nearest neighbour's gap on TSP. No arm without selection improved on its seed program. None of the selected programs beat the strongest published heuristics on the same harness: FunSearch's Weibull heuristic and the published ab members on bin packing, the ReEvo/EoH seed rule on TSP.

  [FIGURE:fig_search_clusters]

  Where the randomness is spent mattered, but not in the way the fork account predicted. Forcing a non-top token, at the entropy maximum or at a random position, bought many more behaviours than temperature in the replication's implementation (17.8 to 186.5 times), where temperature mostly copied the parent. In the first implementation, where temperature wrote new code, branching's advantage over temperature 1.6 was 1.2 times and reversed in one seed, and on TSP branching tied temperature 1.0. Against its random-position placebo, branching was ahead in the first search (2.1), behind in the replication (0.74), ahead in the exploratory seeds (1.47) and tied on TSP (0.95). The committed operator claim needed the gain over temperature and over the placebo in both bin-packing seed sets and on TSP; it failed on every one of those three tests at least once. The instruction to use a different idea found the most behaviours in the first search and on TSP, and was in the same range as forcing in the replication. The artifacts' dated literature searches found no earlier use of a decoding-time entropy fork as the mutation operator of an LLM program search; the nearest work analyses forking tokens in text generation [30] or uses high-entropy tokens during reinforcement learning [139].

  The figure below repeats Tables 448 and 453 for the two primary sets. In both bin-packing searches the tuned ab member, a two-parameter rule tuned with the same budget of 2,000 evaluations, has the lowest binpack3 excess of the plotted programs (3.06%; the published ab-FF(5,24) reaches 3.01%). On the Weibull test set it is beaten by four of the first search's five arm bests and by the replication's placebo and instruction bests.

  [FIGURE:fig_bp_heldout]

  The novelty verdicts disagree between the two bin-packing searches, and the disagreement is a disagreement between two readers. The first search's reader classed 8 representatives as one new idea, preferring a leftover that is a whole multiple of the item size. The replication's reader classed every program built on an item-proportional target residual as known, citing the EoH run-3 and MCTS-AHD programs. The two rules are related but not identical: a target residual of about c times the item rewards one leftover size, while the whole-multiple rule rewards leftovers of 0, one and two items and penalises leftovers smaller than the item. Neither reading was double-coded. Only one judge family passed its gate in the first search and none in the replication, the first search's probe filter did no work, and no ablation tested whether the whole-multiple term causes the improvement. We therefore record the first search's eight programs as candidates that one reader judged novel. They are behaviourally distinct from every corpus program (agreement below 0.9) and better than best fit, but not better than the published ab members. We do not record them as a confirmed new heuristic.

  ## 10.7 Prohibition with an exact instrument: do banned bin-packing rules come back under other names?

  **Why a second task.** The grid result of iteration 9, that a five-name ban is obeyed by name far more than by mechanism, rested on instruments that read expansion order imperfectly: the runtime label and the tracer disagreed, and the tracer failed its gold gate on iterative deepening. On online bin packing the mechanism can be read exactly. A program's bin choices on fixed probe states either match a banned rule's or they do not, and a renamed copy of best fit agrees with best fit on every state whatever it is called.

  **Setup.** The prohibition experiment  asked for one-shot online bin-packing priority functions in FunSearch's interface, with no parents and no evaluator in the loop. Each program was scored two ways. Lexical compliance means no banned rule name or abbreviation anywhere in the extracted program, comments and docstrings included. Mechanistic compliance means agreement below 0.95 with every banned rule on the 2,000 committed probe states, with a stochastic matcher for random fit. The instrument was gated before any ban row: every reference agrees with itself across runs, renamed copies of each rule agree at 1.0, implementation variants of each rule (an argmin one-hot, a reciprocal score, an exact-fit bonus, a Python loop) agree at 1.0, and planted different rules fall below 0.95. Three models ran: Qwen3-8B without thinking (local vLLM with 8-bit floating-point weights) and Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B with thinking (OpenRouter, with the DeepInfra provider and its 8-bit floating-point weights pinned). A baseline cell fixed each model's frequency order over six textbook rules (best, first, worst, almost-worst, last and random fit), and the resulting ban sequence was the same for all three models: best fit, then first fit, worst fit, almost-worst fit and last fit. The cells were cumulative name bans of the top k rules (k = 1 to 5) on three templates, a ban of the five rules described without names, the five-name ban on two held-out templates, and two novelty instructions. We call the one-line request to make a new algorithm the short novelty instruction, and the request for a fully novel algorithm with about 2,000 words of rationale the long novelty instruction. Every threshold, prompt, verdict rule and the analysis code were hash-committed before any sample. Three claims were committed. The renaming claim predicted that both compliance rates are at least 0.7 at one banned name, that mechanistic compliance falls with k while lexical compliance stays at least 0.7, and that the lexical-minus-mechanistic gap at k = 5 is at least 0.3 in at least two models. The described-ban claim predicted that describing the five rules without names raises mechanistic compliance at k = 5 by at least 0.2 over the named ban in at least two models. The bound without an evaluator predicted that at most 0.02 of the samples in any cell beat best fit on held-out data and are behaviourally novel. The OpenRouter cells used the plan's reduction ladder after a container crash: 30 samples per ban and instruction cell for the thinking models (their baselines have 50), and 50 per cell for Qwen3-8B.

  **The renaming claim was partial.** Renaming is large and significant only in the model without thinking (Table 461 and the figure below). Under the five-name ban, Qwen3-8B's lexical compliance is 0.91 and its mechanistic compliance 0.51, a gap of +0.40 (paired Newcombe interval [174] 0.21 to 0.55); its lexically clean programs are a banned rule in 0.40 to 0.63 of cases across k, mostly best fit under names the model invented, such as *tightest fit* or *minimum remaining space* (Table 462). The two thinking models change behaviour when a name is banned. Banning best fit sends Qwen3-32B to first fit in 14 of 30 programs and to other rules in 16, and from k = 2 on their programs sit mostly outside the catalogue. Their k = 5 gaps are +0.04 and -0.13 with intervals that include 0. Lexical compliance there is lower than mechanistic, because some of their programs mention a banned name in code or comments while implementing a different rule. The trend of mechanistic compliance over k is significant only for Qwen3-14B (Jonckheere-Terpstra permutation p 0.038, Holm 0.11). On the held-out templates no model has a positive gap whose interval excludes 0; Qwen3-8B's falls to +0.08. The verdict is the same at class thresholds of 0.90 and 0.98 and on informative probe states only.

  The reasoning traces of both thinking models name the banned rule in every cell (share 1.00), and under the name bans they identify their own program as close to it in 0.90 to 1.00 of traces. The bans cost reasoning: median reasoning tokens rose from 6,342 (Qwen3-14B) and 5,485 (Qwen3-32B) at baseline to 8,350 and 10,889 at five names, and Qwen3-32B truncated 0.20 of its five-name traces.

  **The described-ban claim was disconfirmed, as a weak test.** Each description had to be named correctly by the model in at least 16 of 20 separate queries. Only first fit's description passed; the models named the other descriptions as first-fit decreasing (an offline rule that sorts the items before packing them) or similar rules. The described cell therefore banned first fit alone, a rule these models rarely use, and mechanistic compliance was about 1.0 under the description and under the name alike: differences 0.00 (Qwen3-14B, -0.11 to 0.12), 0.00 (Qwen3-32B, -0.11 to 0.14) and +0.03 (Qwen3-8B, -0.09 to 0.15). The grid question this test was meant to settle, whether a name-free description changes the mechanism more than names, stays open.

  **The bound without an evaluator held.** None of the 1,143 programs beat best fit on both held-out sets by the 0.8 rule. 186 valid programs were behaviourally novel against the 426-member published corpus (maximum agreement below 0.9), and none of them was better than best fit. The committed share of at most 0.02 novel-and-better programs per cell holds as a point estimate only: the Clopper-Pearson upper bounds [170] are 0.07 per cell at 50 samples and 0.12 at 30.

  **Novelty instructions return the default.** The short novelty instruction returned best fit in 28 of 29 programs from Qwen3-14B, 28 of 28 from Qwen3-32B and 18 of 42 from Qwen3-8B. Every program that claimed novelty under that instruction was a catalogue rule (agreement at least 0.95) or a corpus heuristic (at least 0.9) for the thinking models (4 of 4 and 11 of 11), and 6 of 7 were for Qwen3-8B. Under the long instruction 11 of 14, 4 of 12 and 18 of 27 novelty claims were known programs, and Qwen3-32B truncated 0.57 of those traces.

  **Integrity.** The worker container crashed at about 4.2 hours and sampling resumed at 5.9 hours behind exclusive locks. From 21:21 to 22:00 UTC a kill reached a shell wrapper and left its Python child alive, so two samplers ran together; five duplicate Qwen3-32B baseline rows were moved aside, keeping the first, evaluated row per slot. The first naming-check files mixed empty replies with real ones; a clean rerun was committed before any Qwen3-32B described-ban row. The payload files of two commits were overwritten after their hashes were logged, so two lines of the commitment log no longer match the files on disk; the chain itself verifies, and the banned sets of the name cells are identical in every version. The standard-library re-derivation recomputed every agreement, class, lexical flag, cell count, trend statistic, interval and verdict with 0 mismatches, and its four placebos failed as required: 600 shuffled-k trend tests give p below 0.05 in 3.8% of cases, randomly swapped flags give a mean gap of 0.001, 50 random decision vectors are all classed other, and a renamed best fit whose comment calls it the tightest rule is still classed best fit with no lexical hit. The spend was USD 1.42 for 2,497 calls.

  ## 10.8 Discipline against container on the program map, and where the survivor families land

  **Why.** In iteration 9 the program manifold placed unit-weight Dijkstra at the edge of the banned five, and its Bellman-Ford survivors opposite, but that manifold tracked code surface and length as strongly as behaviour (Section 9.4). Unit-weight Dijkstra expands a grid in BFS order through a heap, so its edge position could reflect the same expansion discipline or only similar code. A factorial program set that crosses discipline with container separates the two by design.

  **Setup.** The factorial geometry experiment  had Qwen3-32B (OpenRouter, thinking off, temperature 1.0) write grid path programs for 24 implementable cells of expansion discipline (FIFO order, LIFO order, goal-heuristic order, path-cost order, relaxation rounds, random order) by storage container (deque, list, recursion, heap, two-dimensional arrays, set). Each prompt described the mechanics step by step in three wordings and named no algorithm (0 lint hits over 144 prompts). Every program had to pass the 48-case and 41-case hidden suites, an AST container check, a discipline check (the iteration-9 tracer for FIFO, LIFO, heuristic and cost order, a two-seed runtime check for random order, an AST sweep check plus at least two runtime passes for relaxation, and hand reads for the array cells) and name scrubbing followed by a rerun of the suite. The freeze kept the first 12 verified programs per cell, 287 in all (the relaxation-by-set cell has 11), plus 12 top-ups each for bidirectional BFS, iterative deepening and bidirectional A*; the 12 jump point search top-ups are all paraphrases of the reference. Four programs were rejected on hand read. States were read under iteration 9's neutral-twin contexts with its frozen readout and truncated decoder (Qwen3-8B in bfloat16 at block 17, Qwen3-32B with 4-bit NormalFloat weights at block 33), and the reproduction gate matched iteration 9's frames bit for bit (unit-weight Dijkstra g over median 0.6296 and 0.6725; 113 of 113 placements). The spend was USD 0.25 for 1,138 calls.

  The discipline-against-container claim uses a partial Spearman correlation between the program-state dissimilarity matrix and the discipline matrix given the container matrix (written rho_dc), and the reverse (rho_cd), with a program bootstrap and permutations restricted within strata. The prediction was rho_dc at least 0.3 and above rho_cd on at least one model; the disconfirming outcome was rho_dc at most 0.1 on both.

  **The discipline-against-container verdict is indeterminate.** Discipline is encoded, container is encoded more strongly, and token surface more strongly than either (Table 463). On both models rho_dc is below 0.3 and below rho_cd, and the difference is negative with an interval that excludes 0 on the full set. The bag-of-tokens baseline (mean input embedding over the code tokens) gives rho_dc 0.169 (Qwen3-8B) and 0.156 (Qwen3-32B), and a randomly initialised network 0.072, so the trained states carry discipline information beyond token identity, but less than the bar. A rank regression with surface, length, container, discipline and context matrices gives semi-partial correlations of 0.32, 0.30, 0.13, 0.10 and 0.02 on Qwen3-8B and 0.41, 0.23, 0.20 and 0.13 (surface, length, container, discipline) on Qwen3-32B. Partialling the token-surface matrix out leaves rho_dc at 0.13 to 0.15 (Qwen3-8B) and 0.18 to 0.21 (Qwen3-32B). The noise ceiling across context variants is 0.94 on Qwen3-8B, the cell-cluster bootstrap widens the difference interval to include 0, other readouts give lower discipline correlations (0.09 at the token after the first pop, 0.04 to 0.05 at the 16th code token), and the layer curve is flat (0.20 to 0.26 on Qwen3-8B, 0.25 to 0.30 on Qwen3-32B). Shuffled labels give 0.006 for both partial correlations.

  **The placements.** The placement claims placed 351 programs out of sample on a frame of 464 programs (the 24 cells plus the catalogue) with iteration 9's unchanged placement code (k-nearest-neighbour geodesic distances). The families were 38 unit-weight Dijkstra, 32 grid Bellman-Ford, 18 coordinate-key heaps, 14 random frontiers, 4 raster sweeps, 3 set frontiers and 8 other survivors, 136 covert BFS and DFS programs from the five-name ban and 98 from other ban sets. The frame classifies well: class-level leave-one-out accuracy 0.68 (Qwen3-8B) and 0.83 (Qwen3-32B), discipline-level 0.83 and 0.91, against chance 0.03. Its false-inside rate, the share of left-out non-banned programs whose nearest other class is banned, is 0.46 and 0.47, close to the 53% of its classes that are banned.

  The reading is that the program map places programs by what they do as well as by how they look, but surface and container dominate discipline. Bellman-Ford survivors sit with relaxation programs, covert BFS and DFS sit with their own discipline, and unit-weight Dijkstra sits with the path-cost and FIFO heap programs rather than with the heuristic heap programs; whether that counts as edge or opposite depends on the frame. Every factorial program has one author, Qwen3-32B, while the survivors and covert programs come from several, so placements of programs by other authors are weaker evidence. Geometry here is correlational: iteration 7's in-manifold pushes moved 0 of 300 programs.

  ## 10.9 Which weights hold the default at the fork

  **Why.** Iteration 9 found that post-training sharpened Qwen3-8B's fork and that the sharpening sits at the fork, in late MLPs and in the unembedding, but its component patching was not specific: matched random late-layer sets closed 0.81 of the minimum spanning tree gap. The weights experiment  moved the question from activations to weights. It asked whether the instruct default is stored in the unembedding rows of the fork-class tokens or in the late-MLP weights, tested the row arm again in free generation, and repeated the row test on Gemma. Units, prompts, openings, fork-class tokens, the generation engine and the frozen labellers came from iteration 9. The primary unit is connected components (default class ' find', union-find, against ' dfs' and ' bfs'; 20 prompts); minimum spanning tree (Kruskal-class against Prim-class tokens; 20 prompts) runs beside it. The margin is the log-sum-exp of the default class's fork logits minus that of the alternative class, and a share is the fraction of the instruct-minus-base margin gap an arm closes, a ratio of sums over prompts with a prompt bootstrap. Every decisive prediction was sha256-chained before the computation it governs. The readout-row claim predicted that, at the fork only, the base rows of the fork-class tokens close at least 0.5 of the connected-components gap, against at most 0.15 for the same rows moved in a random direction of matched norm, and that they give at least 10 of 30 correct DFS programs in generation. The late-MLP claim compared base weights in the late MLPs (layers 26 to 35) with Frobenius-matched swaps of early-layer MLPs.

  **Stage 0.** On a different GPU from iteration 9 the gaps reproduced (4.56 nats on connected components against 4.52; 2.09 on minimum spanning tree against 2.06), but the connected-components instruct mean differed by 0.061 nats, above the 0.05 rule (Table 465). A debug round found the ids, hashes and stack unchanged and measured the bfloat16 numerics floor on this GPU: the instruct margin varies by a mean 0.27 and up to 0.55 nats across numerically equivalent batch shapes. The committed fallback applied, and every share below uses this run's own instruct and base margins from the same cached states.

  | Mean instruct margin, here / iteration 9 | 4.516 / 4.455 (difference 0.061, above 0.05) | 1.320 / 1.311 |
  | Mean base margin, here / iteration 9 | -0.042 / -0.064 | -0.770 / -0.748 |
  | Unembedding-only share, CPU decomposition (target 0.85 and 0.43, within 0.03) | 0.842 | 0.416 |
  | Recomputed final norm against captured state | bit-exact (20 of 20) | bit-exact (20 of 20) |

  **The readout-row claim was supported, as readout-level and not token-specific.** Restoring the base model's rows for the three fork-class tokens of connected components, on the instruct residual, closes 0.548 of the gap (Table 466). That meets the committed rule (at least 0.50, with the median of 50 isotropic matched-norm draws at most 0.15 and the arm above their maximum), although the bootstrap interval's lower end, 0.44, lies under 0.50. By the committed specificity qualifier the effect is readout-level but not token-specific: the arm clears the 95th percentile of 50 real row deltas of other tokens (0.405) but sits inside the distribution of 50 random directions confined to the residual's top 64 principal components (p 0.37). The effect is linear in dose (0.137 per quarter step), flips sign under the negated edit, owes nothing to the final-norm gain, and sits almost entirely in the alternative rows: restoring the ' dfs' and ' bfs' rows closes 0.489, restoring the ' find' row 0.060. The base rows raise the fork logits of ' dfs' by 2.23 nats and ' bfs' by 3.14, and change ' find' by -0.27. Post-training therefore wrote the connected-components default mainly by suppressing the alternatives' readout rows, not by boosting the default's. The ' dfs' and ' bfs' deltas point where the fork residual lives (logit leverage 0.069 and 0.085, close to the residual-subspace draws' medians and seven to nine times the isotropic value), which is why equal-norm random edits aimed entirely at that subspace lever the margin more than the real ones. On minimum spanning tree the base rows overshoot (1.25 of the gap), and the readout-residual interaction is large and opposite in sign to connected components (+1.75 against -1.34 nats), so readout and residual are not additive at either fork.

  **In generation the restored rows are too weak at dose 1, and strong at doses 2 and 3.** With 30 common-random-number slots per arm and only the fork step changed, restoring the rows gave 5 of 30 correct DFS programs on connected components against 1 for the unedited twin (4:0 discordant, exact McNemar [169] p 0.125, Holm 0.25), short of the registered 10 of 30; the committed note had warned that 10 needs a share of about 0.75 (Table 467). A preregistered power extension pooled 90 slots: the rows gave 21 of 90 against 4 for the twin (17:0, p 1.5e-5) and against 4 for the median isotropic draw. On minimum spanning tree the rows flipped 24 of 30 programs to correct Prim (24:0, p 1.2e-7), and one of the three committed isotropic draws, the one with the largest teacher-forced share, flipped 19. Fork-Patched Decoding [142], which splices the base model's fork logits, gave 15 of 30 DFS (iteration 9: 18), more than the restored rows (discordant pairs 12:2 in its favour, exact p 0.013). Pushing further along the same row delta, at twice and three times the dose, made Qwen3-8B write correct DFS in 21 and 30 of 30 connected-components programs and correct Prim in 27 of 30 minimum spanning tree programs, with every program passing the hidden tests (Table 468 and the figure below). At three times the dose the real delta beat the median draws of the strong nulls (24:0 against the residual-subspace median, 27:0 against the median transplanted delta). It tied the best of 50 draws of each null. On minimum spanning tree almost any large edit of these rows flips the fork: the median residual-subspace draw at three times gives 28 of 30.

  **The late-MLP claim did not hold.** Swapping the base model's weights into the late MLPs (layers 26 to 35) jointly widened the connected-components gap slightly (share -0.145, -0.31 to -0.03), while Frobenius-matched swaps of early MLPs, paired by the Hungarian method [171] and scaled by 1.19, closed 0.461 (Table 469). Same-layer random deltas of the same norm moved the margin by comparable amounts in both directions. Single late layers 30 and 28 on connected components, and 32 and 34 on minimum spanning tree, beat their own same-layer random deltas, but a matched early layer can do almost as much (early layer 9: 0.205 next to layer 30's 0.236), and the late singles do not add up in the joint swap. The fork-only version of the swap reproduces iteration 9's weight arm within 0.008 on all 12 checks. At this resolution the weights do not single out these MLPs: any MLP edited by the same amount moves the margin as much.

  **Gemma (descriptive).** At Gemma's grid fork, with tied embeddings untied at the output only, the gap is 1.84 nats and the instruct and base probabilities of the default class (0.675 and 0.088) reproduce iteration 9's. The base rows widen the gap (share -0.253, -0.41 to -0.12; default rows +0.376, alternative rows -0.629), so in Gemma the post-training row changes push against the instruct DFS default, and the default sits in the residual. This agrees with Miyashita's report that the structure of the unembedding depends on the model family [168]. The isotropic null had median 0.165 and maximum 1.92; the transplanted-delta null is partly degenerate, because the newline row's norm-matched pool holds a single token.

  **Checks.** The CPU unit tests (readout equivalence 1.2e-5, the identities, null reproducibility, one-to-one matching, the chain) and the GPU tests (bit-exact recompute, swap and restore, generation determinism) passed. The labeller reproduced iteration 9's 240 labels exactly, and 627 of 630 connected-components programs pass both the frozen hidden tests and 128 LeetCode input-output pairs from the declared dataset, with agreement 1.000. The standard-library audit ran 425 checks with 0 mismatches, and a separate float64 re-derivation from the raw safetensors rows reproduced every row share within 4.4e-7, with its placebos failing as required. Two committed files were later extended; their committed versions were reconstructed byte for byte, and the history-aware chain check passes while the strict one does not.

  ## 10.10 Comparisons across this iteration's experiments

  **Single samples against search.** The iteration put the same 8B model's one-shot answers next to its answers inside an evaluator loop, on one task and one harness. Alone, under name bans or novelty instructions, 1,143 one-shot bin-packing programs from three Qwen3 models contained 186 behaviourally novel programs and none that beat best fit on held-out data. Inside a search, programs better than best fit on the selection sets appeared within the first 1,000 calls at temperature 1.0, and every arm with selection produced held-out improvements in at least one seed set, while the same calls without selection never left best fit. On TSP the picture is the same: without selection the best of 252 calls is worse than nearest neighbour, and with selection every arm closes at least 30% of its gap. Selection, not generation, is what moved the score. The second half of the main claim did not survive. It said that randomness spent at the decision token buys more distinct ideas than temperature. Forcing beat temperature only where the prompt let temperature copy its parent, and choosing the forced position by entropy did no better than choosing it at random (Table 459).

  **Renaming under a ban, on two tasks.** On the grid (iteration 9), with instruments that read expansion order imperfectly, five-name bans were obeyed by name far more than by mechanism in ten of ten configurations, and Qwen3-14B with thinking renamed under every reading but one. On bin packing, with an instrument that reads behaviour exactly, only Qwen3-8B without thinking renames (gap +0.40 at five names, rename rate 0.40 to 0.63); Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B with thinking leave the banned rules, mostly to programs outside the six-rule catalogue. The same reasoning model therefore renamed the banned algorithm on the grid and obeyed on bin packing. One difference between the tasks is the cost of leaving the catalogue. A bin-packing priority function that is none of the six textbook rules is one changed expression away and still packs correctly, while a correct grid path search outside BFS, DFS, iterative deepening, A* and greedy best-first is a different algorithm with its own failure modes. The experiments do not isolate this difference, so it is a reading, not a finding.

  **Asking for a different idea.** The instruction to use an idea different from both parents was obeyed in behaviour inside every search: its offspring renamed a parent less often than temperature 1.0's (0.44 against 0.86, 0.67 against 0.96, 0.06 against 0.18 and 0.22), and it found the most behaviour clusters in two of the three searches. The rename-rate prediction, that the instruction would be obeyed in text but not in behaviour, was wrong in every search. Asked for novelty from scratch, the thinking models returned best fit in 56 of 57 programs under the short novelty instruction, and every program that claimed novelty there was a known rule or a corpus heuristic. With a parent to differ from, the instruction moves behaviour; without one, it returns the default with a claim attached.

  **The fork account inside search.** Forcing the argmax back at an offspring's birth token reverted it to a parent's behaviour more often than at random positions in the replication (0.50 against 0.26) but not in the first search (0.40 against 0.36). The two analyses differ in how births and controls were chosen (the replication paired each offspring's highest-entropy deviating token with one random deviating token; the first search used up to three birth and three control positions from a teacher-forced profile), so the disagreement is between two operationalisations as well as two runs. Whether new heuristics are born at single decision tokens stays open.

  **Geometry and weights.** The factorial program set shows that the program map, which iteration 9 read as tracking behaviour, separates container more than expansion discipline, and token surface more than either. Placements still sort by mechanism where the mechanism is distinct: relaxation survivors sit with relaxation programs and covert BFS and DFS inside their own disciplines. At the fork, the weights experiment found that post-training wrote Qwen3-8B's connected-components default mainly by suppressing the alternatives' unembedding rows. That matches iteration 9's finding that the instruct unembedding reading the base residual carries 0.85 of that gap, and it turns the finding into a lever: three times the base-minus-instruct delta of three rows makes the model write correct DFS in 30 of 30 programs. The lever is not unique (the best of 50 random edits of the same size does as well) and it reaches only a known algorithm.

  **Established.** An executable evaluator turns an 8B model's samples into online bin-packing heuristics that beat best fit on held-out data, and constructive TSP heuristics that close at least 30% of nearest neighbour's gap, within about 1,000 to 2,000 calls per arm and seed; the same calls without selection never improve on the seed program. The selected programs recombine known principles (near-exact fits, avoided residual bands, item-proportional targets, weighted distance features) and do not beat the strongest published heuristics on the same harness. Where randomness is spent matters less than the prompt: forcing a non-top token beats temperature by an order of magnitude when the prompt lets temperature copy its parent, and ties temperature when temperature writes new code; choosing the forced position by entropy is no better than choosing it at random. An instruction to differ from the parents is obeyed in behaviour inside a search. On bin packing, read by exact behaviour, a model without thinking renames banned rules (about half of its lexically clean programs under a five-name ban are still a banned rule), and two thinking models obey name bans and leave the catalogue. The short novelty instruction returns best fit from both thinking models. The program map encodes container more strongly than expansion discipline, and surface more strongly than both, while placements still sort relaxation survivors with relaxation programs and covert BFS and DFS with their own disciplines. Post-training wrote Qwen3-8B's connected-components default at the fork mainly by suppressing the alternatives' unembedding rows, and editing those rows at two to three times the base-minus-instruct delta makes the model write the alternative correct algorithm in 21 to 30 of 30 programs.

  **Ruled out.** Decision-token branching as a better exploration operator than temperature or a random-position forcing (disconfirmed on TSP; failed against the placebo in the replication and against temperature 1.6 in the first search). The prediction that instruction offspring rename their parents (rename rates fell, not rose). A late-MLP store of the default specific to layers 26 to 35 (matched early swaps close more). The prediction that the program map's discipline signal reaches 0.3 once container is held fixed.

  **Dead ends.** Decision-token branching, the operator this iteration built on the fork finding, is a dead end at this resolution: in three implementations it never beat its random-position placebo consistently (2.10, 0.74 and 0.95, with 1.47 on two exploratory seeds) and it tied temperature 1.0 on TSP (0.96). The described ban on bin packing could not be built: the models named only first fit's description correctly, so the cell banned one rarely used rule. Temperature 1.6 with top-p 0.95 is greedy under a prompt that invites copying (one behaviour in 4,000 calls). LLM judges at a gate of 9 of 10 controls passed in 1 of 8 judge-family gates across the three searches; they call nearly every composition known. The novelty filter at probe agreement 0.9 did no work in the first search (permuting the corpus left 70 of 70 programs).

  **Not run.** The forced-token arm drawn from the base model's distribution (memory); the grid and shortest path units of the weights experiment (their single-position margin is degenerate); full-unembedding generation (committed total variation below 0.05); an ablation of the whole-multiple-of-item term; a second reader for any manual novelty read; and, carried from iteration 9, the names-against-mechanisms test on weighted shortest path.

  ## 10.12 What remains open at the end of the run

  The run ends here, and five questions stay open. First, whether the whole-multiple-of-item rule is a new heuristic: it needs an ablation of the term, a second blind reader, and a direct comparison with the item-proportional target residuals of the published EoH run-3 and MCTS-AHD programs. Second, where a search should spend its randomness once the prompt is held fixed: the two bin-packing implementations differed in one instruction sentence and reached opposite conclusions about temperature, so a test that varies the prompt and the operator in one design is needed before any operator claim. Third, why the same reasoning model renames a banned algorithm on the grid and obeys on bin packing; a task with a bounded catalogue but cheap departures from it would separate the cost of leaving the catalogue from the task. Fourth, whether a variable for the algorithm exists anywhere in the model: specificity failed at the late fork sites under steering, distributed alignment search (DAS) and cross-model patching, and at the readout rows it fails against random edits confined to the residual subspace. Fifth, the program map with discipline separated from container and surface would need programs by several authors and more non-banned classes above the floor; the current frame has one author.

  # What we have learned so far

  After ten iterations the run has a firm picture of the collapse, a measured place where the algorithm is decided in generation, a law that predicts what temperature does there, and a weight-level account of how post-training wrote the default at that place. It has internal handles in two families that move the algorithm without being the model's own variable, a measured and model-dependent gap between obeying a ban by name and obeying it by mechanism, and an answer to the request's question about truly novel solutions: an executable evaluator makes the model write heuristics better than the textbook rule, but no route in the run produced a confirmed new algorithm or heuristic. One reader classed eight bin-packing programs from one search as a new idea, and the independent replication found none.

  Qwen3-8B [5] writes BFS and Dijkstra almost without exception on the two path search tasks and one algorithm on each of 13 further coding tasks (modal share 1.00 on 12, 0.98 on one). The collapse is not universal. Three of 15 new tasks are already mixed in the instruct twin (trapped rain water, minimum spanning tree weight and valid anagram, with minority shares of 0.13 to 0.36), and on two of them the instruct model is more diverse than its base model. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct [22] attempts more algorithms, but its correct grid programs are BFS 20 of 20; gemma-3-4b-it [76] writes DFS in about 70% and BFS in about 30% of programs for one grid prompt; Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct [124] shares most of Qwen3-8B's defaults. On the grid task eight more open configurations (Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B with thinking on and off, Qwen3-8B with thinking on, gemma-3-27b-it, Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct in bfloat16) write BFS or DFS at baseline apart from a few programs labelled other or invalid, and so does gpt-oss-120b [152] (BFS 45, DFS 5 of 50). The collapse extends to online bin packing for the reasoning models: asked once for a priority function, Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B with thinking write best fit in 50 of 50 and 48 of 49 valid programs, while Qwen3-8B without thinking spreads (25 of its 36 valid programs are outside the six-rule catalogue and 9 are best fit). So the answer to the request's question whether the model always designs BFS is: on the grid, BFS or DFS nearly always, with the split fixed by the model; on weighted shortest path, Dijkstra; on bin packing, best fit for the thinking models.

  The algorithm is decided at one or two generated tokens after a shared opening, the fork, where one can be found. On the mixed units programs share an opening of 18 to 61 tokens and the next token settles the algorithm: ' Kr' or ' Prim' on minimum spanning tree weight, ' n' or ' left' on trapped rain water, ' visited' against a blank line or ' queue' in Gemma. The entropy of the algorithm given the fork token's class is at most 0.19 bits as iteration 7 measured it, at most 0.004 bits on the five Qwen3-8B and Gemma units of iteration 8's blind locator, and 0.63 bits on Llama's grid task, where the fork is reached through many openings. Prefix resampling finds these forks blind on mixed units in Qwen3-8B and Gemma, but not on a collapsed task, where resampling at T 1 never leaves the default. The fork's entropy lies above the 90th percentile of the twin's per-token entropy in all 209 twin samples that reach it, though it can be small in absolute terms (median 0.13 nats on connected components), and it is the single highest-entropy position among the first 64 tokens on most slots of three units but on 2 of 50 and 0 of 37 slots of the other two. On kth smallest a ban decides before the first generated token, and on shortest path no single token decides within 60 tokens. Thought anchors and forks, the logit and tuned lenses and a Jacobian lens were all run on this question; the lenses found no veto layer at the commitment token, because the fork has already happened at the first token. Inside an evaluator search, whether new heuristics are born at single decision tokens is not settled: forcing the argmax back at an offspring's birth token reverted it to a parent's behaviour at 0.50 against 0.26 at random positions in one search and 0.40 against 0.36 in the other.

  Temperature acts on the algorithm through those one or two tokens and reweights ideas the fork already weighs. A law composed over the forks, committed before sampling from teacher-forced logits, predicted the minority share across T 0.3 to 1.3 within a mean total variation distance of 0.029 to 0.054 on three Qwen3-8B units and of 0.033 and 0.014 on two held-out Gemma units; it beats the flat law on 4 of 6 units only (sign test p 0.34), and on Llama's grid task every predictor fails (0.142). Applying temperature only at the fork moves the mix as predicted and raises correct-only Hill-1 on valid anagram from 1.78 to 2.78 at a 2-point pass cost, but on collapsed connected components it reaches DFS in at most 18% of programs. Forcing each of the fork's top 64 tokens reaches one more known idea on three units, each about once in 2 million to 50 million samples at T 1. Lowering T from 1.0 to 0.3 moves the output toward the default, and top-k 10 gives the same programs as top-p 1 because every fork token lies in the top 10. On the collapsed tasks fork margins of 4.85 to 17.04 nats put the alternative out of reach, which is why iterations 1 to 4 changed the algorithm in 0 of 20 seeds under a shared seed while phrasings multiplied. The answer to question 1a to 1c of the request is that a model has few ideas at tight temperature and the same few at loose temperature, in proportions its fork logits fix, with more phrasings of each as T rises; it is case (a), not case (b), and loosening temperature does not turn one idea into several on a collapsed task. Inside a search temperature is not a reliable exploration knob either. Under one prompt, temperature 1.6 with top-p 0.95 found 373 behaviours in 4,000 calls; under a prompt that invites copying the parent, it became greedy and found one; on TSP it halved validity. Temperature is not the creativity knob the request asks about.

  Context seeding does not change the algorithm. Under a random entropy seed prepended to the prompt the grid task stays BFS 100 and shortest path Dijkstra 100, and in a later cell both random seeds give Dijkstra in 30 of 30 programs; the word seed moves the read-position state 1.555 times the paraphrase noise without changing the program. Prompt instructions change claims more than algorithms. Of 574 outputs with a claim record under the long novelty instructions, 484 claimed a new algorithm and 220 of the 295 with code were catalogue algorithms. On bin packing the short novelty instruction (a one-line request to make a new algorithm) returns best fit in 28 of 29 and 28 of 28 programs from the two thinking models, and every program that claims novelty there is a known rule or a corpus heuristic. Inside an evaluator search the picture changes: an instruction to use an idea different from both parents is obeyed in behaviour, lowers the share of offspring that rename a parent (0.44 against 0.86, 0.67 against 0.96, 0.06 against 0.18 to 0.22) and found the most behaviours in two of three searches. An instruction to differ works when there is something to differ from.

  Post-training made the fork margins, and the instruct default is a sharpened choice of the base model, not its mean answer. On the three collapsed Qwen3-8B tasks the instruct fork margin exceeds the base model's by 2.1 to 13.4 nats while phrasing entropy moves by under 0.5 nats, and the default is the base model's second or third choice at the fork. In Gemma the grid fork gains 1.78 nats and post-training reversed and concentrated the base model's preference (base P(BFS) 0.25, 0.663 of base mass unmapped), while the first-and-last-position forks sharpen the base model's own first choice. That post-training shifts concentrate at forks of high base entropy is shown by Cantarero et al. [142] and Sparse but Critical [143], and the run confirms the confound they control: at Gemma's forks the base-instruct divergence is only 0.75 to 1.18 times that of positions matched for base entropy. What the run adds is the algorithm-level outcome on code at counterfactually located forks, and where the sharpening is written in Qwen3-8B. It is not written upstream at the task-specification nodes. In activations it sits at the fork, in late MLPs and in the unembedding, which alone carries 0.43 of the minimum spanning tree gap and 0.85 of the connected components gap. In weights, restoring the base rows of the three fork-class tokens of connected components closes 0.548 of the gap, almost all through the alternatives' rows (0.489 against 0.060): post-training suppressed the readout of ' dfs' and ' bfs' more than it boosted ' find'. The effect is readout-level but not token-specific, because random edits of the same size confined to the residual's top 64 directions do as much (p 0.37). Swapping the late MLPs (layers 26 to 35) back to base does not close the gap, while matched early swaps close 0.461, so no specific late-MLP store of the default was found. At the same three rows, the edit is also a cheap lever over which known algorithm gets written: at dose 1 it gives correct DFS in 21 of 90 slots against 4 of 90, and at two and three times the delta in 21 and 30 of 30, with every program passing; on minimum spanning tree 24 to 27 of 30 programs become correct Prim. Splicing the base model's fork logits (Fork-Patched Decoding [142]) gives 15 of 30. No edit produced a correct program outside the known classes. To the request's hypothesis that the model gives the mean answer and only context pushes it into another subspace, the run's answer is that the default is a sharpened, not an averaged, base choice, and that context moves the algorithm only through the fork.

  A random displacement of the task specification states at early to middle blocks changes the algorithm in Qwen3-8B, and its size has to be counted in the right unit. At the absolute unit of iteration 4, bfloat16 escapes on 26 of 40 directions on connected components and 6 of 40 on shortest path, close to the 8-bit engine's 29 and 8. These pushes do not act through any fitted subspace: their projection on the task band's DAS subspace associates with their escapes at Spearman 0.09, and clamping the subspace back to the twin removes none of 218 escapes. Internal handles exist in both families, and under one protocol none is a certified variable. A rank-4 DAS edit at the fork is a sufficient handle in Gemma (22 of 30 correct BFS against 6 unedited) and no handle at Qwen3-8B's fork, where the edit toward BFS writes BFS in 29 of 30 programs and 24 fail; neither passes the specificity controls, and both show the off-manifold overshoot Makelov et al. warn of [122]. Path-patching circuits for the fork margin show a late stack of fork-position MLPs and heads carrying the fork logit in both families, with different motifs; steering the top five Qwen3-8B nodes rewrites the algorithm with every program passing, but matched random components do nearly as much at the committed dose, and most matched random patching sets repeat a component. The layer-0 condition-span MLP gives about 7.9 nats on the five forced held-out prompts and about 0 on the five padded twins. Specificity fails at the same late fork-position sites under steering, DAS, cross-model patching and, at the readout, row edits. Sparse autoencoder features read Gemma's fork (R-squared 0.66 against 0.18 for text) but steer it less than a difference-in-means direction, and a natural language autoencoder on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct names the algorithm only where the prompt names it. Natural BFS against DFS internals were read within a ban in Qwen3-8B and within one prompt in Gemma, with circuits for the fork in both.

  A single prompt ban, where the model obeys it, removes the default and the output collapses on one replacement: Bellman-Ford/SPFA on shortest path, DFS on the grid, and quickselect, a size-k heap, brute force, index marking and BFS on the bench tasks where Qwen3-8B obeys; on bin packing, banning best fit sent Qwen3-32B to first fit in 14 of 30 programs and outside the catalogue in 16. Shown a correct program of another algorithm and told not to use it, the model goes home to its default. How often a ban is obeyed depends on its wording more than on anything else measured. A ban of the whole repertoire is answered in two ways, depending on the model and the task. On the grid, read by the runtime label (heap priorities, frontier evidence, restarts) and by the expansion-order tracer over 546 programs in ten configurations, lexical compliance exceeds mechanistic compliance by 0.70 or 0.61 (0.66 if unit-weight Dijkstra, IDA* and jump point search count as compliant), in every configuration; the tracer failed its gold gate on iterative deepening, so these numbers are descriptive. Under cumulative bans of one to five names, Qwen3-14B with thinking renames under every reading except the fine tracer on held-out templates, while Qwen3-32B with thinking moves mostly to other known disciplines (by hand reads 0.59 mechanistically compliant at five names, against 0.22 by the runtime label). On bin packing, read by exact behaviour, Qwen3-8B without thinking renames (lexical 0.91 against mechanistic 0.51 at five names; about half its lexically clean programs are still a banned rule, mostly best fit under invented names such as *tightest fit*), while Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B with thinking obey and leave the catalogue (gaps +0.04 and -0.13). Thinking traces name the banned rule in every cell. Renaming is therefore not a fixed property of a model: the same reasoning model renames the banned algorithm on the grid and obeys on bin packing. A ban described without names moved grid compliance by an instrument-dependent amount (+0.58 by the runtime label, -0.07 by the tracer, about +0.21 under the per-cell reading), and on bin packing the test could not be built, because the models named only one description correctly.

  The answer to the request's top-five question, edge or opposite, depends on the map and on the survivor. By hand reads of 76 survivors of the grid ban, 0.30 are unit-weight Dijkstra, which is BFS order on a unit grid, and the rest are known algorithms with other disciplines (grid Bellman-Ford rounds, heaps keyed by goal-independent coordinates, random frontiers). On every manifold built from language (named prompts, name-only sentences and name-free descriptions the model names correctly) unit-weight Dijkstra lies opposite the banned five (g 1.63, 1.20 and 1.08 times the median of the non-banned algorithms); the language manifolds track lexical distance between the names and textbook data-structure attributes, not measured expansion order. On the manifold built from name-scrubbed programs it lies at the edge (0.67), its iteration-8 survivors place at the edge, and the Bellman-Ford/SPFA survivors place opposite on both gate-passing Qwen3-32B frames. The factorial program set of iteration 10 shows what that program map encodes: container more than expansion discipline (partial correlations 0.300 and 0.414 against 0.226 and 0.285) and token surface more than both. On a frame built from it, covert BFS and DFS programs land inside the banned disciplines (0.993 and 0.978), Bellman-Ford survivors sit with the relaxation programs (opposite on Qwen3-32B, robustly), and unit-weight Dijkstra sits with the path-cost and FIFO heap programs, at the edge on the full frame and on one side or the other of the heap frame depending on the model and readout. The geometry is correlational: a push inside the named manifold toward the survivors produced BFS in all 300 programs. Geometry plots in actual activation coordinates exist for every map the run built: at a label-dependent position (iteration 2), at the plan site (iteration 4), for the top-five prohibition and the fork (iteration 6), in fitted DAS coordinates (iterations 7 and 8), at the fork for every dosed arm and for the forced prompts of ten algorithms with the ban prompts of the model that obeys (iteration 8), on four manifolds of the ten algorithms built with and without names in two models (iteration 9), and on the discipline-by-container frame (iteration 10). They use geodesic distances, Isomap [25], MDS and centroids sized or coloured by implemented count under the baseline and under the ban. No circle manifold was found: persistent loops exceed their null only on shortest path at block 18 and two sum at blocks 18 and 23, while a planted circle at matched size and noise was detected every time.

  Where a ban acts depends on the task. On the path tasks it is carried mostly by the prompt states; on the bench, pooled over five gated tasks, the direct route carries 0.744 of the behavioural effect and the prompt states 0.611, with overlapping intervals. The ban is enforced at the opening of the program body, the same place where forks surface. What decides the replacement has measured leads and no confirmed rule: the base model's second choice names the push landing in 17 of 21 recorded events and 5 of 8 held-out events (p 0.053).

  On novelty, the run's single-sample record is empty and its search record is mixed. No instruction, knob, push, transplant, feature clamp, verbal edit, fitted edit, steered circuit, fork dose, forced branch, prohibition, cross-model patch or row edit produced a correct novel algorithm. Iterations 1 to 3 and 5 produced 116 and 130 correct programs outside the catalogue, none new. Iteration 4 found none among 14,206 correct programs, iteration 8 none among 5,543, 1,857, 395, 913, 4,703 and 661 in six experiments, and iteration 9 none among 568 under bans and 237 after fork interventions. In iteration 10 none of 1,143 one-shot bin-packing programs was both novel and better than best fit. The evolutionary search of iteration 7 on kth smallest reached known techniques outside the catalogue at 7.8 times the instruction's per-call rate, none novel. In iteration 10, the route the field's discovery systems use [81, 82], an island search whose evaluator keeps improvements across generations, was run with Qwen3-8B as the mutator on online bin packing (two independent implementations, six seeds, 64,000 calls) and on constructive TSP (10,812 calls). With selection, the model wrote priority functions that beat best fit on held-out instances by the committed 0.8 rule (the first search's core-arm bests reach 1.40% to 2.42% excess on FunSearch's Weibull test set against best fit's 3.98%) and TSP rules that close 30% to 42% of nearest neighbour's gap; without selection it never improved on its seed program. The selected programs recombine known principles, and none beats the strongest published heuristics on the same harness: FunSearch's Weibull heuristic (0.68%), the ab rules of Herrmann and Pallez [162] (3.01% on binpack3 against 3.38% at best) and the ReEvo/EoH TSP seed rule (13.67% against 13.88% at best). One reader of the first search classed eight programs, all built on a preference for leftovers that are whole multiples of the item size, as a new idea. Only one of three judge families passed its gate, so the committed two-judge rule could not apply. The novelty filter did no work there, and no ablation tested the term. The replication's reader, applying the same rule to 40 programs, found every item-proportional residual rule already published. So the answer to the request's question whether LLMs can give truly creative and novel solutions is, at this scale: an evaluator, not a knob, makes the 8B model better than the textbook rule, and whether it makes the model new is unresolved, resting on one reader's eight candidates that a second implementation did not reproduce. Spending the sampling randomness at the decision token, the operator the fork finding suggested, did not buy more ideas than a random-position forcing, and tied temperature on TSP.

  What remains open follows from this. First, whether the whole-multiple-of-item rule is new: an ablation, a second blind reader and a direct comparison with the published target-residual programs. Second, where a search should spend its randomness once the prompt is held fixed, since one instruction sentence decided whether temperature explored or copied. Third, why renaming depends on the task for the same reasoning model. Fourth, whether a variable for the algorithm exists anywhere: specificity fails at the late fork-position sites under every method tried, and at the readout rows against random edits in the residual subspace. Fifth, a program map that separates discipline from container and surface, with programs by several authors. Every part of the request was run. The behavioural analysis in the manner of the inspiration repository, the BFS question, temperature with top-k 10 under the same seed, context seeding and prompt instructions were answered behaviourally. The mean-answer question, natural BFS against DFS internals, thought anchors and forks, natural language autoencoders, sparse autoencoders, the logit and tuned lenses and circuits were answered from the internals. The manifold with centroids coloured by implemented count, with geodesic distances and MDS in actual activation space, and the top-five prohibition with its edge-or-opposite reading were answered geometrically. The circuits are answered only in part (specificity unresolved), and the edge-or-opposite reading is descriptive. The question of truly novel solutions met the one route the run had not tried, an evaluator-guided search, and the outcome is better-than-textbook heuristics without a confirmed new one.

summary: >-
  Across ten iterations a code model's 'idea' proved to be a small known repertoire decided at one or two fork tokens: temperature,
  seeds, top-k and instructions change wording, not the algorithm (0 of 20 shared-seed draws changed it), and no single-sample
  route produced a correct novel algorithm. With an executable evaluator, Qwen3-8B wrote online bin-packing heuristics that
  beat best fit on held-out data (core-arm bests 1.40% to 2.42% excess against best fit's 3.98% on FunSearch's Weibull test
  set) and TSP rules closing 30% to 42% of nearest neighbour's gap, while search without selection never improved on its seed;
  none beat the best published heuristics, the eight programs one reader judged novel were not reproduced by the independent
  replication (0 of 40), and decision-token branching did not beat a random-position placebo (ratios 2.10, 0.74 and 0.95).
  Bans of the whole repertoire are renamed by Qwen3-8B on bin packing (lexical 0.91 against mechanistic 0.51) but obeyed by
  the thinking models there, and at Qwen3-8B's connected-components fork post-training wrote the default mainly by suppressing
  the alternatives' unembedding rows (restoring three rows closes 0.548 of the gap; three times the delta gives 30 of 30 correct
  DFS).
</report_text>

<paper_headline>
The publishable paper's title, abstract, one-line summary and headline measurement, fixed by the
paper draft before this task. The paper is typeset AFTER this task and leads with this headline;
the executive summary leads with the same one. It steers the summary's lead only: the report
stays the chronological record and grades every result, this one included, as the round record
grades it.

title: >-
  A Random Activation Push Changes a Code Model's Algorithm Where Temperature Does Not
abstract: >-
  Sampling temperature is often treated as the creativity control of a language model. We test, on the same random streams,
  whether temperature or a random push of the residual-stream states at a prompt's task-specification tokens changes which
  algorithm Qwen3-8B implements, labelling every program by its runtime behaviour on hidden tests. The push changed the algorithm
  in more seeds than temperature did, by a paired difference of 0.545 per seed (95% CI 0.41 to 0.67), pooled over shortest
  path and k-th smallest (40 seeds). This contrast was pre-registered and held (one-sided sign-flip p = 1.0e-5) in an experiment
  whose pre-registered verdict is partial, because the push moved 4.55 rather than the predicted 5 of 20 seeds on k-th smallest;
  it ran only in an 8-bit (FP8 W8A8) engine and is untested in bfloat16. Temperature from 0.3 to 1.3 itself changed the algorithm
  in 0 of 20 seeds on each of three tasks while phrasings multiplied, a null that the study also observed with reasoning enabled
  and in bfloat16. Prefix resampling shows why: the algorithm is settled at one or two forking tokens, where the default leads
  by 4.85 to 17.04 nats on these tasks. Where that token is contested, a law built from its logits and committed before sampling
  predicted the temperature response on five of six units, including two held-out Gemma-3-4B units, though a no-change baseline
  was nearly as accurate. No control we tested produced a correct novel algorithm.
summary: >-
  On the same random streams, a random push of Qwen3-8B's task-specification states changed the algorithm it writes in more
  seeds than temperature did, by 0.545 per seed (95% CI 0.41 to 0.67), pooled over shortest path and k-th smallest (40 seeds):
  a pre-registered contrast that held, in an experiment graded partial, run only in an 8-bit engine and untested in bfloat16.
  Temperature from 0.3 to 1.3 changed the algorithm in 0 of 20 seeds per task while phrasings multiplied, because one or two
  forking tokens settle the algorithm by margins temperature cannot overcome; no tested control produced a correct novel algorithm.
headline:
  finding: >-
    A random task-state push changes the algorithm where temperature does not, on the same random streams
  artifact: art_Yu6GN6pLxW8f
  dataset: same seed experiment
  comparator: >-
    temperature T 0.3/0.7/1.0/1.3 on the same 40 seeds (shortest path and kth smallest): per-seed change rate 0 (0 of 40);
    effect is the push's per-seed change (union over three directions, alpha 1, T 1.0) minus temperature's
  effect: 0.545
  ci_low: 0.41375
  ci_high: 0.67
  outcome: passed
  scope: >-
    Qwen3-8B, thinking off; pooled over the shortest path task and kth smallest (40 seeds); pre-registered as the experiment's
    single entry in the iteration's secondary family, held (one-sided sign-flip p 1.0e-5); the experiment's preregistered
    verdict is PARTIAL because the plan noise prediction (at least 5 of 20 seeds) fails on kth smallest at 4.55; 8-bit W8A8
    engine only, untested in bf16 (Table 229: 8-bit only, untested in bf16; its per-sample plan noise reproduces in bf16 at
    the absolute unit)
</paper_headline>

- iteration: 1
  name: gen_art_experiment_1
  type: experiment
  title: Where an algorithm ban sends an AI coder
  summary: |-
    Behavioural screen on Qwen/Qwen3-8B (thinking off, vLLM 0.11, T=1.0) of two predictors of where probability mass goes when a prompt bans an algorithm. The proposed predictor is substitution by association: the model's own Borda-aggregated 'standard alternative to X' ranking. The baseline is the typicality ladder: baseline frequency renormalised over the surviving modes. Two path-search tasks are used: T1 unweighted grid path (6 modes) and T2 weighted shortest path (5 modes). The artifact provides:
    (1) A reusable task suite: specs, 48 + 45 seeded hidden tests with per-case time limits, 22 reference implementations, and a sandbox harness.
    (2) A validated labeller: runtime tracer + AST rules + a strategy-blind gpt-4.1-mini judge on disagreements, with a gold set adjudicated by gpt-4.1-mini, gemini-2.5-flash and deepseek tie-break. Both labellers get 22/22 references right; on evaluation gold, kappa runtime-vs-AST is 0.753, runtime vs adjudicated 0.843, combined label 0.966. gate_passed=false is flagged.
    (3) data/samples.jsonl: 3,260 labelled programs in the shared screen schema (task, condition, paraphrase, model, decoding, label, passed, code, ...), poolable with other experiments.
    (4) Frozen, sha256 hash-chained predictions (commitments.log); every event was committed before its generation.
    (5) method_out.json (exp_gen_sol_out) with one example per event plus all analyses in metadata.
    Key results, descriptive only (2 tasks, 2 informative events):
    - Baselines are fully collapsed (T1 100% BFS, T2 100% Dijkstra, also at T=1.3), so the frequency predictor is uniform and its nomination is always tied.
    - Modal bans were obeyed (compliance 0.90 / 0.91) and landed entirely on one substitute: DFS for T1 (38/38 compliant correct samples), Bellman-Ford/SPFA for T2 (86/86).
    - Association hit T2 but missed T1, where the Borda map nominated Dijkstra with clarity 0.20 and ranked DFS last. Log scores were T1 -2.82 vs -1.63 and T2 -0.75 vs -1.41; mean paired difference -0.27 nats/sample; association wins 1 of 2.
    - The model's own free-text 'standard alternative' answers and the listall typicality cue nominated the realised substitute in both events (2/2). A post-hoc gpt-4.1-mini map shows the same ranking-vs-free-text split.
    - Cumulative double bans failed (compliance 0.06 / 0.00): the model re-implemented the banned mechanism under other names ('backtracking' DFS, 'BFS with pruning' = SPFA). 41/94 and 58/100 recurrent programs never name the banned algorithm, so the succession stopped at step 2.
    - Mention twins act as strong recommendations (+56 to +100 pp for 5 modes; 0 for 3), not placebos.
    All 36 headline numbers were independently re-derived from raw files (audit/rederive.py), and placebo runs of the contest and T9 comparisons fail as expected. reproducibility.md gives an exact CPU-only Path A (byte-identical outputs verified, no API or GPU calls) and a full-regeneration Path B. OpenRouter spend was USD 0.27. Next-round implications: the ranking instrument diverges from free-text association; frequency-based typicality is uninformative under full collapse, while listall typicality is informative; multi-name bans need mechanism-level compliance checks.
  workspace: >-
    /ai-inventor/aii_data/runs/run_4VFKidE1bxPG/3_invention_loop/iter_1/gen_art/gen_art_experiment_1
  output_files:
  - method.py
  - full_method_out.json
  - mini_method_out.json
  - preview_method_out.json
  - reproducibility.md
- iteration: 1
  name: gen_art_experiment_2
  type: experiment
  title: How prompt bans move an LLM's path-search choices
  summary: >-
    Behavioural + activation-space screen of Qwen3-8B (bf16, thinking off, T=1.0, HF transformers generate on one NVIDIA L4;
    vLLM could not start) for two path-search coding tasks: T1 grid path (catalogue bfs, dfs, bidir_bfs, iddfs, astar, dijkstra_unit)
    and T2 weighted shortest path (dijkstra, bellman_ford_spfa, bidir_dijkstra, floyd_warshall, dial). Provides: hidden test
    suites (41/42 cases) and catalogue references (tasks/); a validated labeller (runtime tracer + AST rules + blind OpenRouter
    judge; gate kappa 0.90/0.94, runtime-vs-adjudicated 0.96/0.92); 1550 prompts with token ids (prompts/prompts.jsonl); every
    labelled program (data/samples_phase{A,C,D}.jsonl; method_out.json, exp_gen_sol_out, 2310 programs + 7 contest events).
    KEY RESULTS (descriptive, few events): baselines collapse completely (T1 200/200 BFS, T2 200/200 Dijkstra; mention:X keeps
    50/50); prompt bans mostly fail (ban:bfs compliance 0.18: 62 BFS/29 DFS/9 unit-Dijkstra; ban:dijkstra 0.22: 72 Dijkstra/27
    Bellman-Ford); on T1 the displaced mass lands only on BFS's geodesic neighbours on the read-position manifold (DFS 41,
    unit-Dijkstra 58; never A*/IDDFS/bidir at 71-95), T2 goes to the 2nd-nearest (Bellman-Ford). Hash-committed forecasts
    (predictions/, sha256 186f71...): geodesic proximity has the best mean log score (-1.43 primary) vs uniform -1.56; the
    model's own 'standard alternative' rankings are worst (-2.59). R-position probes: named->masked transfer 0.67 (T1 L27)
    / 0.54 (T2 L24) vs shuffled null ~0.2-0.3; T1 baseline decoder fails (R gate flagged). Manifold TwoNN ID 4.2/5.2 vs ~11.9/11.6
    shuffled nulls. C3: ban-vs-mention shifts 61-99% residual, all inconclusive. C2: affine directional ablation of the modal
    mode (pre-declared R-plus-prompt variant, alpha 0.5/1/2, random controls with identical edit norms, common random numbers)
    moved 0/50 on both tasks (outputs 78-90% byte-identical to alpha=0, like random controls); exploratory full variant only
    degenerates at alpha 4. Reusable for next rounds: cache/hR_layer{8..28}.npy + hR_index.jsonl (read-position states; layers
    8-20 and suffix means kept on the run volume only), directions/anchors/basis npz, results/*.json, figures/*. Independent
    audit (analysis/audit_rederive.py): 99 numbers re-derived, 0 mismatches, placebos fail.

- iteration: 1
  name: gen_art_experiment_4
  type: experiment
  title: Steering an LLM to vary its search algorithms
  summary: >-
    De-commitment steering screen on Qwen3-8B (thinking off) for two path-search tasks with hidden tests: T1 grid path (catalogue
    bfs/dfs/bidirectional_bfs/iddfs/astar/dijkstra_unit) and T2 weighted shortest path (dijkstra/bellman_ford_spfa/bidirectional_dijkstra/floyd_warshall/dial).
    Method: list-minus-implement difference-of-means direction d_dc (50+50 held-out frame paraphrases) at the last prompt
    token, layer L*=18 (held-out AUC 1.0 on all layers, d' tie-break), added as c*||h||*d_hat at R and every generated token;
    c swept over {0.25,0.5,1,1.5} + pre-registered bisection, c* chosen on pass rate only (T1 0.1, T2 0.25). Controls: HF
    c=0 hook, vLLM baseline N=200 (engine check passed), two random directions, variable-name placebo, breadth direction,
    cross-task transfer, enumeration prompt, modal ban and mention prompts, succession ban. Labels from sandboxed hidden tests
    + runtime tracer + AST rules, judge for disagreements; R0 and labeller gate pass on both tasks (2 revision rounds). RESULTS
    (verdict PARTIAL): T1 is 100% BFS in every arm except bans; steering never diversifies it (pass 1.00 -> 0.57 at c=0.25,
    still all BFS). T2: at c*=0.25 pass 0.78 vs 0.95, correct programs shift Dijkstra->Bellman-Ford (54 BF/23 D vs 7 BF/88
    D), rarefied Hill-1 +0.65 [90% cluster CI 0.31, 0.97]; but random direction rand1 does almost the same (+0.59; dc-rand1
    +0.07 [-0.26, 0.39]) so the gain is not direction-specific (beats rand2 and placebo). Enumeration prompt gives no diversity
    (T2 -0.08); the modal ban buys +0.79 at 1.5 pass points but most banned samples still use the banned algorithm. Commitment
    test: ban-minus-mention shifts R toward the list frame by 0.04/0.05 of the frame distance (exact permutation p 0.021/0.007;
    enumeration positive control 0.54/0.58). Hash-committed forecasts: on T2 the de-committed forecast scored best (log score
    -0.058 vs -0.219 frequency) on one informative event; T1 forecasts degenerate. Headline numbers re-derived independently
    (results/audit_rederivation.json); vLLM same-seed determinism failed on T1. REUSABLE: directions/ (d_dc per task and layer
    8-28, rand/placebo/breadth), cache/hR_*.npy (R-states, on the run volume), tasks/ (specs, hidden tests, 12 references),
    labeller/ (tracer, AST rules, judge prompt), gold/gold_set.jsonl, data/samples.jsonl (2,940 labelled samples), forecast/

- iteration: 1
  name: gen_art_experiment_5
  type: experiment
  title: Did post-training cause Qwen3's algorithm collapse?
  summary: >-
    Screen of alternate 4 ('instruction tuning installed the algorithm-choice collapse') on Qwen3-8B-Base vs Qwen3-8B (thinking
    off), two path-search tasks: T1 unweighted grid path, T2 weighted directed shortest path. 4140 programs, each run on 47/46
    hidden tests and labelled by a runtime-signature + AST labeller with a blind LLM judge (gemini-2.5-flash-lite) for disagreements
    (reference gate: AST 100%, runtime never wrong; kappa runtime-AST 0.77; inter-judge kappa 0.93). 2x2 weights x format
    (T=1, top-p 1): instruct chat is collapsed (T1 BFS 200/200, Hill_cc 1.00; T2 Dijkstra 193/200, Hill_cc 1.16). The base
    model under the same chat tokens is more diverse (T1 BFS 49/57 correct, Hill_cc 1.58; T2 Dijkstra 63/90, Hill_cc 2.09);
    template-free base code is mostly broken (pass 5%/8%; T2 correct programs Bellman-Ford-modal 16/25). D_weights = Hill_cc(instruct_chat)
    - Hill_cc(base_chat) = -0.58 [-1.01,-0.15] (T1), -0.93 [-1.38,-0.46] (T2). Pre-registered verdicts: T2 INSTALLED_BY_POST_TRAINING;
    T1 MIXED (modal-share gap 14.0 pp, just under the 15 pp bar); no ALREADY_IN_BASE, so the alternate passes the screen (also
    under Hill_all). At the planned N (before the N=300 base extension) both read MIXED. Post-training concentrated the base
    model's existing mode rather than inventing one; the chat format also concentrates the instruct model on T2 (template-free
    Hill_cc 1.93 -> chat 1.16) and switches the base model's T2 mode from Bellman-Ford to Dijkstra. Mechanistic test: the
    paired instruct-minus-base residual difference at the read position (split-half cos 0.998, task-general cos 0.85-0.92,
    logit lens = answer-format tokens) subtracted over layers 8-28 is DESTRUCTIVE at c=0.5/1.0/1.5 (0/100 parseable), while
    norm-matched random directions keep format and algorithm; downstream layers amplify the subtraction (overshoot, gap_closed
    ~0 at L18/L28). Single-layer delta_18 fallback: c=0.25 keeps 94-98% pass with zero algorithm change (NO_EFFECT). R-only
    subtraction flips Qwen3 into thinking-style prose yet stated plans and correct programs keep BFS/Dijkstra. No knob restores
    diversity; the ban prompt does better (T2 Hill_cc 1.16 -> 1.99 at 0 pp pass loss). Hash-committed forecast from the base
    model hit top-1 on both ban events (DFS; Bellman-Ford), log score -0.47/-0.22 vs uniform -1.63/-1.41, but base-chat/typicality
    references did as well. All headline numbers were re-derived by an independent script (0 mismatches; placebo permutation
    tests reject at ~5%). Reusable outputs: runs/samples.jsonl (shared row schema, every sample), runs/labelled_*.jsonl, method_out.json
    (metadata = all analyses: collapse_screen, steering, rows.BUY / rows.PREDICT, labeller_qa, sharpening_direction), data/
    (prompts, hidden tests, references), src/ labeller + harness, activations/ (residual states, deltas, band steering vectors;
    kept on the run volume), predictions/ (committed forecast).
